blocks.blomberg-s01-003: 2): through our own exercises and 3): through instruction
blocks.blomberg-s01-004: From learning arises the spirit of imitation. This learning takes place in childhood. There is indeed some skill that one brings about through imitation; but he who imitates shows the lowest degree of capacity.
blocks.blomberg-s01-005: The first origin of our cognitions is empirical. Many things arise through imitation and many cognitions through imitation.
blocks.blomberg-s01-006: We see what others have shown us and do likewise.
blocks.blomberg-s01-007: The second kind is the exercise of our acquired skill. Through frequent exercise of our insights and talents we arrive at a greater cognition and at new insights, and these can be increased still further through our own experience.
blocks.blomberg-s01-008: The last is to arrive at a cognition through general rules; these are derived from reason.
blocks.blomberg-s01-009: The first method of arriving at cognitions must fall away immediately, as soon as the capacities have obtained the ability to cultivate themselves (excoliren). One must seek to think for oneself and to judge for oneself.
blocks.blomberg-s01-010: This kind of exercise of the capacities attains the same degree even if one thinks contrary to what others have thought.
blocks.blomberg-s01-011: The natural understanding has its own laws, according to which alone it can proceed. These are called natural laws.
blocks.blomberg-s01-012: Besides the natural laws there are also precepts, which are for the artificial understanding. The first is to proceed wholly without laws, and to make use neither of the natural [ ... ] laws nor of the precepts. When one wants to cultivate (excoliren) one's own reason on this basis, one first makes use of the natural laws of reason. This happens when one thinks often, or through exercises and frequent attempts, when one considers an object according to particular as well as general laws.
blocks.blomberg-s01-013: The second use of the understanding takes place according to artificial rules, or according to precepts, and from this arises the artificial understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s01-014: One first learns to walk by being led at first; so too one learns to think by first of all imitating, and then one begins to use one's feet by oneself and alone. Thus we too begin to judge for ourselves, and to use our understanding for judging by ourselves through frequent and self-repeated attempts.
blocks.blomberg-s01-015: The merely natural laws are cultivated (excoliret) through experience, but for artificial use I must have other rules. First one must imitate, then exercise oneself, and last one receives precepts.
blocks.blomberg-s01-016: Through imitation we can acquire crafts, but through precepts a science. Versification can be compared, as it were, with the crafts.
blocks.blomberg-s01-017: We learn to judge beautifully through rules, but to compose poetry beautifully through frequent exercises.
blocks.blomberg-s01-018: All cognition takes place according to rules: these are either merely natural or artificial.
blocks.blomberg-s01-019: The natural rules concern the common and sound understanding and sound reason.
blocks.blomberg-s01-020: The artificial rules are the rules of learnedness. The use of the former we acquire not through imitation but through the frequent use of our reason, whereby the common understanding is cultivated (excoliret).
blocks.blomberg-s01-021: The common use of the understanding is that which is concerned with objects of experience.
blocks.blomberg-s01-022: The artificial use is that which proceeds according to precepts and rules.
blocks.blomberg-s01-023: Nowadays people speak much of sound understanding; it is praised too highly. Some have believed that sound reason differs from the sciences merely in degree. But this gives no distinct boundary where one ceases and the other begins. Sound reason and learnedness are distinguished not merely in degree but also in species; there are two particular sources, one for each kind.
blocks.blomberg-s01-024: One is called a scholar whose learnedness is not grounded on common experience. All understanding is called, according to common usage of speech, a common understanding, insofar as it is found in the majority in an equal degree.
blocks.blomberg-s01-025: But it is a sound understanding if it is correct. It is not sound according to degrees; rather the correctness consists in this, that understanding and reason judge according to such laws as agree with experience. But if there are no other principia than experiences, a sound reason still remains a common reason. There is also an instructed understanding, which could not have been acquired through common experiences; and this is a science. There is a Logica of the common understanding and of sound reason, and a Logica of learnedness. It serves to enrich the common and sound understanding, and to cultivate (excoliren) this sound reason up to learnedness.
blocks.blomberg-s01-026: The Logica of sound reason will have one's own experience as its principium, and will thus be empirical; it will not contain the rules for how one ought to think, but it will indicate the rules according to which one commonly thinks. There are two kinds of rules: A:) the rules according to which one proceeds; these are laws of appearance, and subjective. These subjective laws are the laws of reason according to which it commonly proceeds in judging and thinking. B:) Objective laws, according to which the understanding ought to proceed. These are called dogmata.
blocks.blomberg-s01-027: The subjective laws set forth the errors. One extends sound reason by attending to the rules according to which the understanding ought to proceed.
blocks.blomberg-s01-028: We extend the objective laws through doctrines, but in order to cultivate (excoliren) sound reason one must give no general rules and precepts; learned reason is not grounded on empirical principia.
blocks.blomberg-s01-029: The common understanding is the understanding for judging according to laws of experience; the common reason, however, is reason for inferring according to laws of experience. This reason is called common because it is the lowest degree, in all objects that thus come before us. On the occasion of experience we always have a standard of measure with which we compare magnitudes with one another. So we proceed when we want to find the mean magnitude; namely, we take that of which we want to find the mean magnitude, e.g. man: we reckon the size of each man by the standard of measure, add these together, and divide them by the number of men whom we have never seen in our lives; then the mean magnitude comes out, which is suited to each man. So too the mean magnitude of understanding is brought out, from the understanding that one knows through common experience. The common understanding is the measure. The common and sound understanding is a small but correct understanding, and its cognition has great usefulness. In a stretch of country of peasants far fewer errors are found than in a district of scholars of equal size. For the peasant always goes by the guiding thread of experience: he judges about little, but about the little correctly. The exercises of common and sound reason are also easy; all cognition from experience has more life and more of the intuitive than that which has arisen from general concepts. The first advantage of common reason is simplicity. The second is correctness. The third usefulness. The fourth ease and the fifth clarity and liveliness. For the cognitions arise with the light with which representations of experience are endowed. Sound reason will accordingly be sufficient for the fine sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s01-030: Taste actually requires no learnedness at all in order to be quite perfect. Learned taste is in fact already a false, a corrupted taste.
blocks.blomberg-s01-031: What is beautiful must please universally and everyone. For judging beauty experience is required, and the judgment about the beautiful and the ugly is made in accordance with common and sound reason. Common and sound reason lies at the ground of all learnedness; it becomes ridiculous if it is not grafted onto this stock. In history one needs no sound understanding; the same is the case with many mathematical propositions themselves. But in the philosophical and all other sciences, where not merely an imitation of another's understanding is sufficient, but the spirit of genius itself is necessary, the common understanding is indispensable.
blocks.blomberg-s01-032: The use of all cognitions of scholars and their application is possible only through sound reason. To be sure, someone can also be a scholar without a sound understanding, but that is a ridiculous pedant. All learnedness is either historical or rational. Historical is the cognition that is borrowed, as to form, from common reason, but as to matter from common experiences. Historical learnedness contains history, geography, etc. A historical scholar can also make reflexiones, but these already belong to rational learnedness. The matter in rational learnedness can also be grasped through common reason and experience. The form, however, is wholly different. Human beings find more amusement in the capacity of being able to make some pleasure for themselves than in the pleasure itself. When I derive the particular from the general, I need understanding; but when I infer the general from particular cases, I then need another method. The understanding cognizes everything a priori, sound reason a posteriori. We have cognitions that are empirical, where we ascend from below upward, and in rational ones we descend from above. The Logic that is an organon of rational learnedness does not concern historical but rational cognitions. The Logic that is an organon can prescribe rules for a learnedness already at hand, and then it is called Logica Critica, or else rules by which one can arrive at learnedness, and then it is called Logica Dogmatica; all logics are not dogmatic but critical. Philosophy requires more genius than imitation.
blocks.blomberg-s01-033: The whole of nature moves according to rules; thus water moves according to hydraulic rules; nature works according to rules; even changeable weather has its certain rules, although we do not notice them. Animals move according to rules of which they are often not even conscious. The human being acts according to rules, and makes use of the understanding in particular according to certain propositions and rules. How often do human beings also act according to rules without being conscious of them? E.g. they speak their mother tongue. Often an exercise of our power takes place without our being conscious of it, and indeed 1st because this already lies in our nature. 2nd it often happens through imitation, by means of an example that we imitate, in order gradually to use the understanding as we see that others use it.
blocks.blomberg-s01-034: 3: our own use. Our own exercise brings us to the skill of using the understanding without being conscious of its rules.
blocks.blomberg-s01-035: As the human being learns to walk, so he also learns to think. This understanding so formed is Sens commun. If it is correct, it is called the sound understanding, because the skill of using it is subject to a common use. The frequent use of our understanding on objects of experience finally makes us fit to use it correctly. It can therefore become correct through mere exercise and use. The sound understanding is to be common; the understanding, then, that goes further than its senses teach it in experience, is not common; that would be the learned use of the understanding. The sound understanding thus concerns experience; it must proceed according to rules of which it is itself conscious. It is therefore not undisciplined; only it cognizes these rules not in abstracto but in concreto. Thus a sound, awakened understanding belongs to many trades.
blocks.blomberg-s01-036: The causes of things do not fall so much under the senses as their effects. One must therefore also know the rules according to which one can use the sound understanding. In many cases one cannot rely on one's own exercise; but the sole teacher of the sound understanding is experience. The sound understanding and sound reason are therefore, first, of great necessity, in order to be laid at the ground of all abstract higher cognitions. One commonly opposes sound reason to affected learnedness, to proud school-wisdom. But this will not do, for learnedness always presupposes the sound understanding; art presupposes nature. They are indeed distinctae but not oppositae. But it has become fashionable to praise the sound understanding to the detriment of the honor of the sciences. To be sure, it is no reproach if one denies someone science, but if someone has no sound understanding, he is a natural minor, a child. From everyone, then, we demand at least sound understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s01-037: There are certain middle kinds of perfections; the beauty of a woman, e.g., is as it were a merit, ugliness displeases, but tolerable looks are as it were the middle thing that one as it were demands of a human being. Beauty and ugliness distinguish human beings in particular. So it is also with the size of human beings. Our eyes form a certain idea of the mean measure, and what is particular; thus human beings for the most part agree in it. So, e.g., one speaks of a person's wealth. The mean measure between wealth and poverty we call being well-off; in all our concepts we thus always make a mean measure the standard of measure. So too the sound understanding is the mean measure among the capacities of human beings. Sound reason is not to go a step further than experience leads it. The sound understanding cognizes and judges not in abstracto but in concreto; it draws its judgments from experiences. Yet it can also cognize much of what experience teaches us universally, a priori and in abstracto. The sound understanding is therefore the capacity to judge correctly in concreto. Often very rational people cannot judge in abstracto at all, though they think just as often in concreto; so it is in moral cases, e.g. through an example in an occurrence one cognizes things in concreto. The understanding that can judge in abstracto is called the finer, scientific understanding. The natural capacity for judging is the understanding, the capacity for inferring is reason. Through experience one becomes prudent, but not learned. Prudence does not consist in science; one can be and become prudent without any learnedness. The sound understanding and reason show their utility especially in praxi. A certain lack of the sound understanding and of its application in concreto no science can in the least replace or compensate, although it can otherwise replace much. Our general judgments alone cannot help us. With all rules I must know whether they can be applied to the case
blocks.blomberg-s01-038: 2: how I am to apply them here; thus there can be very learned people without any sound understanding. There is therefore as it were in the use of the understanding something that nature has reserved for genius, and which no art can replace.
blocks.blomberg-s01-039: Through all too great a fullness of learnedness people often become the more insipid, and wholly unfit to judge in concreto. To the sound understanding, which is small but correct, belongs 1. Simplicity. It keeps to the ground of experience, and does not love chimerical ideals. This very simplicity makes the understanding the more correct, secure, and reliable than science. An Academy of Sciences at Paris hatches a thousand times more errors than a village full of peasants. 2. Its cognitions are intuitive through examples and instances. It represents objects to us in natura, whereas the finer understanding shows only the shadow of things. The sound understanding is the controller of learnedness. The common sound understanding grows without instruction. So the common living languages are distinguished from the learned dead languages.
blocks.blomberg-s01-040: To give general rules for how one can judge the infallibility of a witness requires more than mere common and sound understanding; it requires art and learnedness. Languages existed before grammars of them, orators before rhetoric, poets before poetics.
blocks.blomberg-s01-041: If I have general cognitions of the understanding, and also its general rules, I must still have understanding in particular besides, in order to judge whether this or that stands under this rule or not. All doctrine in the whole world is only a general sum total of the rules for using the powers of the understanding, but there must still be an understanding present, which nature alone can give. Persons who possess learnedness but lack a sound understanding are far more insipid than wholly ignorant ones. From this, however, arises pedantry. A stubborn blockhead cannot be called a pedant. Learnedness must always be there, but the ability to apply the recognized general rules in concreto to particular cases must be lacking. Although to be sure a pedant, for all his science, always retains a kind of stupidity. So it is, e.g., with all the introduction of witty remarks in society, with complimenting even according to general precept. The Chinese have books of compliments; general rules always testify to the weakness of our understanding. Just as a lexicon of a language finds in a beginner much regularity without consciousness of the rules, so it is with the sound understanding. The use of the understanding, however, according to rules of which one is conscious, is called science. There are cases where one person without science can go further than another with science, but also where the greatest sound understanding cannot go as far as science alone. So in mathematics, in geometry (surveying), one cannot get on through mere understanding; some science must always be there. So it is also with the art of medicine. For judging morality, right and wrong, on the other hand, no science and learnedness is needed.
blocks.blomberg-s01-042: The human race would otherwise be very imperfect. Here the sound understanding is the judge of science.
blocks.blomberg-s01-043: In all sciences a precept serves well for the development of our capacities for all occurrences. But in every instruction in art it is still always necessarily left to the understanding of the subject whether, and in what degree, these general precepts are applied in individual cases. Thus one cannot possibly become prudent according to universally valid rules and precepts, for prudence actually consists in this, that one can subsume individual cases in common life itself under the general rules of common life.
blocks.blomberg-s01-044: The discipline that contains the rules of the good use of the understanding and of reason in general is called Logica. It determines no individual cases; in all other sciences Logica is applied. Logic stands to the whole use of the understanding exactly as the Grammatica to a language. Grammar has a source of the correctness of the rules, but the proof lies in experience.
blocks.blomberg-s01-045: Logic shows the rules of the use of the understanding and of reason, which can themselves be cognized a priori and without experience, since they do not depend on it. The understanding here sees into its own rules and makes of them a discipline, an instruction, which can however be cognized a priori, and hence it is called a doctrine.
blocks.blomberg-s01-046: In logic reason is not merely applied; rather reason is its object, the object of its consideration in usu.
blocks.blomberg-s01-047: There are many cognitions whose form is not rational, and then it is no doctrine of reason. So, for example, it is with the science of taste.
blocks.blomberg-s01-048: Philosophia is in general the rational science of the qualities of things. By the former it is distinguished from the historical sciences, by the latter from the mathematical sciences. It is called a science of reason, however, because it presents cognitions in abstracto.
blocks.blomberg-s01-049: For the arrangement of the first science, such as logic is, nothing is needed but the common sound understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s01-050: Logic is called, by a particular name properly belonging to it, the science of reason, because this is its object. The remaining many Scientias rationales should be called sciences of reason.
blocks.blomberg-s01-051: Logic is called a science because its rules can be proved a priori by themselves without any use. For this reason neither grammar nor aesthetic is a science. And there really is, properly speaking, no science of the beautiful at all; rather, whatever we know of the beautiful is nothing but a Critica.
blocks.blomberg-s01-052: The Logica will therefore have no other grounds and source than the nature of the human understanding. Of every cognition, and thus also of logic, there are always 1. .. a) objective and b) subjective grounds. In every science one rightly studies the object, what belongs to its greatest perfection, but also ... 2. the subject, i.e. the means, the substrata, for arriving at the object. And so in the sciences of the understanding I must first of all study the human being; but since this happens seldom, or by few, there arise from it, e.g., the many errors in morals especially, from most moralists, who can indeed speak excellently of virtue, praise, recommend and describe it, but are not in a position to instil in their hearers, and to bring forth in them, the desire and love to practice it, because they have not studied the human being.
blocks.blomberg-s01-053: The Logica is a good Philosophia about the good use of reason and its rules. It therefore considers not only the nature of human reason alone but also, in particular, its precepts.
blocks.blomberg-s01-054: The nature of the human understanding is developed from experience and treated by Psychologia. It will therefore also have its sources, i.e. we shall have to learn some subjective laws of the use of reason from Psychologia and experience.
blocks.blomberg-s01-055: We can therefore 1st make the subjective laws of our understanding, according to which we actually make use of the understanding, the object of our consideration.
blocks.blomberg-s01-056: That science which examines the subjective laws, as distinct from the rules, of our use of understanding and reason is called Psychologia.
blocks.blomberg-s01-057: Logic does not properly contain the rules according to which the human being actually thinks, but the rules for how the human being ought to think. For the human being often uses his understanding and thinks otherwise than he ought to think and to use his understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s01-058: Logic therefore contains in itself the objective laws of the understanding and of reason. Thus the portrayal of a good republic is often so opposed to an actually existing republic that it contains precisely the opposite of it.
blocks.blomberg-s01-059: We have, then, basically only two objective doctrines, for there are only two objective powers of the soul: the power of cognition and the faculty of desire. Logic as well as morals have as their object a praxis, an exercise, the use of our understanding, the application of our free power of choice. For that reason, however, they are not yet called practical sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s01-060: We can have a theoretical as well as a practical logic and morals. Disciplines are practical if their effects are practical.
blocks.blomberg-s01-061: Logic is not a mere critic; it is an actual doctrine, which can be proved. Its rules are taken in abstracto, and proved. But not every doctrine is always practical; it can be a pure theory. Now if logic is a mere theory of the conditions under which a cognition is perfect, according to laws of the understanding and of reason, then it is no means of [31a] execution; it would be a theory but not an organon.
blocks.blomberg-s01-062: There is a logic that is called a Scientia propaedeutica, an introductory science.
blocks.blomberg-s01-063: and so it will serve us as a means of critic or as an organon; but that it is not; it only sharpens the understanding in judging about cognitions
blocks.blomberg-s01-064: Logic therefore contains the rules for the use of our understanding and of our reason. Everything else therefore stands under it. It paves the way for all the other sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s02-001: There are many rules of motion and of the understanding; every ship, every fish orients itself by the rules of motion. We ourselves are subject to these laws. We observe them in walking and in other movements. Nature has implanted these laws in human beings and animals. But in respect of them we do nothing more than fulfil them unknowingly, like the animals.
blocks.blomberg-s02-002: It would be unnecessary if one wanted to spy out these laws of motion and to take no step without deliberation. Just as the fish in its swimming observes these rules most precisely through exercise, so we too can acquire a skill in observing them only through exercise. How quickly do we not know how to help ourselves when we are about to fall? But this skill would be lacking to us if we wanted to deliberate beforehand what posture we should assume.
blocks.blomberg-s02-003: Borellus has written a book on regular motion.
blocks.blomberg-s02-004: Besides the laws and rules of motion, however, there are also rules and laws of the understanding. We arrange all our judgments according to these laws. Just as a child in walking learns to observe the laws of motion, so too in judging it seeks to form itself according to the laws of the understanding. But it does all this unknowingly, and attains the skill merely through exercise.
blocks.blomberg-s02-005: For common cognition it is not necessary that we be conscious of these rules and deliberate on them. If we wanted to do so, we would lose a great deal. But if our understanding wants to have ascended to learned cognition, it must be conscious of its rules and use them after deliberation, because common exercise is not enough for it here. These rules, which the understanding has to observe in learned observation, or cognition, are prescribed to us by Logic, which we now wish to expound.
blocks.blomberg-s02-006: The author defines it quite rightly: it is a science that treats of the rules of learned cognition and of learned presentation. A shorter definition would be: Logic is a science that teaches us the use of the understanding in learned cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s02-007: It is also called Philosophia instrumentalis, because it can be regarded, as it were, as an Instrumentum of all the other philosophical sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s02-008: Through frequent observations the rules of the understanding have been spied out. Aristotle already established some; but these were nothing other than signposts to wrong paths. It has already cost much effort to forget such false propositions, to give the understanding its natural perfection again, and to investigate its true rules.
blocks.blomberg-s02-009: A correct logic is like a straight line, such that one must deviate from it neither to the right nor to the left. It would be desirable that logic had already been brought to such correctness and perfection.
blocks.blomberg-s02-010: The author indicates to us in this paragraph from what we must derive its rules if we want to make it so perfect.
blocks.blomberg-s02-011: Namely, the following can serve for this
blocks.blomberg-s02-012: 1. the experiences of the effects of human reason. Baco de Verulam (see his life in Formey's Hist. der Philosophie pag. 293 et sequ. and in Gentzkenii Historia Philosophica pag. 156, 157.) was the first to show the world that all philosophy consists of chimeras if it does not rest on experiences.
blocks.blomberg-s02-013: It would be just as necessary to write an experimental logic as a physics, in which one should investigate how the human being can err through prejudices and through overhastiness, as well as in other ways, so that rules can be prescribed to him for how he is to guard against them.
blocks.blomberg-s02-014: One should furthermore make observations on how one can judge most correctly, and also prescribe rules for this in Logica.
blocks.blomberg-s02-015: 2. we must look to the nature of human reason, so that the rules can be established in conformity with it.
blocks.blomberg-s02-016: It would be foolish to arrange logic for rational beings in general, or even for angels, and to think that it could also be useful to us. This would be just as if I wanted to give rules and precepts to a lame man who had to walk on crutches, as to how he should walk and run as a healthy man. 3. Our rules must conform to the general basic truths of human cognition, with which Ontologia deals. These basic truths are the Principia of all sciences, and consequently also of Logica. We must remark here that we, here at the beginning of Philosophia, are not yet in a position to deliver a perfect Logica; for this, insights are required that can be presupposed only in such hearers to whom the whole of philosophy is known. We shall here strive only to give preliminary rules for learned cognition, by which one will make the learning of the remaining sciences easier for oneself.
blocks.blomberg-s02-017: The aim of the doctrine of reason can be divided into the immediate and the mediate. The immediate is the improvement of learned cognition, and the mediate that of common cognition. The latter can happen if one seeks, in daily intercourse, to improve people's concepts, in which one must not come with scholastic termini if one does not want to be called a pedant.
blocks.blomberg-s02-018: As for the immediate aim of logic, namely the perfection of learned cognition, this concerns scholars by profession as well as others. Everyone can improve his learned cognition through it as much as he wants. Scholars by profession are distinguished from others by certain termini technici, and also by the fact that learnedness is their foremost occupation, whereas by the others, e.g. by kings, it is for the most part pursued only as a side-instrument.
blocks.blomberg-s02-019: It would be fair, since the multitude of the sciences is now so great, that each person be assigned his particular field, because it is impossible to make oneself perfect in all the sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s02-020: Among the persons who are not scholars by profession one could also count women, who can also occupy themselves with learnedness in accordance with their capacities.
blocks.blomberg-s02-021: There are sciences for which acute sense, much reflection, and profundity are required. These are for the male sex. On the other hand there are also such sciences for which wit and a kind of feeling are required, and these are fitting for women.
blocks.blomberg-s02-022: Here philosophy is spoken of. Its object is the general qualities and constitutions of things. But it is well to note that philosophy does not look to quotiens aliquid positum sit? but only to quod positum sit? It considers only the qualities, it weighs only what is posited. Mathesis, on the other hand, investigates how many times the thing is posited, and investigates the quantitates of things, how great they are. Philosophy further considers not the whole qualities, not the whole constitution of things, and all of them, but only those which are found in many things and are therefore called general.

blocks.blomberg-s02-024: The definition that our author gives of Philosophia is the following: philosophy, he says, is a science of the general constitutions of things, insofar as they are cognized without faith. One is also accustomed to say otherwise: Philosophia est Scientia, quae circa rerum rationes versatur. But because philosophy occupies itself not merely with the grounds of things but also often with their constitutions simply, one easily sees that this definition is incorrect. To philosophy belongs a higher use of reason; but it is hard to determine where philosophy begins and where it ceases; just as, e.g., the boundaries between poverty and wealth are to be determined. A man is rich, one says, e.g. if he has 50000 or 20000 Rthlr., but at what number of money does he then cease to be rich, and when does he become rich? – Just as hard are the boundaries between avarice and thrift to determine. At one point philosophy must separate itself from the common use of reason, poverty from wealth, stinginess from thrift; but where this point is, is hard to say.

blocks.blomberg-s02-039: As regards the history of philosophy, the following is to be noted: the Chaldeans had a philosopher in Zoroaster, and among the Persians a Zoroaster is likewise known, who is however wholly different from the Chaldean. The Philosophia of the Chaldeans was very obscure and uncertain. (Theology therefore first extended philosophy, ad pag. 44) It ascends to the highest antiquity, and what one can bring out about it derives from very suspect reports. One must therefore be very cautious if one does not want to mix the teachings of the ancients with the fictions spread in later times. The religion of these peoples was a mixture of the most absurd superstition, a crude and abominable idolatry. The priests deceived the stupid people by all sorts of artifices. Soothsayings, enchantments, interpretations of dreams, childish and extravagant ceremonies made up the whole. If something good still lay beneath this crude rind, it is impossible now to pick it out. This philosophy thus has the appearance of the most perfect folly, but it must also have been a dangerous folly; for from the first times of the Roman monarchy onward the arts of the Chaldeans were banished as suspect and godless. But notwithstanding such obscurity of the Chaldean philosophy, it was nevertheless very famous in all antiquity. Its adherents divided themselves into many sorts of sects, such as: Hipparenes, Babylonians, Orchenes, Marsypers, Borsippenes etc. Zoroaster is given out as the originator of magic, i.e. as the father of the crudest among all deceptions and of the most shameful superstition. It is said: he was killed by fire from heaven. Belus is said to have instructed the priests in astronomia and physica. Berosus, Marmaridius, Zabrates, and Teucrus are known to us merely by name alone.
blocks.blomberg-s02-040: All philosophies of the oldest peoples were to be found among the priests. The Egyptians and Persians were probably the first whose understanding overstepped its limit and began to make speculationes. Astrologia and Cosmologia arose earlier than the physical sciences. The very first object of investigation was the origin of things, for these are without doubt the most important questions, and must have occurred to human beings at once, after they had first attended to the necessities of their bodies. Yet this first inquiry will of course have contained more superstition than philosophy. So much is certain: before philosophy in a nation had separated itself wholly and entirely from the power of the government and the rule of the clergy, no philosophy could properly come about.
blocks.blomberg-s02-041: The originator of the Persian philosophy was Zerdusch or Zoroaster. He lived at the time of the Babylonian captivity; he was the head of the religion. He brought his doctrine together in a work called Zendavesta. His oracle is a book falsely attributed to him by the New Platonists. The priests of the Persians were called Magi, and their chief Archimagus. The doctrines of their philosophy were as follows. The supreme God is the intellectual fire: from it, in order to bring forth the world, two mutually opposed fundamental beings or principia proceeded. The foremost being, from which all the others proceed, and on which the law of emanations also depends, is called Mithra. The 2 fundamental beings are Oromasdes, a very pure, active and spiritual light, and Arimanius, the suffering and material darkness, which was born from the limitation of the light and is bound up with it as a necessary consequence. From the mixture of these 2 fundamental beings all things beneath the moon have proceeded, and thus one must explain the origin of evil on earth. But a time will come when the darkness will be overcome by the light and annihilated. The soul, in their opinion, came from the gods and was, like them, immortal. Their moral teachings recommended chastity, uprightness, fairness, the shunning of pleasures. They expressed this thus: You must follow the light, and guard yourselves against the plague of darkness or the generation of matter.
blocks.blomberg-s02-042: Among the Chinese we note 3 great philosophers: Confucius, Keilau and Janzu, whom they worshipped under the image of a 3-headed idol. They held the opinion of Pythagoras about the transmigration of souls, worship the sun, moon and stars, and indeed not infrequently the devil, so that he may not harm them. They therefore place his likeness on the fore part of their ships, and wear fearsome heads on their clothes. Among the Chinese all philosophy is nothing but morals, some astronomy and mathematics, and a kind of political science and art of government. Confucius was a Solon of the Chinese.
blocks.blomberg-s02-043: Among the Jews, before the destruction of Jerusalem, we note several sects, as 1. the Sadducees, who originated from Antigonus Sochaeus. Out of vexation at the doctrine of good works, by which one can earn nothing with God, he fell into the complete opposite and said: one must serve God without any hope of future reward. Zadok and Boethos misunderstood this doctrine; they therefore denied the resurrection of the bodies, and all rewards after this life.
blocks.blomberg-s02-044: 2: the Karaites, Karaites or scribes, who rejected all allegorical interpretations of scripture, but otherwise accepted all Sadducean propositions. They adhered to the school of Chamai.
blocks.blomberg-s02-045: 3: the sect of the Pharisees; it has its name from the Hebrew word parash, which means separated people. For they believed themselves to be very different from the people, partly through their knowledge, which however consisted only in false interpretations of the law, and partly through meritorious works, which however were nothing further than observances of external ceremonies and superstitious acts. Their doctrine was chiefly upheld by the school of Hillel.
blocks.blomberg-s02-046: 4: the sect of the Essenes. These departed most from the Jewish customs. The persecutions of the Syrian kings, or rather the invasion of Kambyses, gave them their origin. Their way of life was very similar to the monastic orders. They served God in a purely spiritual manner; they had fixed hours in which they attended to certain duties.
blocks.blomberg-s02-047: 5. the sect of the Therapeutae. They flourished in Egypt, and were wholly monk-like.
blocks.blomberg-s02-048: From the times after the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Temple we note the Rabbis: Gamaliel, and Jehuda called the Holy, the foremost originators of the Talmudic doctrine. The Cabbalistic doctrine is in the mysterious books Happlijah, Ha-Bahir, and Sohar. The Rabbis Akiba and Simeon, son of Sohar, propagated it, but as a secret doctrine. Finally the philosophy of Aristotle mixed itself in, although all the Rabbis opposed it. Proofs of this are found in the work Cuzzeri. The famous Rabbi Moses Maimonides was very practised in it. This mixed doctrine has very great similarity with the positive and moral theology that was founded on the interpretation of the divine law. Rabbi Saudius brought the former into a doctrinal system. Moses Maimonides gave it a more philosophical turn, and made 13 articles of faith out of it, which he called roots. Finally the Jews in Egypt adopted the allegorical method, and the very philosophy of this country, namely the concept of emanations, which consisted of a mixture of the opinions of Zoroaster, Pythagoras, and others. All this they sought to combine, as well as possible, with their own opinions. Among the Therapeutae this doctrine was already in vogue, and Philo followed it. The fear of the Jews in the 2nd century of being dispersed moved them to set this doctrine down in writing, and thus they propagated these errors ever further. On this see more in Formey's Histoire de la philosophie, pp. 72, 184.

blocks.blomberg-s03-002: In this paragraph the author wanted to give a definition of representation, but since he was unable to do so, he helped himself out with a rhetorical flourish, as commonly tends to happen when one cannot say anything certain. To this end he says that a representation is related to an image which the painterly skill of the soul draws in its interior. What representation is cannot actually be explained at all. It is one of the simple concepts that we necessarily must have. Every human being knows immediately what representation is. Cognitions and representations are the same. Concepts, however, differ somewhat from them, as we shall see in what follows. Cognition and representation are taken in logic as the same. Every representation is something in us, which however refers to something else, which is the object. Certain things represent something, but we represent things to ourselves. Logic does not teach us at all how we are to represent something to ourselves through consciousness, but rather presupposes consciousness of something as a matter of psychology.
blocks.blomberg-s03-003: In every cognition we find something material. But also something formal.
blocks.blomberg-s03-004: The object that we represent to ourselves is the object; the manner of the representation, however, is called the formal. If, e.g., I represent virtue to someone, I can partly look at what I represent to myself, partly at how I represent it to myself; the latter is the formal, the former the material of the representation. Logic, however, has for the most part to do with the formal of cognition. But cognitions can have different form in one materia. blocks.blomberg-s03-005: When we distinguish a representation and its object, to which it goes, from other representations, then we are conscious of the representation. Consciousness accompanies each of our states; it is, as it were, the intuiting of ourselves.
blocks.blomberg-s03-006: Yet we are not conscious of most of the most powerful and most forceful representations. Who would imagine that? Only for those representations of which we are conscious can we prescribe rules. Consciousness cannot be spoken of more fully here. The doctrine of it actually belongs in metaphysica, and in order to have a correct concept of it, much from metaphysica is laid down as the ground.
blocks.blomberg-s03-007: Here distinct and confused representations are spoken of. If in a composite representation I distinguish from one another the parts of which it consists, then that is a distinct representation. But if I do not distinguish its partial representations from one another, then it is a confused representation. E.g., if I see a cheese mite, my representation of it is at first confused. But if I take a microscope in hand, and in it become aware of a maw full of teeth, 2 rows of feet, 2 black eyes, then I had also represented all this to myself before. But I was not able to distinguish these partial representations of the individual limbs from the whole body. Through the microscope, however, my cognition becomes distinct, in that I thereby represent to myself the individual parts of a cheese mite, and distinguish them from its whole body. Likewise, when I regard the Milky Way with the naked eyes, I distinguish nothing in it from anything else. I am conscious of no parts in the representation. But if I regard the Milky Way through a telescope, I see that it consists of fixed stars. These fixed stars I represent to myself as parts of the Milky Way and distinguish the representation of one fixed star from the representation of another, and therefore have a distinct representation, because precisely for such a one it is required that I distinguish the partial representations from one another, and the partial representations of the fixed stars are partial representations of the Milky Way.
blocks.blomberg-s03-008: A simple representation, and simple cognitions, can be neither confused nor distinct, nor become so. Confusedness and distinctness therefore occur only in composite cognitions.
blocks.blomberg-s03-009: A main property of logic will therefore be to unfold a confused cognition and to make it distinct.
blocks.blomberg-s03-010: Indistinctness is opposed to distinctness, but confusion to order. Something can be confused even though I am conscious of the partial representations and it has distinctness. A distinct representation is not yet always orderly. The more we reduce our representations to simple ones, the more we remove the confusion.
blocks.blomberg-s03-011: In the distinct representation the material is just the same as in the confused. In the one case we represent just as much as in the other. In the confused representation we have the partial representations just as in the distinct. For if we did not have them, we would not have the total either.
blocks.blomberg-s03-012: In the confused, however, we do not distinguish the partial representations. A cognition can be distinct only insofar as it is a total representation. Likewise only a total representation can be confused. A simple representation is neither confused nor distinct. For in it I cannot distinguish any partial representation from another. The distinct, as well as the confused, occurs only in total and composite representations.
blocks.blomberg-s03-014: 1 mo in intuiting, when we can distinguish well the marks of that which we intuit. That is distinctness in intuition.
blocks.blomberg-s03-015: 2. in thinking, when we connect clear concepts and representations with the intuiting. One can often intuit something distinctly without thinking anything distinctly in connection with it.
blocks.blomberg-s03-016: We arrive at distinctness of intuition through more attentiveness per Synthesin; but distinctness of concepts requires the dissection of what I think, of what I already actually conceive in thought, i.e. distinctness of the understanding per Analysin. The whole of morals has nothing but concepts of the understanding. Empirical distinctness is acquired a posteriori through attentiveness to the objects of experience. Distinctness of reason, however, is acquired a priori through attentiveness to the actions of my understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s03-017: A ground is that from which something can be cognized, and a consequence is what can be cognized from the ground. With this definition we can make do here. In metaphysica, however, we shall not be content with it. A ground from which everything in the consequence can be understood, to which therefore nothing is lacking, is a sufficient ground, and one where only something is cognized is an insufficient ground. E.g., if we say: that the moon has inhabitants because mountains and valleys are found in it, then this is an insufficient ground. One sees from it only that it is possible and probable that there are inhabitants in the moon. But if, e.g., a merchant has 100000 Rthl. in property, and one says: 50000 Rthl. he has acquired through trade, and 50000 Rthl. he has inherited, then this is a sufficient ground. The relation of the ground and the consequences is the connection; e.g., the tree is connected with its fruits, the tree is the ground, and the fruits are the consequence.
blocks.blomberg-s03-018: Every truth has its ground, i.e. that from which one can distinguish it from the false and hold it to be true. This is here in logica. Of sufficient grounds is properly spoken in metaphysica.
blocks.blomberg-s03-019: If I merely the ground of a consequence , the cognition is not yet rational on that account. E.g., if one gives saltpetre as the ground of the thunderstorm. But if one sees distinctly how the consequence arises from the ground, e.g. how the storm comes from the saltpetre, then our cognition is rational. The author here already speaks of rational cognition, without first having spoken of distinct cognition. He should have called it a cognition of reason, which itself arises from reason.

blocks.blomberg-s03-030: 2 do that it has an effect on our feeling and our taste. The former is a logical, the latter an aesthetic perfection, but both a formal perfection. We have a logic that makes, and can make, our cognitions logically perfect, and another that makes our cognition aesthetically perfect. The former teaches us to make representations that are in accordance with the constitution of the thing, which is what the logic does that we now want to treat. The latter, however, which contains aesthetics, must deal with those representations that have an effect on our feeling. blocks.blomberg-s03-031: We can say that the cognition or representation is rational in which reason is employed, in which I cognize the grounds; but truth in particular belongs to the logical perfection of a representation. Another means to objective perfection is distinctness. Thus, e.g., a demonstration is logically perfect if the proofs adduced are secure, distinct, certain, and agree with the properties of the thing. A proof can also be easy, however, although this property does not properly relate to the object, but rather to the subject. Hence one and the same object can be hard to grasp for one subject and in turn easy for another.
blocks.blomberg-s03-032: One must ordinarily sacrifice something of logical perfection if one wants to attain an aesthetic one, and expend something of the aesthetic if one wants to attain a logical perfection. Something can never be quite distinct without being somewhat hard, and never quite lively without being somewhat indistinct, et vice versa.
blocks.blomberg-s03-033: No one has yet been able to combine, determine, and find out accurately the right measure of aesthetic perfection with the logical. A great deal of delicacy belongs to this. What favors our life, i.e. what, as it were, sets our activity into play, pleases. Something becomes easy for us when it is in order. E.g., if someone has great knowledge of natural history, and does not cognize it in connection with its grounds, then he has no rational but only a historical cognition. The beautiful in a cognition is diminished when the rational and distinct is promoted in it, just as the beauty of a woman vanishes when one regards her through a microscope. blocks.blomberg-s03-093: In the 26th §, the author speaks of the magnitude of cognition as likewise a perfection. In every magnitude there is always a multitude, but in every multitude there is not yet a magnitude. In every magnitude I can consider the extensive and the intensive. In the first case, when I consider the extensive of a magnitude, I look to the multitude of units, to their number, how many there are of them. In the other case, however, namely when I consider the intensive magnitude, I look especially to the magnitude of each unit. And so it is also with cognition. If I consider only the multitude of objects that I cognize, I look merely to the extensive magnitude of cognition; but if I cognize a single object wholly and quite perfectly, then the cognition is certainly intensive. With the latter it properly depends on the degree to which I cognize each unit.
blocks.blomberg-s03-094: Truth is a perfection that belongs both to the logical and to the aesthetic perfection of cognition. It is a chief logical perfection on which all the others depend. If I cognize the thing as it actually is, my cognition is true. Truth is also required for aesthetic perfection. Hence Milton is censured for having represented death and sin as it were as persons, because this is not in accordance with their constitution. Yet in the aesthetically perfect not so great a truth is required as in the logical. In the aesthetic, something need only be tolerabiliter true. In this way it is aesthetically true that Milton represents the angels in Paradise Lost as fighting and engaged in combat, for who knows whether this cannot take place? A good fable must always contain an aesthetic truth in itself. So, e.g., in Aesop's fable of the wolf there is such truth when he says of the lamb and the wolf at the river that the patient lamb excused itself quite meekly against the wolf's malicious accusation and endeavored to appease his anger, but that the bloodthirsty and unjust wolf thereupon answered, or at least signified by his worthless answer: In short, I am hungry now, I must devour you –.

With children one should begin from the sensible. Geography could be presented to them in such a way that they always feel and are moved in the process. Thus, instead of having them learn the names by heart verbosus, one could rather relate the curiosities of the sea, the particular customs of foreign nations and peoples etc., and not, as is commonly done, merely point out to them on the map, without anything to remark about it: that is Paris, that is London etc. From history one could in turn present to them the events that have occurred in the liveliest and most moving way, so that their feeling and desires would be improved thereby. With riper years one could also begin various exercises of the understanding with them. One could let them read skillful, selected poems and good speeches, and think about them.
blocks.blomberg-s03-124: But one must not, as is commonly done in school, force them, often before they can even think, to an oratory which afterwards does them no good at all, except that they forget it; for what one has had to learn unwillingly, or even by means of compulsion, one forgets very soon, and of itself. Dry cognitions, which are nevertheless so much in favor, such as reciting the names of places, emperors, the dates etc., corrupt the youth in the worst way. The child learns them with vexation, and does not retain them, but seeks only, from fear of punishment, to have its lesson ready to recite etc. That what it has once learned should always remain in its memory is not at all its intention. Even if one tells it that otherwise it cannot be and become happy, it pays no heed to that at all; it is still entirely disinterested, and content only with its present pleasure, and therefore abhors everything that would diminish this for it. Naturally, therefore, it will retain, and seek to retain, only what pleases it and moves its feeling. If now everything is presented in such a way, it would also be able to retain everything gladly and with pleasure.
blocks.blomberg-s03-125: To be truthful is the greatest virtue in the world, on which all the rest are grounded, and all the other virtues are in fact, without truthfulness, nothing but dissimulations. This virtue, then, ought to be presented to children first, and at the same time accustomed everywhere, where not yet by words, then at least by looks.
blocks.blomberg-s03-126: One ought above all to endeavor to implant in children a strong disgust at all and every untruth, under whatever pretext one might excuse it, just as, e.g., at a caterpillar or other vermin. Afterwards they will gradually accustom themselves to lie as little in their lives as to touch a caterpillar. They will always be honest and hate every possible dissimulation.
blocks.blomberg-s03-127: Every human being, furthermore, has a natural drive to benevolence, as it were innate in him. Just as we rejoice when we can make another laugh with our ideas, so we rejoice still more when we have made others happy through us, or have merely put them into joy, pleasure etc. (only a few malicious minds, who wish their fellow human beings misfortune, or even promote it, are excepted from this). One would therefore have to know how to preserve this in a child too. One should, e.g., give a child something to give to other children who are poorer, but not first when these, as beggars, ask for it, since they are wretched. For thereby one accustoms them merely to pity, which is still very different from true compassion; rather one would have to let the child share something with others, merely in order to give it, because it is beautiful and praiseworthy to share what one has to spare; because those deserve it, even if they do not ask for it or do not have the heart to.
blocks.blomberg-s03-128: When one has instilled so much in it through feeling, this will certainly at once improve its moral character, and it will take pleasure in moral narratives.
blocks.blomberg-s03-129: Once this has been attained, one can teach it to read; then it will itself see what the skill of being able to read helps it. It will itself get pleasure in it, it will endeavor to attain a skill in it the sooner the better, since this reading puts it in a position to read letters, poems, moral occurrences, and other beautiful books itself, and henceforth not to need to ask others to tell it something. When this has now happened, one should seek to promote its historical cognition, because this must lie at the ground of the rational. One should by no means burden it with a monstrous multitude of names; from this it naturally sees no use at all, and consequently has no desire for it.
blocks.blomberg-s03-130: One should grasp the histories morally; then it will take pleasure in them, and will indeed regard the names only as side matters, but yet retain them.
blocks.blomberg-s03-131: Finally, one should also seek to extend and promote its rational cognition. One should tell it the grounds when it asks the cause of something, yet one should not burden it with remote grounds. If it asks why no grain grows in this or that field, one should tell it: because it is sandy etc., but not give it a lengthy explanation of fertility; this serves for nothing but to confuse its understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s03-132: In this §pho the author says that one must let small perfections go when greater ones are thereby hindered. To small aesthetic perfections greater logical ones must be preferred, and greater aesthetic ones again to smaller logical perfections.
blocks.blomberg-s03-133: If one follows this rule, one will write both logically and aesthetically beautifully, and be able to express oneself in a presentation.
blocks.blomberg-s03-134: The opposite of any perfection is always twofold, namely either the contradictory opposite, when the perfection merely is lacking, or secondly the real opposite, which entirely cancels the perfection that might otherwise be there on another ground. An example of the first would be, e.g., such medicaments as help not at all but also do no harm, such as can often be prescribed; this is aptly compared with the contradictory opposite of healing; but those medicines that not only do no good but even do harm have the real opposite of healing. And so it is also with cognitions.
blocks.blomberg-s03-135: The imperfection that is the contradictory opposite is called the lack, and the imperfection that is the real opposite of the perfect is called the fault. Thus, e.g., ignorance of the immortality of the human soul is the contradictory opposite, whereas error, in which one even believes that the human soul is not immortal, is the real opposite of the cognition of the soul's immortality. In ignorance only grounds are lacking; it can therefore be easily remedied. In error, however, there are actual grounds, which are opposed to the true cognition as counter-grounds.
blocks.blomberg-s03-136: Faults: vitia, must therefore be avoided far more than lacks, Defectus. It is indeed far worse if I cancel what has already actually been proved on other grounds than if I know nothing yet, because in the latter case I can be instructed sooner than in the former. E.g. he who defines something not at all can get by with his common cognition, whereas if he makes false definitiones and afterwards applies them, a far greater and more important harm arises from it, which could not have arisen from a lack. With the vitia, however, the cognition is not only not increased, but rather diminished; but even what is already there is actually cancelled.
blocks.blomberg-s03-137: Common and historical cognition can be far more perfect than learned cognition. They are to be regarded as Heterogenea, but can nevertheless also be considered against a Focus Perfectionis, e.g. whether they are lively, fruitful and so on etc. By historical cognition we understand not the aesthetic but the merely dry cognition. This dry cognition in a man, e.g., of the circumstances of his life and his occurrences is much more fruitful and extensive than the learned.
blocks.blomberg-s03-138: A mathematician who otherwise possesses much cognition will nevertheless not get as far in praxis with his engineering science as another who has not studied the theory but has acquired for himself a merely historical cognition of praxis itself.
blocks.blomberg-s03-139: Machiavelli, e.g., had a great learned cognition of how to draw up an entire army in battle order, but when he was actually once commissioned to command an army, he put the entire army into disorder instead of arranging it, because he had no historical cognition of the incidental circumstances.
blocks.blomberg-s03-140: In many respects the scholar with his solid cognition really accomplishes by far not so much as another whose cognition is historical, because the first is not so universally useful as the other.
blocks.blomberg-s03-141: Rousseau holds that the sciences have brought more harm than benefit. We have capacities that are far greater than is necessary for this life. Our theoretical capacities are stronger in us than the practical ones. The former we can improve more than the latter; whence a disproportion, a monstrosity, in which the head is too large en régard of the other members of the body. If we had no other life to expect, learnedness would certainly be more harmful than useful to us. For here we often have by far not advantages enough for the trouble that we take. Meanwhile learnedness has also already procured us many advantages here. Navigation, the art of government etc. would certainly, without it, have remained still very obscure and imperfect. What a great benefit it is that through it alone, as through a light, the darkness of superstition has been dispelled, and that superstition has been so happily eradicated. Many old women can now grow old with honor and end their lives in peace, whereas before, they very often fell under suspicion and quite possibly had to lose their lives wretchedly.
blocks.blomberg-s03-142: Learned cognition considers the universal, and therefore gives occasion for inventions and improvements.
blocks.blomberg-s03-143: If learned cognition is at the same time beautiful, it is the most useful and serviceable, especially in praxis. One knows how the cognition of the Scholastics, those dry philosophers bound to a very constrained method, has as it were annihilated the moral qualities and capacities of human beings and degraded them to superstition. An irreplaceable loss! All this, however, could not have been otherwise, and came about merely because their cognitions, and consequently also their presentations of morals etc., were merely learned and not also at the same time beautiful, but rather entirely dry. So harmful, then, is a beautiful but unlearned cognition, and a learned but dry one.
blocks.blomberg-s04-001: The extensiveness of learned cognition is opposed to its paltriness. This concerns either the material or the formal. If someone lacks historical cognition, he is in complete ignorance. So, e.g., the ancients were in complete ignorance of the existence of the new world; they had no historical cognition of it. The common man is still completely ignorant with regard to many things. But one can also be in ignorance with regard to the grounds of a thing: 1. in that it is wholly unknown to us, so that one has no historical cognition of it. E.g. when one does not know at all whence thunderstorm, rain, snow etc. arise.
blocks.blomberg-s04-002: 2 Second, when one does not see the Nexus of the thing with the ground at all, although the grounds are known to one. E.g. when I do know that ebb and flood have the moon as cause, but do not yet understand and see how it comes about that ebb and flood derive from the attraction of the moon.
blocks.blomberg-s04-003: As for ignorance, it can be divided
blocks.blomberg-s04-004: 1: into a necessary, and on the other hand
blocks.blomberg-s04-006: Where no data are given us for determining something, ignorance is necessary. E.g. for determining where the human soul will be after the death of the body; item, of the generative power of animals and human beings.
blocks.blomberg-s04-007: Thirdly, the place that we have in the world makes ignorance necessary to us. If, however, on the contrary, from certain motives we voluntarily renounce some things, so that we purposely do not want to know them, when we see that something is too difficult for us or without use, this is a logical ignorance.
blocks.blomberg-s04-008: Logic is more a doctrine of skill, which belongs to the youth; the doctrine of wisdom, however, belongs to the man.
blocks.blomberg-s04-009: That circle within which we can see things is called our horizon. The sum total of all things that man can cognize in a learned manner without detriment to his other perfections is the horizon of learned cognition. What is above the horizon can be seen in the geographical sense. Here, however, it is to mean such things as one cannot cognize even if one wanted to, ignorance of which is necessary. Of many things we are even in ignorance in historical cognition, e.g. of the joys in heaven, of the mysteries, because perhaps they cannot be expressed through our words; of some things we are often in ignorance because of our weak capacities, of others, however, with regard to circumstances, time, and place.
blocks.blomberg-s04-010: We determine the horizon of cognition
blocks.blomberg-s04-011: 1. logically merely through the faculty, through the measure of our powers
blocks.blomberg-s04-013: One believes it is always good to know more than one may, and that it is better to know too much than too little. But all effort to a greater degree on one aim is superfluous and badly applied. It is therefore necessary that all our efforts be commensurate with the purposes that we have once set ourselves; otherwise man squanders the capital of his powers, which is after all very limited; we say: something goes beyond our horizon when it goes beyond the capacities of our cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s04-014: Many more things are above the learned than above the historical horizon. The former is therefore far smaller than the latter. Much that I cognize historically I cannot always cognize in a learned and beautiful manner. E.g. of the commercium animae et corporis I have indeed a historical but not a learned cognition. We must therefore not engage ourselves with all objects, but always bear in mind that we have a horizon in cognition. Thus it is also not necessary to engage in inquiry into the state of the soul after death, which is above our horizon.
blocks.blomberg-s04-015: It is very hard to determine what is properly above our horizon. If something often seems to me as if it were above my horizon, so that I even hold it for an impossibility, it can nevertheless in time, through inquiry and diligence, come under my horizon. It is the true philosophy of the lazy when one asserts of all things that they are above our horizon.
blocks.blomberg-s04-016: But if someone says: I can indeed cognize something, but I do not need it, it is superfluous to me, or even it is harmful to me, I ought not to cognize it, that means just as much as: it is above my horizon. According to taste one determines the horizon
blocks.blomberg-s04-017: 1. According to the taste of the human being.
blocks.blomberg-s04-018: 2. According to the taste of the age.
blocks.blomberg-s04-019: But if it is true that most human beings draw their horizon of cognition only according to taste, it is only a superficial cognition, in order to seem learned in everything, to be able to judge learnedly of everything. This, however, is as it were only the froth of cognition, for which a certain impudence itself is required.
blocks.blomberg-s04-020: Our age is almost such a one. But the harm of it is also unavoidable, namely that in the end all sciences are treated only superficially, according to the surface.
blocks.blomberg-s04-021: The more a science is restricted to a single aim, the greater a degree of perfection it can obtain. One would almost think in our times that everything was refined and learned. Women, instead of doing, as before, coarse housework, now read refined writings. The logical horizon with regard to our capacities is 1.) historical, which is the most extensive, and must be.
blocks.blomberg-s04-022: 2.) Rational, however, it is very narrow.
blocks.blomberg-s04-023: The historical horizon is to be cultivated especially in our youth, yet the aim must also be known according to which I acquire the historical knowledge for myself.
blocks.blomberg-s04-024: The polyhistor is he who has command of all historical cognition of all possible sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s04-025: Philosophy is the field of all historical cognition, of the theologian, physicist
blocks.blomberg-s04-026: A polyhistor brings together the materials for a science; his head is a veritable Bibliotheca. But to polyhistory there also belongs in particular philology, the science of the tools of learnedness.
blocks.blomberg-s04-027: The more perfect a science is to become in its kind, the narrower it becomes. Those who have command of all historical and all rational cognition are the great, universal minds, but there are only very few of them.
blocks.blomberg-s04-028: Everyone must think that, according to his capacities, be they great or small, he has a determinate horizon suited to them. E.g. he who knows something of geometry, supposing it is not yet much, must and can well think that finding the quadrature of the circle is beyond his horizon.
blocks.blomberg-s04-029: Our horizon of cognition changes with time. What is now above it will, when I acquire more capacities and cultivate them properly and better, in time well come to lie below it.
blocks.blomberg-s04-030: Commonly a beginner thinks that nothing is above, but everything below his horizon, that he is perfectly able to cognize and settle everything. blocks.blomberg-s04-031: How many there are also among the so-called and merely nominal philosophers who are vain of their outward glitter and quite conceited, indeed even think they are in a position to be teachers of philosophy, whereas that is very far removed from their horizon.
blocks.blomberg-s04-032: Things are lowered beneath the horizon of learned cognition when they are unworthy of our learned cognition. Some absurd opinions of the ancient philosophers are not even worthy of our historical cognition, such that we should make ourselves acquainted with them.
blocks.blomberg-s04-033: In and about nature, however, nothing in the least is unworthy of our historical cognition, unless one wanted to devote oneself to it so much that one neglects more important things on that account.
blocks.blomberg-s04-034: Delusion and methods have also brought a great deal beneath the horizon of our cognition. E.g. the examination of urine is now almost held to be indecent, owing to people's delusion, although it serves very much for the distinguishing of illnesses.
blocks.blomberg-s04-035: Things are outside the horizon of our learned cognition that are excluded because they make us neglect more important things on their account. With an unrestricted understanding nothing can be outside the horizon; rather, this occurs only with a restricted one.
blocks.blomberg-s04-036: We must deal sparingly with our capacities, so that we can also apply them to important things.
blocks.blomberg-s04-037: What therefore does not belong to the science that we have actually chosen to cultivate thoroughly is already outside our horizon, be it above or below it.
blocks.blomberg-s04-038: To occupy oneself chiefly with foreign matters, and with the neglect of more important ones, is properly called to overstep one's horizon. blocks.blomberg-s04-039: As the understanding grows, so ever more and more objects come under our horizon, and it widens little by little.
blocks.blomberg-s04-040: Rousseau says quite rightly that all who have written on education, and likewise most parents, want to make perfect men out of children, whereas they should first form a perfect child out of them. blocks.blomberg-s04-041: Within our horizon is that which is not below, or above, or outside it.

blocks.blomberg-s04-043: People of insight, who have themselves gone astray in their own way, can best determine the horizon. They will show the pupil what is necessary and what is unnecessary, and how one can very soon go astray here.
blocks.blomberg-s04-044: It is better to seek first to gain insight into very many things than to want to learn only a few, and these quite thoroughly, because the former is much easier and more attractive for a youth. It is therefore very perverse when parents want to determine their children's horizon and way of life already in the cradle, when they, e.g., want to infer from the fact that a child makes a serious face and can cry and scold lustily that it will suit the pulpit well, and, because another in his youth liked to examine, dissect and take apart all sorts of things exactly, want to conjecture from this that he must someday become a skilful anatomist.
blocks.blomberg-s04-045: Ignorance is always an imperfection, and therefore can certainly never be praiseworthy; but it can well be blameless, namely when one forgoes certain objects so as not to neglect more important cognitions on their account.
blocks.blomberg-s04-046: Leibniz could have had a blameless ignorance in many things, e.g. in chemistry, in antiquities, and in general in very many other matters that overburden a great genius all too much.
blocks.blomberg-s04-047: One can divide ignorance into the common and the learned. For a scholar to see for the first time properly that he knows nothing, great learnedness is required.
blocks.blomberg-s04-048: Quantum est quod nescimus! blocks.blomberg-s04-049: Socrates first counted it as his greatest learnedness that he saw that he knew nothing. – A beginner believes he can define and demonstrate everything, but does not at all see what a labyrinth so many matters are for him; this, however, he learns to recognize when he already possesses more learnedness. blocks.blomberg-s04-050: When one has already made many investigations, learned much, researched much, then one first learns to recognize one's ignorance. blocks.blomberg-s04-051: A cognition that is extensively great, or that comprehends very many objects within itself, the author calls a polyhistory. blocks.blomberg-s04-058: One must at all times be concerned to extend one's learned cognition. If we do not move forward, we shall certainly always move backward.

blocks.blomberg-s04-060: Certainly, we should never overload our head with learnedness and do ourselves harm, if we observe this properly and take the easy before the difficult.

blocks.blomberg-s04-064: Hippocrates says wisely: Ars longa, vita brevis. Negligent people commonly complain about the length of the time in which they still live.
