blocks.blomberg-s05-010: I think little of many objects.
blocks.blomberg-s05-011: But there is another cognition through which one cognizes much in few things. The previous fault arises for the most part from one's always thinking in abstracto, and many others arise from this. Baumgarten says: beauty is a perfectio phaenomenon, perfection in appearance. But can one really already notice beauty in objects, in cognitions, from this explanation? Because a cognition contains much under itself, it contains all the less in itself. The lack of a cognition is not always blameworthy, provided it does not contradict a purpose set. But as soon as it does, an error arises from this lack. From this it then follows of itself that those who promise to give a definition of a thing entangle themselves in the danger that even the slightest missing mark is at once imputed to them, which would not have been done to them if they had indicated that they did not want to develop the thing completely, but only to explain it in accordance with a certain consideration. It is just so with demonstrationes and proofs.
blocks.blomberg-s05-012: The limits that we set to our desire for knowledge are so necessary that without them we hardly cognize any other science properly. In order to attain to being able to cognize a cognition completely, we must therefore voluntarily impose upon ourselves, as it were, an arbitrary lack with regard to others, and to the cognition perhaps opposed to this cognition, i.e. a kind of ignorance of them, so that we may devote all diligence to this one and insight into it quite perfectly.
blocks.blomberg-s05-013: Defects, defectus, are nothing other than the limits of a thing that is to begin. They are therefore the termini, the boundaries of it, and the lack consists very well indeed with the perfection of a beginning.
blocks.blomberg-s05-014: For the estimation of cognitions acuteness does not belong at all, but only feeling. The mathematici can be very acute and yet have no taste for metaphysics, or for any other logical or moral investigation.
blocks.blomberg-s05-015: Often cognitions seem to us dry and of no use. Afterwards, when we first wander through them and penetrate into their interior, their advantages soon reveal themselves. Thus, e.g., electricity was nothing but a fine plaything; afterwards, however, its use has shown itself such that it may now serve for the cure of many an illness. Perhaps one will even be able, with the help of electricity, in time to drive away thunderstorms.
blocks.blomberg-s05-016: Euclid discovered many properties of the circle with it, and only now, in time, did one see the extensive advantages of it. Many things have been despised, and become contemptible, merely through misuse. E.g. the Wolffians spoke so long and so much about the monads that they were mocked by merry poets.
blocks.blomberg-s05-017: The expressions concerning monads, the best world, the sufficient and insufficient ground have been so dishonored by the learned rabble that one now really already hesitates to make use of them. Much that is in fact possible and good can also very soon be made ridiculous and represented as absurd.
blocks.blomberg-s05-018: Thus, e.g., Voltaire made Maupertuis's thought ridiculous when the latter is of the opinion that the Egyptians, in order to make an immortal name for themselves, should rather have buried books in the earth instead of pyramids, so that he becomes quite ridiculous, though he was perhaps one of the greatest men of his time.
blocks.blomberg-s05-019: Meanwhile, let everyone not apply his learnedness to useless objects, nor carry it along into common company, as, e.g., happened with the doctrine of the best world, which in the end people applied to everything possible.
blocks.blomberg-s05-020: Finally it is to be noted that many a thing is passed off as useless brooding because one is too weak for it and not in a position to be able to see and cognize it.
blocks.blomberg-s05-021: »As many a man often despises a beautiful woman because he cannot obtain her as he pleases, and as the fox cries out that the grapes are unripe when he cannot snatch them. –«
blocks.blomberg-s05-022: One can never, or at least very seldom, see and know in advance the whole use of this or that cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s05-023: Where did Euclid, when he discovered his propositions, ever think that from his propositions one would find out the distance of the heavenly bodies?
blocks.blomberg-s05-024: The author says that the intermediate truths must not be neglected, since they are often very necessary in the case of the main truths. Because a cognition is difficult, it is for that reason not yet to be highly esteemed.
blocks.blomberg-s05-025: Because something is imposing, it sometimes pleases, even if it is of no use. blocks.blomberg-s05-026: If many trifles come together, they finally make up a great cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s05-027: A cognition can be great on account of its many consequences, even if these consequences are not very great and correct. It is so, e.g., with the art of reckoning.
blocks.blomberg-s05-028: What is great for one is small for another. The Latin language, as well as metaphysical questions and investigations, are important and great to learned men.
blocks.blomberg-s05-029: For women, however, they are unnecessary. So too, not all cognitions are necessary for persons of rank, princes, etc.; rather, they can rely on the learned in many sciences and in many matters, just as someone who does not understand this or that single trade relies on the craftsman when he commissions him to make something. For such lords as princes etc. it would be unnecessary to enter far into metaphysica and its investigations.
blocks.blomberg-s05-030: On the other hand, one should instill in them the true learnedness that is necessary to them, that is, one should teach them preeminently and first of all justice, the worth of man, of their subjects, hatred of flatterers and of flattery, true care for the citizens of the land, and to distinguish the true advantages of the state from the false, and impress the knowledge of all this firmly upon them; then many a monarch now ill-disposed will be full of noble magnanimity and of exalted dispositions worthy of his rank. We shall have happy princes, subjects, and lands. A great mind, according to its feeling, does not busy itself with trifles; it sees what is important, and chooses it as its object.
blocks.blomberg-s06-001: The universal supreme question of one who wants to learn logica is quite natural: What is truth?
blocks.blomberg-s06-002: To answer this question, which is so fitted to the understanding of man, and especially of a beginner, will cause more difficulties than one would think, and there have already been people who well saw that one is not really in a position to give a distinct, complete, precise concept of it.
blocks.blomberg-s06-003: It has always been so: none of the ancient Roman jurists, e.g., could actually say what is right and not right (quid sit jus), and nonetheless the concept one has of it is complete for use and good enough.
blocks.blomberg-s06-004: But in order to see the difficulties that can occur with the concept of truth, we note the following. First, if a mark, criterium, of truth is to be given, a judgment of it, a rule, will have to be given. The supreme criterium therefore cannot be given.
blocks.blomberg-s06-005: If a cognition does not agree with the constitution of the thing that we represent to ourselves and want to cognize, it is false, since it cannot subsist with truth. If, on the other hand, a cognition conforms to the constitution of the thing we represent to ourselves, it is true.
blocks.blomberg-s06-006: The skeptic, however, said on the contrary: Something is true if it agrees with the object. But now I cannot see this without first considering and cognizing the object. It is therefore nothing other than that truth will consist in the cognition of the object agreeing with the cognition of the object. But this is indeed identitas, idem per idem, nothing, said the skeptics, is a circle in the explanation of truth. This argument was called diallele, and since the skeptics concluded thus, they finally derived the main conclusion from it that all distinction of the true and the false was nothing.
blocks.blomberg-s06-007: In false cognition I do not cognize and comprehend the thing itself that I want to represent to myself, but another. E.g. if I represent the polyp to myself as a worm, I have a false cognition of a polyp.
blocks.blomberg-s06-008: False learned cognitions are those that are supposed to be learned, or also seem learned, but are not so in fact. This, however, always happens when one clothes the indistinct common cognitions in termini occulti, whereby one in fact obtains no correct concept of the thing, but merely idem per idem is explained. E.g. if one asked after the cause of the propagation and multiplication of human and animal understanding, and wanted to have a distinct concept of how this came about, the ancients said with an affected learned air: the cause of the propagation of humans and animals is the vis plastica, propagating force.
blocks.blomberg-s06-009: One then imagines that one has given a real ground of the thing, and yet says nothing more than what one actually asked and wants to know, but in other words.
blocks.blomberg-s06-010: One clothes the concept of such a thing somewhat differently, puts, so to speak, a feather plume on it, and then esteems it exceedingly highly.
blocks.blomberg-s06-011: In the writings of the ancient philosophers one finds such qualitates occultas very frequently, and in the writings of Crusius they are as frequent as they ever could have been among the ancients. He says, e.g.: something is true because no one can regard and hold it otherwise than as true.
blocks.blomberg-s06-012: The one means just as much as the other; this is therefore a qualitas occulta.
blocks.blomberg-s06-013: If one now will not let oneself be asked further about the cause of this or that, one often gives a ground that is none. E.g. if I ask why one yawns and looks at another, the ancients said gravely that the ground of it is sympathy. This word, however, indicates nothing other than a fellow-feeling. They said therefore with it nothing other than that it came about because the one must have fellow-feeling with the other. But how is this applicable to yawning? Thereby, then, they explain nothing.
blocks.blomberg-s06-014: In the truth of learned cognition the formal aspect is also at issue. The cognition itself must really not be a common but rather a learned cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s06-015: The material aspect of a cognition can very often be true; the cognition can conform to the constitution of the thing, and thus have truth as a common cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s06-016: But if the same cognition is supposed to be learned without really being so, it will thereby become a false learned cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s06-017: To spread qualitates occultas is the grave of philosophy. One then believes one possesses a real learned cognition, though it is nothing other than a mere common one.
blocks.blomberg-s06-018: What Crusius says in his writings about probability pleases very many quite well. But it is in fact nothing other than what one already knows through merely common cognition, only that it is presented with a certain pomp, which is always very characteristic of Crusius.
blocks.blomberg-s06-019: Hence it follows naturally that it carries with it the semblance, but not the essence, of a learnedness and of a learned cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s06-020: The first in every matter, cognition, science, art etc. causes great difficulty.
blocks.blomberg-s06-021: Truth and error never lie in concepts, but merely in judgments. Whoever therefore never judges will also never err, but he will also never speak a truth.
blocks.blomberg-s06-022: The concept is always the datum about which I am to judge. Concepts are the materials for judging.
blocks.blomberg-s06-023: There are methods of avoiding all error, but these are so simple that for that very reason one does not heed them. They consist, however, briefly in this: do not judge so much, do not decide often, indeed very seldom, except in certain cases where it is also necessary. Do not always, and very seldom, settle whether something is true or whether it is false.
blocks.blomberg-s06-024: There is therefore, and it is necessary in order to avoid error, a certain moderation in thinking and in judging.
blocks.blomberg-s06-025: But how many philosophers of our times like always to decide.
blocks.blomberg-s06-026: To this bold assertion of opinions once adopted or hatched out by oneself, to these decisive judgments on propositions of reason, already customary in ancient times, Pyrrho cried out in opposition: »Non liquet«. – Many authors entangle themselves in such doubtful circumstances through decisive judgments and side-thoughts, which are often taken as errors.
blocks.blomberg-s06-027: A household remedy against errors is: to distinguish nothing, to judge little; hence it comes about that one finds a village full of peasants has by far not as many errors as an academy of sciences; thoughtlessness preserves them from errors.
blocks.blomberg-s06-028: Yet in order to avoid all errors we shall therefore be allowed to resolve to leave many things unweighed.
blocks.blomberg-s06-029: This tells us, and only indicates, what the limits of our judgments are, and it is precisely about these limits that one must judge. blocks.blomberg-s06-030: Ignorance is an empty space in our head and for that reason does not hinder any true knowledge, if it does not spread it. Error, on the other hand, is a hindrance to truth.
blocks.blomberg-s06-031: As long as our cognitions are only speculations, we can well still venture to err; but as soon as an error becomes harmful, and this happens as soon as it bears on the practical, it is very dangerous to retain it
blocks.blomberg-s06-032: Judgments are actions [207a] of the understanding and of reason.
blocks.blomberg-s06-033: The senses, however, do not judge; not all concepts arise from the understanding, but some from the senses; all judgments, however, come merely from the understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s06-034: Often human beings take a secure judgment of their understanding for a sensation and representation of the senses, though it is anything but that.
blocks.blomberg-s06-035: About a sensation there is no disputing. It is a datum, and not yet an error. But often such a sensation is properly the judgment of the understanding on the occasion of such sensations.
blocks.blomberg-s06-036: Appeals to such feelings and sensations are very much in fashion at present; often some want to feel and sense right and wrong in a masterly way, and indeed through an inner moral feeling peculiar to them alone. Ridiculous. In this the understanding must necessarily be in play.
blocks.blomberg-s06-037: Truth is nothing other than the agreement of a cognition with the laws of the understanding and of reason, and conversely the conflict of a cognition with the laws of the understanding and of reason is nothing other than falsity.
blocks.blomberg-s06-038: No force in nature deviates in its actions from its laws, or the conditions under which alone it can act; the understanding taken alone can therefore not possibly err.
blocks.blomberg-s06-039: All judgments agree with the laws of the understanding; all judgments of the understanding are therefore true. Even in our erroneous judgments the understanding must always have done something, and so it can never be that everything in them is false, but there must still always be something true.
blocks.blomberg-s06-040: It is quite impossible for a human being to err wholly when he judges.
blocks.blomberg-s06-041: In error there is therefore still truth. But we judge there in a mixed way, and intermingle the effects of the remaining powers of the mind, and from this arises the erroneous, which is so very contrary to the understanding, and of which we nonetheless falsely think, and often believe quite certainly, that it is an effect of the understanding. Whereas it is in fact nothing other than, as it were, a bastard of sensibility and the understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s06-042: Since, then, as we have already shown, every judgment does not take place without an ingrediens of truth, it follows necessarily from this that we shall have to moderate very much our judgment on the criticam of truth, and on the judgments or also errors of others. For it is a certain principium: one can never come to truth if one is always disputing, if one is always contradicting the other.
blocks.blomberg-s06-043: Every discovery of an error that is in fact gross and manifest is very sad. One would therefore rather not make such sad discoveries, but help one another jointly and in a friendly spirit, support one another, and not always act one against the other.
blocks.blomberg-s06-044: Instead of refuting a thing, one will therefore have merely to examine it, whether there does not really lie truth in it, what is lacking to supplement it, and so to act jointly everywhere, and then to make it comprehensible to the one who errs in a way that bites least, but is rather loving, how it is not at all to be wondered at, since he could very easily and gladly have erred.
blocks.blomberg-s06-045: This moderate way of judging, this well-applied good-heartedness of dispositions, is just as necessary for the attainment of upright cognition as it ever may be in common life.
blocks.blomberg-s06-046: But naturally, therefore, there is no total error. Otherwise the understanding would have to contradict itself and its prescriptions, and to act against them.
blocks.blomberg-s06-047: Errors, however great and important they may seem, are nonetheless all only particular.
blocks.blomberg-s06-048: One can instruct no one except through the remainder of understanding that is still in him. One can improve no one himself except through the remainder of the good that is still in him.
blocks.blomberg-s06-049: In the instruction of the understanding and improvement of the will I must in any case still always presuppose something true and something good.
blocks.blomberg-s06-050: Every other human being's judgment is after all always a judgment of one of those human beings whose judgments all taken together are my judge, and the greatest assessor of all my products of understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s06-051: A contradiction is indeed nothing other than an occurrence in which the one says: yes, but the other, on the contrary: No.
blocks.blomberg-s06-052: It follows therefore that it must naturally disquiet every rational person to a certain extent. But it is a universal duty of a philosopher, in a case of this kind, always to take the part of humanity in general, and to think benignly thus: these opinions that seem so bizarre and absurd are perhaps not at all so badly thought, not so absurd as they may well seem.
blocks.blomberg-s06-053: Everything that makes human beings united and agreeable contributes really very much to promoting the perfection of the whole human race. Conflict, however, brings nothing forth. It holds everywhere, and so too in the whole world among the learned:
blocks.blomberg-s06-056: Furthermore, the limits, i.e. the narrow boundaries by which the human understanding is surrounded, are not in the least to be regarded as sources of errors, as so many supposed philosophers hold them to be; indeed they are in fact causes of man's ignorance in many respects, but not of error; but as soon as a conceit, a presumption, a learned arrogance of judging more than one knows and is in a position to, combines with this ignorance, error can arise from it.
blocks.blomberg-s06-057: The sole cause of error is therefore the ill-applied presumption of overstepping the limits and boundaries of one's own understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s06-058: The understanding alone does not err. The senses alone also do not err; they are passive, and do not judge at all.
blocks.blomberg-s06-060: There must therefore also be certain materialia, stuffs, for judging.
blocks.blomberg-s06-061: The understanding must necessarily combine with sensibility in order to be able to judge, and this does not depend in the least on choice
blocks.blomberg-s06-062: There are therefore naturally also subjective conditions of our understanding and of thinking, and these we reckon all to sensibility.
blocks.blomberg-s06-063: Sometimes the understanding is, as it were, in a certain way at a loss. blocks.blomberg-s06-064: To every distinguishing of the true from the false there belongs cognition by inner sense, i.e. I must be and become conscious of what actually lies in my concept, and what I think.
blocks.blomberg-s06-065: Inner sense is often dull, and its horizon clouded, and does not give us help enough.
blocks.blomberg-s06-066: But since inner sense also belongs to sensibility, and without it the understanding cannot judge, the understanding must judge by the help of sensibility, and precisely this combination and intermingling of the understanding with sensibility is the source of all errors, namely when the effects of the understanding are held to be effects of sensibility.
blocks.blomberg-s06-067: As we thus see, the understanding and sensibility alone cannot err; so we see how an error is possible.
blocks.blomberg-s06-068: All errors are, so to speak, curved lines, which we determine by being driven on the one side by the understanding, but on the other side by error.
blocks.blomberg-s06-069: We see before us the play of the things of the world, but we do not on that account yet have a complete concept of their motion.
blocks.blomberg-s06-070: The senses do not judge. Inner sense, which alone teaches us by what means we become aware whether we have all the requisita of cognition or not, does not always do us the right service, and from this then arises the appearance as if something were lacking to the objects themselves for their cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s06-071: One can, e.g., have correct rules for reckoning, and nevertheless fail in carrying them out. There it is commonly a fault of inner sense; this happens through oversight.
blocks.blomberg-s06-072: The only means of avoiding error will therefore be that I find out certain criteria by which I can properly distinguish, in every judgment, what stems from the understanding from what the outer or inner senses supply to us.

blocks.blomberg-s06-076: The former are objective; they contain the ground why something is properly true or false. The latter, however, are subjective; they contain certain circumstances by which one is in a position to presume truth or falsity in a thing.
blocks.blomberg-s06-077: That by which true cognitions are distinguished from false ones is the mark of truth
blocks.blomberg-s06-078: The proposition of identity is the formal mark of truth in affirmative judgments, and the Principium Contradictionis in negative judgments.
blocks.blomberg-s06-079: Material marks are the Notae intermediae, by which I prove a judgment, the Principia materialia.
blocks.blomberg-s06-080: In a simple and wholly simple Idea neither truth nor falsity is naturally to be found; rather, it occurs only in comparison.
blocks.blomberg-s06-081: When I attribute to the thing a mark that either contradicts it or is even wholly contrary to it, or deny of it a mark that is nonetheless identical in it.
blocks.blomberg-s06-082: That, however, by which I recognize that the comparison with a thing is right or not is called the Nota intermedia (Principium materiale), e.g. if I want to prove that a body is divisible, I assume a Nota intermedia, that it is composite, and infer in the following way: everything that is composite is divisible, atqui every body is composite, ergo every body is divisible.
blocks.blomberg-s06-083: Some propositions are so constituted that they have no material mark of truth at all, but carry only the formal one with them. These are properly the immediate judgments that we have of a thing, which we cannot prove or derive from anything further. E.g. that a body is composite.
blocks.blomberg-s06-084: Simple concepts have the mark that they are always true. E.g. if I represent the moon to myself as round, this is a true concept, because I actually think it so.
blocks.blomberg-s06-085: But if I compare this representation of the moon with the representation of other planets and doubt whether the moon is round or oval, then I can very easily err in this, and my cognition can be true as well as false.
blocks.blomberg-s06-086: Among all marks of truth, the first inner indication, or chief mark, of it is inner possibility.
blocks.blomberg-s06-087: Through experience we are instructed about the possibility of many things that one would otherwise really not have held to be possible.
blocks.blomberg-s06-088: Possibility is nevertheless still far from a sufficient ground of truth: because something is possible, and because we can represent it well to ourselves and think it through our reason, it is not yet actually true.
blocks.blomberg-s06-089: Yet possibility is at least a ground of probability: if something is possible and can be thought by us, we at least believe and hope that it could be true, supposing that we are not in a position to assert it with certainty.
blocks.blomberg-s06-090: Impossibility, on the contrary, is always a sufficient and Sufficient ground for the infallible proof of the untruth or falsity of a thing.
blocks.blomberg-s06-091: If we see that something is entirely impossible, we commonly also hold it at once to be false.
blocks.blomberg-s06-092: Yet it is to be remarked here that we can err in both cases. We very often hold something to be useful, and per Consequentiam also true and correct, which, when we examine it more closely, is actually entirely impossible and false. And conversely we hold many a thing to be impossible and false that is actually possible and at the same time true, or, if not true, at least useful.
blocks.blomberg-s06-093: If the consequences of a cognition are true, then the cognitions themselves are also true. E.g. It is true, and settled for all, that there are fire-spewing mountains, warm baths, etc. Just as this is true, so it may well also be true that there is a central fire in the earth.
blocks.blomberg-s06-094: With some ground we can indeed always infer from this to the central fire of the earth, for these fire-spewing mountains, warm baths, etc. can with much conjecture, indeed even probability, be regarded as consequences of such a central fire, and from the consequences one can very often infer correctly to the ground.
blocks.blomberg-s06-095: If all consequences of a cognition without exception are true, then the cognition too is certainly true. For if even some falsity were to be found in the cognition, falsity would also have to lie already in the consequences. But if this is not so, nothing in the cognition can be false.
blocks.blomberg-s06-096: If, for example, a fortunate engagement is announced to us in the newspapers and the victory of a hero is made known; if its publication even takes place from the pulpit, if solemn arrangements are made and thanksgiving feasts held on account of it; in short, if all its consequences are true, then the engagement itself must also be true.
blocks.blomberg-s06-097: Sometimes, however, we cannot cognize all the consequences of a thing, and then some false ones may well sometimes have been mixed in among them and be present, even though we hold the cognition itself to be true. E.g. if we assume the central fire to be found in the earth, it will follow from this in turn that the strata of the earth that lay not very far from this central fire would be entirely parched and ruined by excessively great and violent heat, and would finally even have to collapse into one another.
blocks.blomberg-s06-098: But since, as one readily sees, this consequence is false, it is also quite easy to notice that the central fire too cannot be held to be wholly beyond doubt certain, and cannot be reliably asserted.
blocks.blomberg-s06-099: If a cognition is to be possible in connection, it must have correct grounds and weighty, also true, consequences.
blocks.blomberg-s06-100: The cognition of the possibility of a thing arises from experience; reason cannot instruct us about it. E.g. that the magnet attracts iron.
blocks.blomberg-s06-101: The possibility of composite bodies we can see through reason, if we are convinced of the possibility of simple effects.
blocks.blomberg-s06-102: But the first possibility of causes and effects becomes evident solely through the senses from experience. Hence reason also raises no objection against the impossibility of a thing whose possibility or actual existence we clearly see through experience. For experience, through the actuality of a thing, naturally also instructs us about its possibility.
blocks.blomberg-s06-103: Reason, however, can derive from these examples of experience certain laws of the possibility of this or that thing, but the first Principia Data and Materialia of possibility must necessarily be given to us from experience and arise from it.
blocks.blomberg-s06-104: But we must not hold something to be impossible because we cannot think it or represent it through the senses: e.g. one born blind cannot make for himself through reason any representation of colors, because experience denies him the Data for it; nonetheless he can and may not at all infer to their impossibility. blocks.blomberg-s06-105: There are logical truths. These are those that relate merely to understanding and reason.
blocks.blomberg-s06-106: On the other side, however, we can also think of an aesthetic and a practical truth. The former relates to the relation of taste, the latter, on the contrary, to the rules of the free will.
blocks.blomberg-s06-107: But logical truth is not always aesthetically true, nor does it always bring practical perfection with it.
blocks.blomberg-s06-108: Every truth is always in itself a logical perfection, or a perfect cognition, according to the rules of the understanding and of reason.
blocks.blomberg-s06-109: Much can be aesthetically true without being logically true; it need only charm and please. E.g. so it is with novels.
blocks.blomberg-s06-110: Even practical truth need not always be grounded on understanding and reason. E.g. if I slander someone to another, I can thereby arouse his affects, and in such a way his will, although this slander is not logically true.
blocks.blomberg-s06-111: Logical truth is distinguished from aesthetic truth in that, when something delights and moves me, I can relax somewhat about its truth. Logical truth can thus very often yield to the aesthetic.
blocks.blomberg-s06-112: Truth often does not please us most; rather, even the lie does. We are far happier in fables than in logical truths. Whoever, e.g., takes nature as his ground in painting does not always accord with delight, charm, and pleasure. Fiction often moves much more.
blocks.blomberg-s06-113: Our wishes often belong among the fictiones. They often aim at something better than what nature actually offers us. So, e.g., enthusiasm in friendship pleases us, and we are moved by the earthly pastoral life. It is indeed true that in aesthetic truth too there must always be a certain logical truth, but the more we look to the aesthetic true, the less logical truth can be found in the subject that we want to represent to ourselves. So, e.g., it is aesthetically true that man, when he is dead, will not rise again. Although this runs directly counter to logical (not to mention moral) truth.
blocks.blomberg-s06-114: What all men say is true according to the rules of taste, and thus aesthetically true. For a universal Consensus is sufficient for that. Meanwhile, what is true according to the rules of taste is very often false according to the rules of reason.

blocks.blomberg-s07-001: All grounds of cognition are either inner or outer. blocks.blomberg-s07-013: 1: The marks that I cognize of a thing are internal when I consider the thing solely and merely in itself.

blocks.blomberg-s07-019: But absolute knowledge of things is far more difficult than the cognitions one acquires through comparisons. For the latter are far easier and more natural to us, because it already lies, as it were, in our nature that, in comparison with others, we become aware far more easily of agreement or difference in objects, and are able to notice it. Thus, e.g., ugliness en comparaison with a beauty, and a true beauty, strike the eye when she is found among many ugly persons, and the human being himself, when he undertakes an appraisal of himself, mostly asks not how good he is and how much he still lacks, but rather whether he is not as good as, or perhaps even better than, others. Hence it comes about that Herr von Wolff, and even our author, hold marks and characteristics to be one and the same.
blocks.blomberg-s07-020: In the beginning it is mostly so that most things are held to be, if not wholly the same, then at least only very slightly different; with time the differences gradually come to light, and the more one attends to the things, the more and more marks are also found. But this gradual search for the marks of a thing also requires much subtlety of understanding, just as it does in order to be able to find, among things where the greatest differences seem to be, or really are, nevertheless a certain similarity, a sameness, and agreement.
blocks.blomberg-s07-021: In this § the author speaks of mediate and immediate marks. If a thing can be cognized through a certain mark without the mediation of a mark that is different from it, then this is an immediate mark. A mediate mark, on the other hand, is a mark of a mark: e.g., perishability is a mark of the human being, but an immediate one, for perishability is a mark of a mortal being, i.e., of a body, but the human being is mortal and has a body.
blocks.blomberg-s07-022: There are therefore degrees of remote marks, and so there are degrees of mediate marks. The first degree is: when a thing can be cognized only through a nota intermedia. But among all marks, of which one is the mark of the other, a relation of subordination is always to be found. But there is also a relation of coordination, and this occurs with immediate marks, where each particular mark is a new ground of cognition of the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-023: Through experience we cannot become aware of, and cognize, anything other than coordinated, i.e., juxtaposed, marks of a thing. But reason alone is able to supply us with subordinated marks of a thing, i.e., to present to us series of marks.
blocks.blomberg-s07-024: With the subordination of marks I have nothing more than a single immediate mark, and the remaining Notae are marks of marks. But with the Coordinatio Notarum all marks are immediate.
blocks.blomberg-s07-025: In the series of the subordinated, i.e., of marks subordinated to one another, there is always a first, i.e., the concepts are limited.
blocks.blomberg-s07-026: But in coordination there is no limitation.
blocks.blomberg-s07-027: There are countless marks that belong immediately to a thing, and our understanding is not able to see into all properties and to determine them exactly.
blocks.blomberg-s07-028: In subordination the immediate mark is called Nota infima, and the last mark of all marks is called the Nota Summa.
blocks.blomberg-s07-029: Through the subordination of marks I obtain a deep, i.e., intensive magnitude; through the coordination of marks Notarum, however, one attains an extensive magnitude, i.e., a cognition worked out according to its ground and extensive.
blocks.blomberg-s07-030: The series of marks coordinated with one another is, as it were, a line without boundaries, which is infinite; for it is still always possible, indeed to be presumed, that posterity will in time still be able to discover ever more immediate marks of a thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-031: But the series of marks subordinated to one another is bounded and has its limits, and indeed often very soon, when no mark of a mark can be given in it any more.
blocks.blomberg-s07-032: Metaphysica is that science by means of which we seek out the Terminum a priori of the subordinated marks. Through it we obtain simple and irresolvable concepts.
blocks.blomberg-s07-033: Too much beauty also does harm and really arouses suspicion. Beautiful simplicity is often found through nature. But the greatest art consists in concealing the art that is actually applied somewhere in such a way that it is not noticeable at all, but seems to be pure nature.
blocks.blomberg-s07-034: Profundity is in a certain way opposed to beauty; cognition becomes dry the more it is abstracted. Merely abstract cognitions in general cannot be fully understood unless I present and see into a case in Concreto. But the dry also often falls into the droll, and this often requires art: thus, e.g., with witty remarks in company; and one is accustomed to call this simplicity.
blocks.blomberg-s07-035: In all description one seeks more to understand the thing than to see into it. But in all explanation, conversely, one seeks more to see into the thing than to understand it.
blocks.blomberg-s07-036: The multitude of marks coordinated with one another increases experience.
blocks.blomberg-s07-037: The extensive magnitude of a cognition is, as it were, its volumen, but the intensive magnitude is its density. In certain cases the extensive magnitude of cognition is more useful, in others the intensive. In morals, e.g., the intensive magnitude of a cognition is more necessary, but in Physica and medicine the extensive magnitude of cognition is very often more indispensable.
blocks.blomberg-s07-038: Dry cognitions are not at all suited to sensibility, and therefore not to beauty either. But thorough, deep, solid cognitions can and must be dry without reproach. This dryness, however, one compensates for when one considers the abstract in concreto in a certain case. (Analysis proceeds ascendendo, but synthesis descendendo.)
blocks.blomberg-s07-039: Through negative marks of a thing I think to myself something that is not actually to be found in the thing. Through affirmative marks, however, I think to myself that which is in fact present in the thing. But negative marks are possible only in that one first represents to oneself the marks opposed to them, which are affirmative. Thus, e.g., I cannot know what darkness is unless I first have a clear Idea of light.
blocks.blomberg-s07-040: But negative marks serve only to avoid errors. E.g., animals have no rational soul. But affirmative marks serve to obtain an extensive, unelaborated cognition of a thing. E.g., God is omniscient, etc. Gold loses nothing of its massa and weight in fire, is ductile.
blocks.blomberg-s07-041: Besides ignorance there is another, still more dangerous evil in the understanding, and this is error. Through affirmative marks we avoid ignorance, but through negative marks, error. This is the purpose of both kinds of marks. Through negative marks one admittedly obtains no new cognition at all; nonetheless they are altogether very necessary and important, for one guards oneself thereby against erroneous cognitions.
blocks.blomberg-s07-042: The fewer means we have at hand to arrive at true cognitions, the more negative marks we shall need in order not to err in the cognition of the thing. Thus, e.g., in no science is there a greater multitude of negative marks than in rational theology, in natural Theologia. For in it we have no means at all at hand to arrive at extended cognitions. Thus, e.g., we are at every moment inclined to err in the concept, Idea, and representation of the divine being and of God himself in general, because we are very fond of comparing him sensibly with the things we perceive on earth, but these can be no measure of God at all. God, after all, cannot be cognized by us through the senses, and consequently our whole knowledge of him can only be very much limited.
blocks.blomberg-s07-043: If, therefore, we consider God in Theologia naturali and take away all the negative marks through which we speak of him, nothing will remain for us but the Idea of the most sufficient and most perfect being.
blocks.blomberg-s07-044: Negative judgments are really often foolish, because that which is denied is often already impossible in itself. E.g.: the human being has reason, therefore he is no stone. It is true, that is an established truth that no one will doubt. But because it is also obvious that no one will let it occur to him to take a human being seriously for a stone, this judgment is in vain.
blocks.blomberg-s07-045: Every mark is a ground of cognition, which is estimated by its consequences. Now according as the consequences are of worth with respect to reason or to our perfection and happiness, so too the marks as grounds of cognition will be of worth.
blocks.blomberg-s07-046: From the former consequences the logical worth of the marks is to be derived, from the latter consequences the practical worth.
blocks.blomberg-s07-047: If many consequences are to be derived from one ground, then it is fruitful, or it has an extensive magnitude; e.g., from the sun many consequences flow with respect to the earth. So the rules of morals are very fruitful, in that they have an influence on our life, i.e., on our conduct, which is very great.
blocks.blomberg-s07-048: A mark is extensively great if I can cognize many consequences of a thing. But a mark is intensively great when I can cognize from a thing not so much many as great and important consequences. The former mark is called fruitful, the latter, however, correct.
blocks.blomberg-s07-049: Empty speculations have a logical worth. They are often of many consequences with respect to reason, although they admittedly have no influence on the happiness of human beings, e.g., that the moon is inhabited, etc. This proposition has no influence on the will, on the state, etc. No one becomes more perfect, happier, or better with respect to his outer understanding through this cognition, although with respect to his reason he becomes somewhat more perfect.
blocks.blomberg-s07-050: Other cognitions are aesthetically correct because they stimulate our taste and pleasure, e.g., poetry delights because it is in accordance with our taste. But all importance of cognition exists only when it is considered by itself alone, without comparison with other cognitions.
blocks.blomberg-s07-051: The marks either suffice for our purposes, and then they are comparative Sufficientes; or suffice to distinguish a thing from all others, thus for all logical purposes, and then they are Notae absolute Sufficientes.
blocks.blomberg-s07-052: All experiences have only a relative Sufficientiam. E.g., if I look closely at a pear tree, I can easily distinguish its leaves from the leaves of all other trees in the forest. This cognition is therefore sufficient in relation to other cognitions.
blocks.blomberg-s07-053: The Sufficientia relativa, or comparativa, suffices to distinguish a thing from such things as we have merely known up to now, but not from all things that are possible, that could ever exist. E.g., gold is distinguished from all other metals by its weight, but one has already discovered a metal called platina, which is of white color but has in itself the same weight as gold. Consequently this mark, and ground of distinction, of gold from all other metals is not sufficient enough.
blocks.blomberg-s07-054: Things that fall within our senses can be cognized and distinguished only through marks that are sufficient relatively, but not by means of such marks as suffice absolutely.
blocks.blomberg-s07-058: The former consists in the marks of a thing being sufficient to distinguish it from other things through comparison. The latter, however, consists in one mark of a thing sufficing to derive from it all the other determinations of the same. From this Sufficientia arises the division of grounds of cognition into
blocks.blomberg-s07-060: From the latter one can derive nothing, e.g., gold has a yellow color, the human being is an animal that laughs. But the former are fruitful, so that much flows from them.
blocks.blomberg-s07-061: External grounds of cognition can often be very important in themselves, but with respect to internal sufficiency be unfruitful and useless.
blocks.blomberg-s07-062: Necessary marks are such ad Essentiam pertinentia, without which the thing cannot be thought at all. Pertinent autem ad Essentiam 1: vel Solum ut Causae aut 2: ut Causata

blocks.blomberg-s07-064: extension B. Attributa. E.g., the divisibility of bodies. Contingent marks, however, are Extra Essentialia, without which the thing can nevertheless be thought, e.g., learnedness in a human being.
blocks.blomberg-s07-065: If the Essentialia are marks, then they are not subordinated to one another but coordinated; the attributa, however, are not coordinated with the Essentialibus but subordinated, for they follow from one another.

blocks.blomberg-s07-068: The latter are also called relations. But the internal ones are again
blocks.blomberg-s07-072: 1. Complete, or marks that are sufficient to derive from them everything that is contained in the thing, or
blocks.blomberg-s07-073: 2: incomplete. When the marks do not suffice to derive and cognize from them everything that belongs to the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-074: The internal contingent relations are called Modi. The modification of the external relations does not modify the human being himself, although among the things of nature a change of relation also seems for the most part to be connected at the same time with a change of modification.
blocks.blomberg-s07-075: Summer and winter are strictly speaking no changes in the sun itself, but only altered Relationes, and relations of the sun to our earth.
blocks.blomberg-s07-076: Modi are nothing other than internal determinations and changes that can be thought in a thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-077: Relationes, however, are: changes that occur with a thing in relation to others, and in reference to other things.
blocks.blomberg-s07-078: But we now raise the question whether, with the Completudo Notarum, necessaria interna, a Praecision cannot also take place, so that superfluous marks are found in it which are no longer necessary to distinguish the thing from all others and to derive from it all the proper determinations, so that everything is omitted which, even if it is lacking, is nevertheless so constituted that even without it the concept will still be complete?
blocks.blomberg-s07-079: Responsio Yes. It often works. The Nota,e Rei necessariae internae Sufficientes constitute the Praecision.
blocks.blomberg-s07-080: If the marks contain no less than is necessary for the distinction of the thing, then this is a Praecision.
blocks.blomberg-s07-081: If, finally, the marks of a thing are wholly commensurate with it, then they are Notae adaequatae.
blocks.blomberg-s07-082: The adequate concept of a thing, insofar as it can no longer be derived from any other, is the concept of the essence, Essentia.
blocks.blomberg-s07-083: The essence of a thing is the first sufficient fundamental concept, which suffices to derive everything that belongs to the former.
blocks.blomberg-s07-086: The former constitute the Essentialia, the latter the attributa. E.g., in the triangle the 3 angles are just as necessary and indispensable as the 3 sides. But the former one derives in turn from the latter, and they are therefore attributa; the sides themselves, however, are fundamental concepts, Essentialia.
blocks.blomberg-s07-087: In order to cognize what is essential to a thing, the following is necessary: in order to cognize the attributa I must cognize the internal necessary marks, which, however, are accompanied by others. But in order to cognize the Essentialia I must see that the marks can no longer be derived from any other; in order to cognize the Essentia itself I must know that the marks, and Essentialia, are complete and, taken together, sufficient for the cognition of the whole.
blocks.blomberg-s07-088: The coordination of marks that is complete constitutes the Completudo.
blocks.blomberg-s07-089: The fundamental concept of all that is necessary to a thing is its essence. To investigate the essence of things, this is the business and the purpose of philosophy.
blocks.blomberg-s07-090: The marks which, taken together, constitute the essence of a thing are the Essentialia. The consequences, the Rationata sive consectaria, from the essence, those are the Attributa. Modi sunt Notae internae, quarum possibilitas tantum per Essentiam determinatur.
blocks.blomberg-s07-091: The Modi are therefore not rationata Essentiae with regard to their truth, but only with regard to their possibility. Modi are therefore nothing other than contingent marks.
blocks.blomberg-s07-092: Modi as well as relationes do not belong to the essence at all, ad Essentiam non pertinent, neither as constitutiva nor as attributa.
blocks.blomberg-s07-093: All marks of a thing belong either to the essence of a thing, Essentialia, or not Essentialia: ad Essentiam pertinentia sunt vel Essentialia, vel attributa. Extraessentialia autem sunt vel notae, sive notae internae, vel relationes, sive Notae Externae, quarum Possibilitas tantum per essentiam determinatur.
blocks.blomberg-s07-097: The complete fundamental concept of a thing is in general its essence.
blocks.blomberg-s07-098: But the first ground of everything that is thought by me in the concept of the thing is the logical essence. The first fundamental concept, however, of all that belongs to the thing truly and in fact is the real essence.
blocks.blomberg-s07-099: From this it follows naturally that the logical and the real essence must necessarily be very different from one another.
blocks.blomberg-s07-100: When I utter words and connect a certain concept with them, then what I think in connection with this word and expression is the logical essence. E.g., when I utter the word matter, then everything that is inseparable from the concept which I connect with the expression matter is the logical essence of matter. The logical essence one can always represent and think by itself alone. Thus, e.g., with matter I always think an extension, an impenetrability, a certain constant inertia and lifelessness, so that it is not able to change its place or to move of itself, but only through the addition of another, foreign force.
blocks.blomberg-s07-101: All this are the Essentialia of the word matter, and consequently, taken together, constitute its logical essence.
blocks.blomberg-s07-102: The subjective fundamental concept is that which is contained in an internal concept of the thing. But this does not yet prove that more marks can be present in the object; rather I connect with the thing only what I represent to myself. Hence, e.g., with the word matter still more other properties can take place.
blocks.blomberg-s07-103: The logical essence is the subjective fundamental concept. But this concept is valid only for me, and not for others. Another can represent to himself more or fewer marks with the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-104: The essence of our concept is not always, indeed seldom, the essence of the thing itself.
blocks.blomberg-s07-105: The logical essence is far smaller than the real essence. The logical essence is a concentrated fundamental concept of a thing; it comprehends in itself only what we represent to ourselves in the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-106: This contracting, combining of concepts is really very suited to the human understanding, and quite necessary; it must deal sparingly with its powers; such a compendium, however, is just as good as an extended concept of the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s07-107: The real essence comprehends in itself, in general, everything that can ever actually belong to a thing. This Eduction is the only means of making our concepts quite distinct.
blocks.blomberg-s07-108: But distinctness is one of the most essential logical perfections. Through this my cognition becomes far more serviceable for use, but through the real essence it becomes more extended.
blocks.blomberg-s07-109: But the logical essence must not be confused with the real essence. For in my concept that I have of the thing I do not yet think to myself everything that lies in the thing and belongs to it, or can lie in it and belong to it. E.g., if we take the concept of matter, more recent Philosophi have discovered that the force of attraction still lies in the essence of matter; this property I would certainly never have thought to myself at once with the word matter, and perhaps far more marks that have not yet been discovered, and which only a philosopher will cognize, can belong to matter.
blocks.blomberg-s07-110: From this it is evident that infinitely more is contained in the real essence than in the logical essence.
blocks.blomberg-s07-111: Of no single object of experience or even of the senses can we properly cognize the real, or objective, essence. At most it is possible for us to see into its logical or subjective essence properly.
blocks.blomberg-s07-112: What we think in connection with the word of a thing is very small and slight, indeed often very little; but all that which really, revera, belongs to a thing is often immeasurable and cannot be determined at all.
blocks.blomberg-s07-113: To seek out the real essence of concepts of experience, and of objects, is therefore a wholly vain endeavor, but one can well represent the logical essence of concepts of reason and clarify it properly for oneself.
blocks.blomberg-s07-114: Our concepts of experience are very changeable, because our experience is extended more and more daily. The logical essence is therefore also very variable and changeable, because with the concept of a thing one, in time, thinks ever more determinations
blocks.blomberg-s07-115: to oneself. But all moral concepts are pure concepts of the understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s07-116: That is to say, there are such pure concepts of the understanding which have their origin not from experience but solely from pure reason. Whoever wants to find the real essence must know all the marks that belong constantly to the thing. Then he must further seek out their ground and be at pains to investigate it, and this is then the real essence. E.g., a body that grows through internal unfolding belongs to the logical essence of a plant. But the fundamental concept of its constant determination is the real essence, to which it may also belong that plants beget their like.
blocks.blomberg-s07-117: The concept that water is a fluid element, without smell and taste, 14 times lighter than quicksilver, etc., is the logical essence of water, for if I am somewhat versed in physical knowledge, then I think all of this as soon as I name the word water. From this I cannot by any means derive all the remaining properties which are determined for water, belong to it or can belong to it, and perhaps are not yet all discovered, although we do not think them along with it at all times; consequently it is not yet the real essence.
blocks.blomberg-s07-118: Of individual things we can never give the real essence, but we can of the Genera, e.g., of body in general.
blocks.blomberg-s07-119: Nevertheless we do not know all the concepts and determinations of all things that can belong to them constantly, and then we are also not at all times able to give at once the true ground of all these determinations; we can consequently only very seldom indicate their real essence.
blocks.blomberg-s07-120: Here the clear and obscure cognition is spoken of. The author first dealt with confused and distinct concepts in the first section of the Logica, without first thinking of clear and obscure cognition. How then does it come about that he now begins to speak of it?
blocks.blomberg-s07-121: Responsio: the concept of clear and obscure cognition is, at the beginning of logic, something that can be assumed without proof, and so must be presupposed and laid at the ground. But here one can already derive it again from what has been treated beforehand.
blocks.blomberg-s07-122: Here it is therefore just the reverse. But a representation is obscure (to return to our subject) of which one is not immediately conscious. Mediately, however, one can indeed become conscious of this cognition by means of reason, and so there remains a way to make an otherwise obscure cognition nevertheless [329 (339)] clear, distinct, and thus its insight easier. E.g., with the naked eye, when I look at the Milky Way, I see nothing there but a white streak; but if I take the telescope to help, then I at once become aware of its individual parts as individual stars, and I judge at once by means of reason that these must be the very same stars which I saw with the naked eye only as a mere white streak. Of this representation I am thus conscious mediately, but immediately not: so it is at first only obscure, but afterwards mediate distinct, or clear.
blocks.blomberg-s07-123: A cognition is either obscure in and for itself, so that, despite all effort applied, it cannot become clear at all; or it is relatively obscure, so that in certain circumstances it can become clear, but in others not.
blocks.blomberg-s07-124: But the former, cognition obscure in itself, is, according to its description, wholly impossible, for everything can become clear, however difficult it may seem to us; and what seems to us most obscure is, when we investigate it, always only relatively obscure.
blocks.blomberg-s07-125: Logic prescribes to us the rules which we are to apply in order to know how we should proceed with cognitions of which we are conscious that we really possess them.
blocks.blomberg-s07-126: All clarity is the right way to arrive at distinctness. But clarity itself is not yet a logical perfection, which distinctness nevertheless is. Logic therefore already presupposes clarity, it supposes it and does not itself bring it forth; it deals with cognitions and representations already made clear.
blocks.blomberg-s07-127: Distinctness is therefore also not the proper object of its occupation. Distinctness, Disjunctio, is to be well distinguished
blocks.blomberg-s07-128: from evidentness, Dispicuitaet. Insofar as clarity of the marks takes place in a cognition, to that extent the cognition is distinct.
blocks.blomberg-s07-129: But a cognition is brought into Perspicuum only when it is so bright and clear that even the slightest understanding sees into it; imperspicua, or non perspicua, on the other hand, is a cognition when it is too great for the whole horizon of the whole human race, when it can be called incomprehensible. Perspicuitaet, on the other hand, means nothing other than comprehensibility.
blocks.blomberg-s07-130: often a cognition ceases to be comprehensible in the degree to which it ought to become really distinct. But this cannot be avoided at all, without not speaking of the thing at all.
blocks.blomberg-s07-131: If we now go back to the distinction of clear and obscure cognition, we have further to remark: but all obscure cognitions can be
blocks.blomberg-s07-133: B) Subjectively obscure; if we are to say it properly, the former does not take place, but only the latter.
blocks.blomberg-s07-134: But if the relation of a thing to the limits of human cognition is so constituted that it cannot be cognized clearly enough but always remains obscure, one mostly ascribes all the blame not to him who does not cognize the thing clearly enough, but to the thing itself or to him who presents it; whereas it often lies more with the former than with the latter. One then calls this cognition, which the other does not see into and cannot see into, objectively obscure. But a cognition is subjectively obscure when the fault, that the thing remains obscure despite all effort applied, lies not with the thing and cognition itself but with the one who wants to cognize something, namely because he either possesses a great ignorance and is therefore naturally not able to cognize the thing, or also because he does not apply the diligence required for it at all sufficiently.
blocks.blomberg-s07-135: But this latter obscurity is not founded at all in the nature of the cognition itself, or even, as some hold, in that of all human beings and their understanding. For if this were to take place, then the cognition could not be clearly cognized by a single human being; rather it lies solely either in the incapacity and ignorance, or in the negligence, of this or that individual subject.
blocks.blomberg-s07-136: Hence it comes about that the same cognition which is clear to one subject can be obscure to another, and, conversely, the very same cognition which is obscure to one subject can be clear to another.
blocks.blomberg-s07-137: Few human beings even have a proper concept of what it means to have a proper clear concept of a thing, or cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s07-138: No human being can, so to speak, any longer properly understand himself; he always judges that everything he says is perfectly clear to him, and just hence it comes about that he is also prevented from properly examining whether he understands himself properly or not.
blocks.blomberg-s07-139: Metaphysica and morals, these 2 pure sciences of philosophy, are of such a kind and so constituted that the human being is never able to represent distinctly to himself the slightest concept in them unless he can first acquire for himself a complete and full concept of the whole, i.e., of the whole science.
blocks.blomberg-s07-140: Either someone who wants to study Metaphysica has a quite pure, quite distinct concept of it, or he knows nothing at all of it. There are only these two ways; there is no middle course between them at all.
blocks.blomberg-s07-141: On the other hand, someone can be very comprehensible, especially if he knows nothing yet, or at least no errors, and he who hears him goes away again just as clever as he came to him; this is very easy, and such a presentation, which harms nothing but also benefits nothing, can also be very comprehensible and graspable.
blocks.blomberg-s07-142: It is therefore not possible in some cases to combine easy comprehensibility with complete distinctness, and those certainly judge wrongly who hold the easiest presentation to be the best, and who regard a somewhat harder, less childish presentation, arranged to prompt reflection, as obscure, unintelligible, indeed exaggerated.
blocks.blomberg-s07-143: To make the obscure clear is so difficult that no human being has yet discovered a universally valid means for it.
blocks.blomberg-s07-144: Exhaustiveness is the sufficiency of a cognition for a certain aim. The consequence, if it serves to pursue and to judge the aim, is called the end.
blocks.blomberg-s07-145: With all Completudo we therefore compare the cognition with a certain aim. But this Completudo is
blocks.blomberg-s07-146: a) Externa, which appears in the comparison of the cognition with others.
blocks.blomberg-s07-147: B) interna, which takes place in itself and lies in the cognition itself.
blocks.blomberg-s07-148: But the Completudo Comparativa can often be so very useful to us that we have no need at all of the completudo absoluta, or interna, and can dispense with it. blocks.blomberg-s07-149: Philosophia has the aim of instructing us how we are to learn to understand ourselves ever better.
blocks.blomberg-s07-150: All new cognitions that deviate greatly from the customary way of judging are at first wholly obscure and are not understood by the best head. And indeed this often happens not because the cognitions are obscure in themselves, but because it is commonly very difficult to deviate from the customary way of judging and to observe this or that thing from another side. Whoever, e.g., has learned to dance with a poor master and then is to begin to learn with a skilled one, finds it really very hard to unlearn the old steps and shifts of the feet once habituated, and to follow the newer, better method. Just so it goes with cognition: everything is hard to understand and obscure that departs from the old, once established manner of cognition, of presentation, of writing, etc.
blocks.blomberg-s07-151: All inventors of new methods in all the sciences are therefore obscure at the beginning; indeed, for this very reason, because one loves the old too much and will not depart from it, they are even often despised, until one has in time accommodated oneself to this new method too; whereupon one then finds that it is often far better than the old.
blocks.blomberg-s07-152: Locke and Newton have experienced this fate, that their writings were at the beginning exceedingly obscure and unintelligible, or at least seemed to be, until one afterwards considered them more closely and discovered their merits.
blocks.blomberg-s07-153: The doctrine of obscure cognitions is not logical at all, but only metaphysical. Logica is not a science about the nature of the subject, of the human soul, in order to cognize what really lies hidden therein; rather it already presupposes clear concepts and treats of the use of our understanding and our reason.
blocks.blomberg-s07-154: In our soul all cognitions already lie really hidden, and nothing more is actually necessary than merely to develop these cognitions and to bring them into a brighter light.
blocks.blomberg-s07-155: Rational philosophy teaches us nothing new, but seeks only to make distinct to us what we already know and to bring about a consciousness of it in us.
blocks.blomberg-s07-156: Empirical philosophy, on the other hand, occupies itself with bringing us new cognitions that we have not known until now.
blocks.blomberg-s07-157: In this Paragraphus the author speaks of exhaustive clarity.
blocks.blomberg-s07-161: The former consists in the marks that are attributed to a thing sufficing to distinguish it from all other things.
blocks.blomberg-s07-162: The latter, however, consists in the marks of a thing being sufficient to derive from them all possible remaining determinations of it.
blocks.blomberg-s07-163: The Completudo externa always presupposes the Completudinem internam; where the latter is not, there the former is certainly not either, and conversely the former, namely the Completudo externa, can be attained by means of the completudo interna. blocks.blomberg-s08-142: On the other hand, we would in the same degree also be capable of removing at will at all times everything that could bring about sadness in us and cause vexation. blocks.blomberg-s08-153: A judgment is dogmatic when one either actually accepts or affirms a proposed cognition, or on the other side rejects and denies it. blocks.blomberg-s08-154: The sceptical in judging, in which one passes no decision at all, settles nothing, but leaves everything unsettled, and harbours doubt about everything of which one can assert nothing with certainty, until [496/7] one has proper grounds of proof for either accepting or rejecting a cognition. This cautious and prudent procedure in judging, in which one takes great care not to affirm outright anything of which one is not wholly reliably convinced, and to deny nothing whose impossibility, or non-being, one does not see quite distinctly, this procedure is really most suited to distinct truth, and most advantageous; provided only that one does not have in doing so the constant resolve never to distinguish anything, to doubt everything forever, and to leave everything undecided. Hence it comes about that a true philosopher inclines greatly not to squander his assent needlessly everywhere, but always to withhold it, until he has sufficient and fully adequate grounds of truth. blocks.blomberg-s08-156: One of the chief causes, however, that very often seduce human beings into passing a false judgment, or into an error, are further the affects.

blocks.blomberg-s08-237: But everything true that has been brought forth by means of one prejudice or another is formaliter false, although it can be and is materialiter correct. How wretched is the education that seeks to ground true moral rules in young people through prejudices and errors.
blocks.blomberg-s08-238: Many prejudices are thus so constituted, and of such a kind, that if one dared to attack them, to want to eradicate and remove them, they would nevertheless make the mind of the human being all the more embittered, indeed would stupefy him even to hearing and to attention to true doctrines and important dogmata that have great consequences for them.
blocks.blomberg-s08-239: There are truly quite comfortable prejudices in which the human being feels quite well, and it would therefore be a great folly to wrest from another such prejudices, which would be in a position to contribute so very much to his well-being, and often really do.
blocks.blomberg-s08-240: It is otherwise, however, with harmful prejudices, which can have an influence not merely on a single case or person, but quite often even on the welfare of an entire Republique. blocks.blomberg-s08-241: We must therefore also not despise other people if they are perhaps, whether with or without their own fault, filled very much with prejudices.
blocks.blomberg-s08-242: The common man has and harbors very many prejudices, to which he also very often clings very stubbornly; but it is just as certain that the learned man, even the greatest, always has just as many of them, and far more dangerous ones. Only there is this difference, that the prejudices of a learned man are hidden under the name of canones, those of the common man, however, under the name of proverbs.
blocks.blomberg-s08-243: The author here distinguishes the prejudices from one another. He calls some prejudices logical, as if he had in mind to indicate thereby that there are other kinds of prejudices that are not logical.
blocks.blomberg-s08-244: Otherwise the aesthetic is commonly contra distinguished from the logical, and hence the prejudices will be, and can be divided,
blocks.blomberg-s08-247: The former consist in this, and take place when our cognitions are contrary to the rules of the understanding and of reason; the latter, on the other hand, consist in this, that our cognitions are contrary to the rules of taste.
blocks.blomberg-s08-248: Fashion is properly nothing other than a prejudice of taste, according to which one holds something to be beautiful or ugly through a prejudice. blocks.blomberg-s08-249: Imitation and habit are the greatest sources of aesthetic prejudices.
