blocks.blomberg-s08-250: If everyone were to dress according to his own liking and taste, we would finally have the most excellent kinds of clothing; now, however, the right taste in clothing is really lacking, and indeed because fashion prevails therein, which everyone follows incessantly and constantly.
blocks.blomberg-s08-251: All fashion in general is more harmful than useful, for it is contrary to the rules of pure reason as well as even to the rules of taste. And he who is, or wants to be, fashionable in his judgments of taste, or even of reason, certainly has no reason at all. He shows thereby his very poor talents and his complete lack of all taste. Nevertheless it is still far more tolerable to be fashionable in taste than to be fashionable in thinking, in judging, and in sentiments; to be fashionable in clothes is tolerable and often good. But to want to be fashionable in sentiments, that is the real, logical prejudice. The prejudice of taste, however, prevails not only in clothing, but even in style.
blocks.blomberg-s08-252: Almost every century has a style, or a form of its own
blocks.blomberg-s08-253: At one time a great pomp of inflated words prevails in the manner of writing; at another, anxious contortions of wit prevail; at another again a quite shallow manner of writing, which one is pleased to call natural, because it is easy, costs little or no effort, and can be produced without art. At another time one again loves in all things such a manner of writing as one was properly accustomed to use in all letters. At another time one again loves above all a heavy, obscure, riddling, and enigmatic manner of writing, which one prefers to the easy, complete, and distinct, which is supposed to betray a certain profundity and a deep-thinking learnedness in the authors, because one must guess for a long time and has as it were a riddle to solve, until one comes to guess what the author meant by it, to be able to discover the actual sense and meaning of the author, and to find what the author thought thereby.
blocks.blomberg-s08-254: All taste is very much spoiled by imitation, a fertile source of all prejudices, in that one borrows everything and holds nothing to be a beauty that one might perhaps oneself invent and hit upon, except what others have already devised and previously cognized, and what has been declared a beauty by them.
blocks.blomberg-s08-255: If, therefore, everyone were to endeavor not so much always to imitate, but rather to be an original himself, and to strive for it, we would certainly soon behold the greatest geniuses, who would be sublime and great in judgments of taste.
blocks.blomberg-s08-256: Just so there are again various kinds of prejudices in the various fine arts and sciences, e.g. in music, in poetry, in painting, in sculpture, etc. Everywhere, in every taste, prejudices always prevail, indeed even in moral taste.
blocks.blomberg-s08-257: Habit and examples bring it about, and are therefore the causes why so many prejudices, so many fashions, prevail in them.
blocks.blomberg-s08-258: It has been remarked that the English nation has far more, and greater, originals than the French and other nations. This, however, truly comes from the freer and less constrained form of government. For there nearly everyone is his own master, at least of his own genius. He thinks, judges, and acts therefore naturally for the most part without being moved in anything by examples, or at least without conforming to them, following them, imitating them. Everyone thus thinks and judges there according to his taste, and hence there are so few copies there.
blocks.blomberg-s08-259: Countries and states, on the other hand, in which a monarchical form of government is introduced and prevails, are naturally not in a position to bring forth such originals, or at least not so many for long, for here one commonly conforms very much to the examples, which often become the norm in thinking, in acting, and in judging, and indeed, as usual, the magnates of the realm, the great ones of the realm, and at court for the most part the originals, the models, after whom one is wont to seek to form oneself and to imitate them.
blocks.blomberg-s08-260: The author here further divides prejudices into the prejudices 1.) of excessive trust, and 2.) of altogether excessive mistrust; but both kinds of prejudices are in fact one and the same, and inseparably connected and united with one another.
blocks.blomberg-s08-261: The cause of the prejudices of altogether excessive trust, however, is properly nothing other than the desire to extend one's cognitions, but without acuteness and true judgment of that with which one wants to enrich them; and diligent observation teaches that this takes place for the most part especially in youth, whereas old age, which already has more experience and cognitions than youth, has also already endured more delusions, often reflects more and looks to see whether it is indeed worth it and worth the trouble to strive for the attainment of this or that cognition, and whether it is indeed correct, or not. And by means of this thinking back and forth and often repeated doubt it often finally falls into the prejudice of altogether excessive mistrust, and for the most part it thus turns out: the older we gradually become, the less credulous and the more mistrustful we then become.
blocks.blomberg-s08-262: In the prejudice of altogether excessive mistrust, however, we give certain persons a certain precedence over ourselves; we must therefore ascribe to them more prudence, more learnedness, etc. than to ourselves, and so choose them as originals after whom we endeavor to form ourselves.
blocks.blomberg-s08-263: Distinguished people are for the most part of such a kind that one is possessed of very many prejudices toward them and with regard to their skills and qualities. One always holds them to be prudent, learned, exalted, noble-minded, etc.; even clothing often makes learned and prudent; a person in gold braid even awakens respect, he seems at once to possess more understanding than others, although he nevertheless very often sits in the greatest shadow of darkness.
blocks.blomberg-s08-264: What a distinguished man says is often noticed far sooner than what a common or poor man brings forth, although the latter is very often more prudent than the former. There is further a prejudice of altogether too great a multitude, in that one assumes and persuades oneself that many persons are in a position to judge something more and better than few. This is the common and lowest prejudice of authority.
blocks.blomberg-s08-265: Hence many a one is frightened when he is to give a public speech, address, etc. before a large assembly for the first time. Before 2 or 3 persons he would perhaps not be frightened, but before several 1000 one is afraid. One judges namely that what finds approval with everyone is true and must really lie in the object itself, although this is often quite false.
blocks.blomberg-s08-266: The prejudice of altogether too great a multitude arises for the most part from the prejudice of imitation. A great number of people, all of whom attend to me alone and observe me alone carefully, must necessarily have something venerable for me.
blocks.blomberg-s08-267: With regard to morality, however, the prejudice of the multitude becomes very harmful, detrimental, indeed disgraceful; hence it also comes about that the human being, even in his actions that have an influence on morals, so gladly follows the great crowd; he hopes, as it were, when he does something evil, to hide among it, and thus unseen to escape the eye of the eternal heavenly judge.
blocks.blomberg-s08-268: From a great multitude a like judgment can easily be brought forth; none has so much the spirit of imitation as a great multitude.
blocks.blomberg-s08-269: If something is already so constituted that it receives the general approval of the people all at once, as soon as it appears and at first sight, then it is very often to be feared that it is not worth much; and a reasonable man must be not only not pleased but very much humbled by a general and unanimous approval that he receives all at once. Books that, as soon as they have come to light from the press, are certainly for the most part very shallow.
blocks.blomberg-s08-270: That which is good and in fact excellent, which brings forth correct but new truths, commonly always finds at the beginning very great opposition, and this lasts until, after closer examination and investigation, after exploration and discovery of its proper properties and its difference from other cognitions, one also discovers its beauties, and what is especially distinguished in it above other writings, and begins to esteem them highly.
blocks.blomberg-s08-271: All prejudice of altogether too great authority, however, can fittingly be divided into three kinds. – – –
blocks.blomberg-s08-272: namely 1mo) the judgment of altogether too great authority in which others stand with us.
blocks.blomberg-s08-273: 2do) the prejudice of altogether too great authority that we place in ourselves.
blocks.blomberg-s08-274: 3.) the prejudice of altogether too great authority that a cognition has in us, on account of some perfections that it carries with it, and from which one infers that still more perfections must be found in it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-275: As regards the first kind of prejudices, we are for the most part inclined to ascribe and attribute more to others than to ourselves. We believe that another knows better something that we do not know. This prejudice arises not only from the consciousness of our own weakness, for this is no ground for ascribing more to others than to ourselves, but from a certain respect that we have for the whole human race, in that we judge that what is lacking to us will nevertheless be found in others.
blocks.blomberg-s08-276: Another prejudice arises from a certain laziness.
blocks.blomberg-s08-277: There is nothing more convenient than imitating and drawing one's cognitions from others. From this prejudice arise the various and manifold citations in books, in which one adduces the judgments of others and their opinions of this or that matter, and presents these citations as proofs.
blocks.blomberg-s08-278: There is truly in this a certain kind of laboriousness, an assiduity, but no difficulty. One must work long, though without a certain exertion of the powers. This prejudice of altogether too great authority that others have with us thus flatters comfort very much. One need not think oneself at all, but can rely entirely on the genius, on the understanding of the other, and merely imitate others.
blocks.blomberg-s08-279: Yet another kind of prejudices of authority toward others arises from vanity. One thereby really, as it were, subjects oneself to others, one makes oneself thereby the slave of a great man, and of the understanding, the power of judgment of another. This, however, often happens also only in order to be able to command others much, to have a great dominion over others who are lower than we.
blocks.blomberg-s08-280: Nowhere, however, is there found greater bombast, nowhere greater pride, anywhere, than in polyhistory. One namely exalts in it other great scholars out of ambition and vanity, in order under this cloak to be exalted oneself, to be able to exalt oneself, and thus as it were to raise oneself far above the so-called learned rabble. One namely presents to the eye of the learned world a great and glorious scholar, and seeks to persuade all others firmly that, in spite of all the diligence, labor, and effort they can possibly apply, they would still always act in vain, since they could never be in a position to equal this great man or come near him; indeed, since one regards the pronouncements of this great archetype as irrefutable and unimprovable oracula, one rejects outright all their opinions merely because they contradict, or seem to contradict, the judgment of this great man. One frightens, or seeks as it were to frighten all others off from ever wanting to endeavor to become equal to this scholar, as if it would be a futile undertaking to strive after it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-281: In just this way it comes about, e.g., that most proud people, who do not like to be subject to many and to obey, or who envy their fellow citizens one power or another, would most like to have in a state the unlimited form of government of a monarch, and also help to promote it, and indeed in order then to be equal to one another and not to have to fear any of their fellow citizens, and this is in fact the true origin of all monarchies. But there is truly nothing more harmful to the human race than always to set up others as an unattainable example and to take them as it were as a model for imitation. Thereby one copies more the faults than the good qualities of the original set up, since everything in the world is imperfect, and so these models too cannot be wholly excluded from it. Holy Scripture itself says: we should never choose anyone else as a model but God, this being most perfect in all respects. But to be always directing and forming oneself after other human beings who are, just like us, most highly imperfect, this brings about more harm than benefit.
blocks.blomberg-s08-282: Such prejudices of authority and of imitation, however, are very much grounded by a bad upbringing and unskillful instruction, namely when, for the confirmation of one's judgments of the understanding, one adduces not one's own reflection or experience but the judgments and opinions of others, cites, alleges them. And although this method, whether in an oral or a written presentation, is very agreeable and a witness to great reading, it nevertheless often grounds only the prejudice of authority.
blocks.blomberg-s08-283: Of the prejudice of authority that one places in a great multitude of people we have already spoken above. It is to be presumed that what all people accept is universally valid. There lies in our nature already a particular inclination to communicate our opinion to others, as we have already indicated above, so that if someone were in a desert and had to stay there without any company of human beings, all his judgments would seem to him to be in vain and futile.
blocks.blomberg-s08-284: This inclination arises not at all from vanity, but from a particular and preeminent communicative constitution of human reason. When namely one judges alone and for oneself, one is never quite sure whether the judgment does not arise from a certain illusion that might be putting something over on us. Hence one is eager to test and examine it precisely on the understanding of other human beings. One makes here as it were an experiment and tries whether what we think is universally valid, whether others accept it, or whether it does not agree with reason. One thus sharpens, so to speak, as it were, those judgments that one has, i.e. whose inventor one is, on the sure touchstone of the understanding and of the insights of other human beings.
blocks.blomberg-s08-285: To this inclination of human reason to communicate its judgments to others is opposed logical egoism, of which we have also already said something above, in that one namely believes and fully persuades oneself that one needs in a judgment of the understanding not at all the help of the judgment of others. It is indeed true that the judgment of others judges nothing in matters of the understanding. But it is nevertheless not at all superfluous or dispensable on that account. The understanding of the human being is by instinct communicatio. If it is thus communicative, it must also rightly be participatory, and let itself be concerned with what others judge of it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-286: The prejudice of authority in which other people stand with us is, further, the prejudice of antiquity, or the prejudice of novelty, on which the liveliness of wit depends. The prejudice of antiquity is grounded on the high regard for the old. What remains of the old down to our times always already has the appearance of being good, for one infers: it would hardly have remained and come down to us if it were not good and worth nothing. Just as we also hold those buildings to be good which, though old, still always stand without having fallen into ruin, whereas others have fallen into ruin through the length of time.
blocks.blomberg-s08-287: No judgment is more general than that the world gradually grows old. Everything in the world deteriorates: animals, horses, etc. become worse when they have lived long, bodies, e.g. clocks, become worse with time. And just this judgment one passes on the whole world, on the whole of nature in general: it deteriorates more and more, it ages gradually. Hence one admires old and yet healthy, robust people, and says: where would one find such a one nowadays among us? It goes so too with books, which remain among thousands of others that have been lost; one holds them for that reason, and not without all ground, to be preeminently good, because in spite of the usual decadence that is wont to befall such writings, they have nevertheless maintained themselves in esteem for so long a time.
blocks.blomberg-s08-288: Young people incline for the most part to the prejudice of novelty. Old age, however, to the prejudice of antiquity. »Just as youth is for the most part wont to be generous, but old age miserly.« Yet it is indeed also true that the cause of these prejudices can often be the change of temperament.
blocks.blomberg-s08-289: To the old belong diligence and assiduity.
blocks.blomberg-s08-290: To the new, however, genius, liveliness, and wit without constancy. We do indeed see the individuals of nature fall to pieces and pass away, all works of art pass away. blocks.blomberg-s08-291: but this prejudice is quite incorrect. Only in more recent times has one reflected on this matter more and better than in ancient times.
blocks.blomberg-s08-292: What nature brings forth has such great constancy that nothing, no time, no age, can alter it. If one excepts the time before the general Flood, then after it everything in the world is equally good, equally strong, procreation and the power of procreation just as good, just as possible, although indeed a single nation can have some advantage in this over another, to which indeed the particular circumstances of the climate, of the means of life, etc. must contribute something.
blocks.blomberg-s08-293: Many books one can tell at the very first moment they appear before the world that they will not be esteemed and highly regarded for long. Other writings, however, which contain much thoroughness, are of such a kind that they are handed down from one age to the next and remain always in their authority.
blocks.blomberg-s08-294: From this it follows naturally that one harbors a kind of high regard for them and holds them to be valuable.
blocks.blomberg-s08-295: When one considers how time sifts out everything poor in the sciences, one may well say: how will it one day fare with our present learnedness?
blocks.blomberg-s08-296: A living language is always changing, a dead one never; all authors are inexhaustible sources of it. The German poet of the present day will certainly look bad after 100 years. The dead languages have the advantage that they remain eternally beautiful and independent.
blocks.blomberg-s08-297: Our present languages will perhaps never become dead, for only Holy Scripture and religion make a language dead. Thus the theologians are the true preservers of learnedness, and with them many languages would cease entirely.
blocks.blomberg-s08-298: The corpus Juris is certainly the greatest and surest proof of human profundity. The discovery of the Pandects at Naples in the 11th Saeculo, however, is the best find that human beings have ever been able to obtain among books. In general, though, the ancients are always inimitable models in manner of writing.
blocks.blomberg-s08-299: If one considers the old world as a whole, and all the individual creatures upon it, one easily finds that the longer the series of copies subordinated to one another is, the greater again is the deviation from the original.
blocks.blomberg-s08-300: The first creatures were very perfect, but through generation and propagation they have become more and more dissimilar to one another, at least. Notwithstanding this, one nevertheless finds that no change at all has taken place in the species and genera of creatures, but that everything is still constituted as it was at the creation of the world and of all things. It is therefore always a prejudice when one esteems the old so exceedingly.
blocks.blomberg-s08-301: Besides this, the high regard that we have for the old also arises from a certain kind of illusion of our understanding and our reason.
blocks.blomberg-s08-302: We always esteem learnedness highly; even in ourselves we always feel a certain high regard, an estime toward ourselves, when we are learned.
blocks.blomberg-s08-303: To learning the old belongs, and is required, learnedness. This is a further ground of the prejudice of antiquity. To cognition of the old there often belongs great learnedness; hence it comes about that we hold the old in high esteem, and indeed for this reason, because we are capable of understanding it only through learnedness. This high esteem of the old, however, also often falls upon old authors, because they have written something for the understanding of which learnedness is required. This is a kind of inner deception. One namely aestimates the old and per consequentiam also the ancients.
blocks.blomberg-s08-304: The language of the ancients is itself already a learnedness; from this it follows that whatever is written in such a language already acquires a certain kind of high regard, because for the knowledge of the language alone a certain learnedness
blocks.blomberg-s08-305: is required, without which one is not in a position to understand it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-306: Hence so much already comes to the ancients' benefit; one sometimes does not even notice their errors, indeed one is not even in a position to recognize whether there are errors in an old writing or not. It seems quite fair, however, to esteem the ancients highly with gratitude, since we are only their pupils. We ourselves hope, after all, that we too will one day be called the dear ancients by our descendants, and then promise ourselves from them the same high regard and the same thanks that we now pay to the ancients. The ancients are for us the original itself, and hence those who are exalted above all judging and above all critique. What a prejudice, when an author is such that his language is no longer criticized or judged at all, but is accepted as already perfectly beautiful and unimprovable in itself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-307: When one comes upon twisted turns of phrase in a Cicero, Horatius etc. and other such authoribus classicis once accepted as unimprovable, one will not say: Cicero etc. should not have spoken so; he could have avoided a fault if he had expressed it somewhat differently etc.; rather one approves it, and we are permitted to speak thus too, merely because Cicero etc. did it so perversely. Likewise the old poets, for all their faults, have the Licentiam poeticam on their side. Here one sees what prejudices spring from the authority that one has toward antiquity. Hence there are so many champions of antiquity who, as soon as something is invented in more recent times, immediately show that the ancients already knew all this too; so that it is really nothing new, but only something sought out from the writings of the ancients and brought somewhat to light.
blocks.blomberg-s08-308: Here, however, we must ask whether we do not have reason to pass a certain provisional judgment in favor of antiquity and of the ancients as to their cognitions and insights?
blocks.blomberg-s08-309: Answer. Certainly; the ancients quite surely had the advantage over us that they at least had no models set before them, no originalia, which they could have followed and were to copy. Hence they had to furnish originals themselves, and became so, whether they wished it or not, because they had no other guidance than nature and their reason.
blocks.blomberg-s08-310: Nowadays, however, through the far too great multitude of originalia nothing but copies are produced, and many a possible new originalia is stifled.
blocks.blomberg-s08-311: Another advantage the ancients had with regard to their thinking was that their realms were for the most part all divided into very many small lands and republics, which were all very free and did not have to sigh under the pressure of a monarchical and strict rule (for freedom in thinking originates from the free form of government, as we have already had occasion to remark above); this free condition, so very advantageous to the expansion of the arts and sciences, was found preeminently in the land of the ancient Greeks. Here one knew of no monarchy, but everything followed its own inclination and governed itself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-312: This way of life, this form of state and of government naturally brought it about that among them there appeared and showed themselves to the world such great, inimitable and excellent geniuses and minds in the especially beautiful sciences, and in particular in painting an Apelles etc., in eloquence a Demosthenes, in poetry.
blocks.blomberg-s08-313: Even today we find that in the countries where the spirit of freedom reigns, much and far more is invented, many more originalia arise, far fewer copies appear, than where a despotic monarchical form of government has been introduced.
blocks.blomberg-s08-314: England furnishes us an example of this; here one still today finds the most and the best archetypes and models. Everyone there thinks for himself, speaks and writes for himself etc., without choosing a model and imitating it, wanting to follow it everywhere.
blocks.blomberg-s08-315: Countries, on the other hand, where monarchs and individual princes rule despotically, and where one has to command over all, bring forth nothing but copies, and seldom originalia. The court is here for the most part the original, and everyone strives to imitate what goes on at court. The manner of writing of the court is the manner of writing of all others (just as one gladly wears the clothes that are customarily worn at court). One sees this nowadays e.g. in France; there one seldom meets with an original, but for the most part nothing but copies. Everything there is fashionable, in clothes as well as in judgments and writings.
blocks.blomberg-s08-316: The manner of writing of the English authors is therefore also very easily distinguished from all others. One always says something other than what the other has said. The French, on the contrary, always write after one and the same manner of writing; one makes use of almost the same turns of phrase as the other. Hence it also comes about that one French author is not easily distinguished from another, and one very seldom meets among them with anything special, excellent, new and unusual.
blocks.blomberg-s08-317: Now we come to the prejudice of novelty. This is grounded partly on the provisional judgment which we for the most part pass in favor of and to the advantage of the new. One has reason to pass favorable judgments for the old, but also often for the new.
blocks.blomberg-s08-318: All those sciences which presuppose an extensive, historical and correct cognition become ever more perfect in more recent times, for it is well known that the more recent learned men exert themselves more and more to extend historical cognitions. In empirical cognitions the new always has an indisputable advantage over the old. In sciences, on the other hand, for which sustained diligence and perpetual effort are required, the new likewise has a more favorable judgment than the old, and indeed not because it contradicts the old, but because it often adds still more to it. But if one esteems the new highly because it contradicts the old, this is really a very harmful prejudice. Partly, however, the prejudice of novelty is also grounded on a certain illusion of our understanding, our reason and our imagination. The old man loves the old, but a young person the new. Age makes a person very inclined to defend antiquity, youth in turn to speak in favor of novelty. If youth owes its cognition and all science to the ancients, and has merely learned it from them but not itself invented it, it has no merit of its own, and is therefore also very much inclined to invent new sciences and to add more to the ancients.
blocks.blomberg-s08-319: Whole nations are often very much inclined toward the old, and others again toward the new. The Spaniard and the Portuguese love the old, the Frenchman on the contrary the new. Sluggish, slow, melancholic and reflective temperaments love the old very much; lively and cheerful ones, on the contrary, love the new. The former are enemies, the latter friends of new fashions. The Frenchman is fashionable in clothes, in systems, in medicaments etc. The Frenchman is the first author and founder of all and every fashion, and also the only one who will always remain so. He alone has the necessary requisite flightiness and lightness for it. The French are therefore too much given to the prejudice of novelty, which arises
blocks.blomberg-s08-320: 1.) from the fact that the new contradicts the old, or 2 do from the fact that one loves the new because it first retains the old, but also second adds something new to it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-321: Inclination is also a great source of favorable prejudice. To this belongs the insinuation, e.g. of outward bearing, of mien, of the name, e.g. in books the title. »A good title sells its book«, and indeed, according to the present fashion, a French, light, frivolous, impertinent title, e.g. when Beaumelle publishes a book with the title: Mes Pensées etc. Should we not esteem highly the ancient inhabitants of Greece, since in this favorable climate all learnedness flourished, as we spoke of above?
blocks.blomberg-s08-322: A kind of recommendation, however, which impels toward high regard for someone, also originates from this: when we have despised someone and then discover and become aware of something unexpectedly great, a fine insight, a genius that exceeds all our expectation, we then esteem him all the more highly for it, we admire him all the more, because we had previously despised him. So it is, e.g., when we hear a woman, of whose insight and skill we have only very poor concepts, speak with great insight, wit etc.; we admire her all the more, and our contempt or low esteem soon turns into reverence. Likewise, e.g., we come to esteem and revere very highly the great sage Epicurus, of whom we perhaps at first formed poor concepts, when we examine his conduct, his speeches, his judgments, his knowledge more closely. etc. Whoever is already eager to regard everything from the worst side, and takes pains everywhere to seek out faults rather than good qualities, certainly has a very malicious heart.

blocks.blomberg-s08-327: Question. Would it ever be possible to eradicate and root out all and every prejudice in human beings?
blocks.blomberg-s08-328: Answer. It seems almost impossible. The human being is already accustomed to having springs of action in his soul which he cannot resist, and which run ahead of the judgments of the understanding, and in this way form a prejudice.
blocks.blomberg-s08-329: To be sure, the human being can learn to distinguish what springs from springs of action and what from the understanding; that is indeed already very much, and he then admittedly can no longer, and not so often as hitherto, be deceived and defrauded, although the propensity to it is indeed still there at every moment; but to rid oneself of it entirely and completely, and to get free of it, this seems to be impossible and would never succeed. Nevertheless, every and any pious fraud, in common life in morals as well as here in logic in the application of the powers of the understanding, is wholly unpardonable, i.e. the intention and the endeavor to want to bring forth something true with the help of prejudices; this philosophy pursues always.
blocks.blomberg-s08-330: A proposition is no prejudice, be it ever so false. For a prejudice is nothing other than the mere desire to want to judge, yet without the proper acuteness or reflection.
blocks.blomberg-s08-331: How, then, do our prejudices arise?
blocks.blomberg-s08-332: The propensity of the mind to judge according to authority, according to inclination, according to custom, according to fashion, that is prejudice. Proverbs are for the most part false, for many of them are of such a kind that one can use them indifferently.

All the prejudices of which we have spoken hitherto therefore arise either
blocks.blomberg-s08-336: The prejudice of far too great confidence which one places in oneself is nothing other than egoism. Egoism, however, is vel cosmologicus, when one holds that there is no other thinking being, no world at all outside me, vel Logicus when one holds that one alone judges rationally, but that no other is in a position to judge anything or to see it better. This latter, namely logical egoism, seems at the beginning actually to be permissible. One has, to be sure, no need then to consult the judgments of others when one itself cognizes something correctly; one need not seek to bring about an agreement of others with the cognition which one has oneself. But on closer examination one finds that one cannot be certain whether one has judged correctly or not if one does not compare one's judgments with the judgments of others and test them on the understanding of others. For a cognition is not correct when it agrees with my private understanding, but when it agrees with the universal laws of the understanding of all human beings. Hence every human being, as we have already shown above, has an inclination to communicate his judgments to others
blocks.blomberg-s08-337: and to impart them. This is the true friendship of sentiment. The logical egoist therefore deprives himself of a great and exceedingly important advantage, one very conducive and necessary to the enrichment and improvement of his understanding, namely of being able to distinguish the true from the false correctly per Communicationem judiciorum, et mutuam dijudicationem eorum invicem. Logical egoism, however, also sometimes arises from a certain kind of humility and faintheartedness, when one trusts oneself and one's insights far too little, and believes that one's judgments would not be worthy of becoming known to others in the whole learned world.
blocks.blomberg-s08-338: Opposed to logical egoism, however, is yet another prejudice: namely when one builds all one's judgments on the reason of others, judges nothing oneself, but merely imitates, in that one raises others above oneself and trusts oneself with nothing. These, to put it briefly, are the prejudices of the lazy.
blocks.blomberg-s08-339: There are, however, certain arts and sciences which are of such a kind that they can, indeed must, be learned through mere imitation. To these belong, e.g., all and every handicraft, likewise mathematics, in which one need only set forth certain propositions to someone and demonstrate and prove them properly, which he grasps into his memory, and thereby is in fact able to become a real mathematicus. Other sciences, on the other hand, are of such a kind that they cannot be learned at all through imitation, but genius is required for learning them. To this belongs, e.g., the whole of philosophy. One may be sure that one will never be able to become a true philosopher [619a] if one does nothing more than merely imitate the philosophers of former times, leaf through or read through their writings once or twice, and accept as true what they have said, and, so to speak, entirely forget oneself in the process; if one therefore trusts oneself not in the least, and also passes no judgments oneself, but swears in verba magistri.
blocks.blomberg-s08-340: Nothing is more harmful than to imitate in philosophy. Nothing is more wretched and ruinous for the understanding than, e.g., to take up a Wolffius or a Crusius or others, to learn their definitiones by heart most strictly and word for word and to impress them upon oneself, and to esteem them as stars of the first magnitude and oneself as nothing; rather one must learn to think for oneself, to judge for oneself, to reflect on objects oneself, and, in order to be able to become and to be a philosopher, to learn to philosophize. Worldly wisdom, however, can be learned not in the least through books, but only through one's own reflection and one's own meditation.
blocks.blomberg-s08-341: We have, however, two kinds of prejudices which relate to learnedness: namely a judgment for, and again a prejudice against, learnedness, and for common sound understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s08-342: Learned men, and also other common people, have a prejudice for learnedness. They often accept everything that has been said and taught by learned people. The moralists, on the other hand, have a prejudice for common and sound understanding, which praejudicium is also proper to many common people. This latter prejudice comes from the fact that no one denies himself sound understanding. For there has never yet been a human being who believed he had no Sens commun, Sensum communem, common sound understanding. That one has a poor, deficient memory, one readily and willingly admits. Another in turn admits that he has no quickness in comprehending, no wit, no witty ideas, no genius for this or that particular science, no taste for poetry. But everyone believes he possesses the Sensum communem. No one will so easily deny it of himself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-343: Since now the fewest of those who have a sound understanding are learned people, and it is nevertheless a well-known but true proverb: ut ars non habeat osorem, nisi imperitum, it is indeed not at all to be wondered at if from this it very easily comes about that learnedness is by very many, whether from ignorance or from envy, if not despised then at least held in low esteem, and the common sound understanding, on the other hand, is infinitely exalted.
blocks.blomberg-s08-344: The author here adduces further the prejudice of the accepted system. In almost all parts of learnedness the prejudice of unity takes place.

blocks.blomberg-s08-350: The prejudice of lazy confidence arises from a certain kind of gross ignorance and sluggishness in attaining to this or that cognition, and from a contempt of this cognition arising therefrom, but very ill applied and worthy of contempt, merely because one cannot partake of it. blocks.blomberg-s08-351: In almost all parts of learnedness the prejudice of unity does indeed take place
blocks.blomberg-s08-352: When very many properties and determinations of a thing are to be derived from one ground, one is commonly accustomed for the most part to pass the provisional judgment and to have the presumption that all the remaining determinations of the same thing will probably also be derivable from it, and that this one ground, which one has of this thing, will therefore be nearly the true and fully sufficient ground of this whole thing. One namely sometimes assumes a ground, and then infers from the consequences that this is the only true ground, although this is very seldom fully certain.
blocks.blomberg-s08-353: E.g., if one entertains a presumption or another that this or that man is a thief, one often infers merely from the consequences whether this presumption may well be true or not, but false. If one finds, e.g., that this or that person who stands in connection with us at first had and possessed nothing at all, but afterwards suddenly squandered a great deal of money, and that this happens at the time when this or that money went missing from me and was presumably stolen, one believes with certainty that he must be the thief of our money, although this presumption can very often be false and incorrect, indeed even insulting and sinful. From this provisional judgment arises the prejudice of unity, when one namely finds a ground of a thing which has very many consequences and determinations, and then derives all the remaining consequences and determinations from it. So it went, to give an example of this, e.g., quite in the beginning with electricity. One namely explained at that time each and every thing at all wondrous from it; indeed there were even some fine spirits who went so far as to want to assert that electricity had an influence on religion, in that they namely wanted to endeavor, e.g., to explain even the healing of the woman with the issue of blood by Christ from the powers of electricity.
blocks.blomberg-s08-354: In general, whoever finds, or at least believes he finds, in one ground the source of all wisdom and cognition is always very much inclined to ascribe to it still further more than is actually to be found in it. Another believes he has sound understanding, and yet also wants to amuse and delight himself; but he is far more inclined to satisfy his inclinations as much as possible, far rather than to take the path of reflection and of labor, and in this way one often falsely holds an understanding which is neither exercised nor cultivated for the merely common understanding. For this understanding one can rightly call, in a good sense, a plain understanding. For although one now connects with this expression a bad concept and a harmful interpretation, it is nevertheless well known that the dear ancients had the proverb: plain and right, and thereby good; and took the word plain here in a very good sense.

blocks.blomberg-s08-361: Often there arises in us even a prejudice against, but also again a whole science, and indeed for this reason, because it has perhaps often erred, and we have exactly noticed and taken note of its errors. blocks.blomberg-s08-377: »Every cognition from merely insufficient grounds is uncertain.« If a cognition is cognized from merely insufficient grounds of truth, so that I see far more grounds for than against the matter, then it is plausible. If, however, there are finally more grounds for than against the cognitions, or at least more than half of the grounds are for the cognitions (whether I see these grounds or not), then it is probable.
blocks.blomberg-s08-378: Plausibility rests merely on the subject
blocks.blomberg-s08-379: Probability on the object, so that I thereby actually cognize more grounds for the matter than grounds for asserting the opposite of the matter are possible. In plausibility an error is actually to be found, and indeed in the form that one is not aware of the insufficient grounds. The first rule is therefore: in all cognitions, even in true ones, seek first of all to become aware of the uncertainty which arises, and could ever arise, from the insufficient grounds; one should place oneself, as it were, in the situation of the opponent, the doubter, who believe themselves to have sufficient grounds for asserting the opposite of these cognitions; for otherwise one will actually almost always, for the most part, err and deceive oneself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-380: One can never know whether one cognizes more grounds for than against the matter, and cannot learn to see this before one has a cognition of the sufficient ground.
blocks.blomberg-s08-381: Therefore in all cognitions one must first make oneself acquainted with the sufficient ground, or want to know and cognize how many grounds are actually required for the complete certainty of a thing, so that one can properly distinguish whether something is plausible or probable.
blocks.blomberg-s08-382: If one does not cognize the sufficient ground of a thing, one also cannot determine how many grounds for the truth are necessary in order merely to make the cognition probable in the first place.
blocks.blomberg-s08-383: If I subtract the grounds of holding-to-be-true from all possible ones that are necessary and required for certainty, and hold this properly against one another and weigh it, then the remaining ones are the grounds of the opposite. Hence I can quite easily see which grounds, whether the grounds for or the grounds against the cognition, are preponderant. Plausibility can change very much, for its weight is grounded in the subject, probability, however, always remains unchanged the same, and indeed merely for the reason that it is grounded in the object.
blocks.blomberg-s08-384: The manner of writing is naturally very changeable, and indeed especially for this reason, that one can cognize today more grounds for and tomorrow again more grounds against this matter, according as one directs one's thoughts variously upon this matter, and investigates and reflects more upon this or that, and endeavors to seek it out. blocks.blomberg-s08-385: It is still a ground, even if it is not complete. blocks.blomberg-s08-386: All our conviction and assurance of any cognition must necessarily run through all such elements. First we merely presume that something is true. blocks.blomberg-s08-387: True sagacity is always, as it were, a spying out, a scenting of the truth already beforehand. It is one of the foremost talents of good minds, and of reflection. So it goes, e.g., with the discoveries of the world.

blocks.blomberg-s08-389: No ground can be more than sufficient, for otherwise it is entirely and altogether no ground, just as nothing can be more than true, more than false, more than good, more than evil, for otherwise it is nothing.
blocks.blomberg-s08-390: The sufficient ground already comprehends everything in itself, but the concept of everything also contains at the same time a unity. blocks.blomberg-s08-391: Probability is a fraction, in which the sufficient ground of truth is the denominator, while the insufficient grounds of holding-to-be-true which I have are the numerator.
blocks.blomberg-s08-392: One can actually calculate mathematically the degree of probability or the degree of improbability of one or another empirical matter. blocks.blomberg-s08-393: With our philosophical truths we cognize nothing other than a plausibility of this or that matter.
blocks.blomberg-s08-394: We have certain grounds for the truth of the matter, and cognize fewer for the opposite of it, in that there is no one who is in a position to bring forward more grounds against than for the truth of the matter; our cognition is therefore nothing more than plausible.

blocks.blomberg-s08-397: All plausible judgments, on the other hand, change daily, according as one cognizes more or fewer grounds for and against the matter. blocks.blomberg-s08-398: But in order to know whether the grounds for the truth of the matter are greater than the grounds of the opposite, or whether the grounds for the cognition make up more than half of the sufficient ground, one must first of all always endeavor to attain a solid and upright cognition of the sufficient ground, as has already been remarked above. Mathematics alone is the science that is of such a kind that in it we can cognize the sufficient ground of a thing. In philosophy, however, this is quite impossible, and hence it comes about that all our cognitions in philosophy that are not indubitably certain can never be probable, but can always be only plausible. For in probability we do not judge what is actually the case, but only what is possible under certain conditions.
blocks.blomberg-s08-399: But this possibility always remains unchangeable under one and the same conditions.
blocks.blomberg-s08-400: By means of probability we therefore properly cognize the degrees of possibility; if these degrees are great, a great probability obtains; if they are small, a small probability obtains.
blocks.blomberg-s08-401: A cognition is doubtful, taken subjectively, when the grounds for the matter that I cognize are equal to the grounds against the matter, i.e. to the grounds of the opposite. blocks.blomberg-s08-402: Something can be subjectively practically certain, although objectively it contributes only very little to the sufficient ground.
blocks.blomberg-s08-403: As for certainty, there are three particular and entirely different kinds of it, namely
blocks.blomberg-s08-407: Logical certainty is certainty according to the rules of the understanding and of reason, and thus an objective certainty, which is grounded in the matter itself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-408: Aesthetic certainty is a certainty according to the rules of taste.
blocks.blomberg-s08-409: Practical certainty, finally, is a certainty according to the rules of the free will.
blocks.blomberg-s08-410: Someone is practically certain when the grounds of holding-true a cognition that he has are sufficient to determine him to actions; but if he nevertheless does not want to act, then these grounds are still far from sufficient to make him logically certain. E.g. when it comes to condemning someone, sentencing him to death, etc.
blocks.blomberg-s08-411: One can be aesthetically certain when one holds the opposite of a matter or cognition that one has to be impossible, merely because it does not please him. blocks.blomberg-s08-412: In this way the human mind is actually subject to very many illusions and delusions, merely because, often, something pleases us, we hold it to be certain, and merely because something displeases or vexes us, we hold it to be uncertain. blocks.blomberg-s08-414: Practical certainty, finally, is a certainty according to the rules of prudence and of morality. The latter, however, is a moral certainty. The possibility of a thing can produce in us a practical certainty, e.g. if someone merely believes that it is possible that there is a God, this thought must nevertheless necessarily have an influence on his life, just as if he were fully assured and convinced of this cognition.

A practical certainty is that which, with a view to certain actions, brings about just the same as a complete certainty. E.g. if something of value disappears in my house, and my servant happens to stay away at exactly the same time, then my practical certainty is there that this absent servant has stolen what is missing from me, although there is as yet no logical certainty at all, and the servant may have gone away, got away, for entirely different reasons and in another way.
