blocks.blomberg-s08-421: If a cognition that is in itself probable is just as secure a ground of actions according to the rules of prudence as if it were fully certain, then this is a pragmatic certainty.
blocks.blomberg-s08-422: But if a cognition that is in itself probable is just as secure a ground of actions according to the rules of morality as if it were fully certain, then this is a moral wisdom.
blocks.blomberg-s08-423: Even what is logically improbable can nevertheless be morally certain, e.g. if I demand money from someone, and I do not know whether I have already received it or not, and the other, my supposed debtor, knows just as little whether he has already paid it to me or not: then according to morals I can demand nothing more from him, although it is logically uncertain whether something has already been paid or not? A logical certainty can also be attained of the existence of God, although this is very difficult. But all human beings can attain moral certainty even without great logical speculationes. If one only sharpens the moral judgments in someone, one can thereby easily bring him to conviction of the existence of God.
blocks.blomberg-s08-424: A logical certainty of a future life is very difficult to attain, but one can indeed attain a moral certainty of it if one considers that here on earth happiness is not always a consequence of good conduct, and that therefore another world is to be hoped for, in which this will take place.
blocks.blomberg-s08-425: Moral certainty, or uncertainty, must be spoken and treated of at greater length in morals itself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-426: Most, and nearly all, authors do not know moral certainty at all, but hold it to be any probability whatever, e.g.: It is uncertain whether there are inhabitants in the moon, but it is nevertheless always somewhat probable. Some accept this as a moral judgment, but this does not hold, for such a judicium has no influence at all on conduct. It is a logical probability, and mere speculation.
blocks.blomberg-s08-427: Nothing is a moral judgment except what has a relation to my actions. If someone therefore is to and must act, and the grounds are merely probable, then the grounds that have the greatest probability constitute practical certainty.
blocks.blomberg-s08-428: Every ground of the opposite of a matter of which one is aware is called a doubt. Every hindrance to holding-true is a logical difficulty, and this is
blocks.blomberg-s08-431: The latter, that is the subjective difficulty, is properly the incomprehensibility, where I do not reject a cognition, but notice that I cannot come to terms with it. This subjective hindrance of the understanding is a fine task for a philosopher who wants to study human beings. The study of scruples is of great importance.
blocks.blomberg-s08-432: The study of doubts is somewhat easier. To find scruples in ourselves, before we can say that we cannot comprehend a cognition, is very difficult. Scruples hinder a person from holding-true, and can be resolved neither by the person who has the scruple nor by another.
blocks.blomberg-s08-433: But scruples can become doubts [672a], namely when one becomes aware of them, and this is also highly necessary.
blocks.blomberg-s08-434: One transforms a scruple into a doubt by considering the cognition that is accompanied by the scruple in all sorts of different relations and under different circumstances, whereupon one will at once, without any trouble, discover and notice which is the side on which we cannot yet be fully decided, and which, on the other hand, is the side on which no scruple remains any more.
blocks.blomberg-s08-435: Scruples in themselves are therefore not at all to be despised, or straightaway blamed and rejected.
blocks.blomberg-s08-436: But there are subjective scruples, which lie in the one who has this or that cognition, and these one must not heed. The objective scruples, however, which lie in the cognition itself, one must seek to make clear. If someone presents to me nothing but plausible propositions, I have a scruple, and do not yet give him my assent right away. E.g. I consider the proposition: that all moral judgments are supposed to lie in a particular feeling and sensation; I give it my assent, yet a scruple still remains for me; I cannot refute the proposition, and nevertheless I cannot trust the cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-437: When I consider the scruple more closely and reflect better on the matter, a doubt arises from it. I see that if I accept this proposition as true, it necessarily follows that anyone who does not have this feeling and this sensation must be incapable of passing moral judgments, which yet seldom, or even never, takes place.
blocks.blomberg-s08-438: From this doubt, however, something else must necessarily arise again, namely: that I will then make various objections against the truth of the proposition; and upon these objections there finally follows a complete refutation from certain grounds, which is otherwise also called merely an answer.
blocks.blomberg-s08-439: If I refute the doubt from grounds that only one person holds and accepts as correct, sufficient, and adequate: then these grounds, as well as this answer, hold only for a single subject; this is then a so-called responsio, et refutatio ad hominem.
blocks.blomberg-s08-440: This already happens with a kind of reluctance, and happens merely in order to get one's opponent off one's neck as soon as possible. But if, on the contrary, I refute the doubt from grounds that hold for everyone, and are consequently universally valid, but also so convincing and assuring that no one is any longer in a position to object anything against them, then this is an actual categorical refutation, refutatio categorica, and this takes place for the purpose of actually bringing the truth to light and, as far as possible, clearing false cognitions out of the way.
blocks.blomberg-s08-441: Scruples often remain permanently in a cognition, and cannot be removed.
blocks.blomberg-s08-442: The development of scruples is a very fine science. Through it a scruple is drawn, as it were, out of the dark, and then, as a significant objection, it must be formally refuted, after it has been properly placed in the light.
blocks.blomberg-s08-443: But it is indeed impossible to think of a more wretched condition of man than the condition that leaves us undecided. The condition of indecision, especially when it concerns our interest. This condition of indecision is far more burdensome than the condition of speculation.
blocks.blomberg-s08-444: Everything that detains us and makes us inactive, that puts us in a certain kind of inaction, is very much opposed to the essential determinations of the soul. Man would even rather know a future misfortune in advance than remain uncertain in the presumption of it, and hover between fear and hope.
blocks.blomberg-s08-445: Physicians are often themselves to blame for the cowardice of their patients; they mostly feed them always with empty words, and conditions, imaginings.
blocks.blomberg-s08-446: Young people in particular are mostly of such a kind that they very much dislike being in suspenso, for it is their nature: they always want to get further. Yet despite all this uncertainty a certain kind of certainty can still always take place, namely in this, that all our cognition must be only very much restricted and bounded, and consequently only very imperfect and deficient.
blocks.blomberg-s08-447: For we can always cognize the grounds of uncertainty with certainty and reliability; that is a certainty of subjective philosophy.
blocks.blomberg-s08-448: Established truths are those truths against which no further objection can be made.
blocks.blomberg-s08-449: To these belong, e.g., the res judicatae, that is, matters settled in foro by a legally binding judgment, e.g. thus after a completed trial it is an established matter that, once the judge has pronounced a verdict, this person or that must, according to it, pay to that or this person a certain assigned sum of money.
blocks.blomberg-s08-450: All and every new truths always find at the beginning very many opponents and much resistance; a certain time must be necessary and required to settle them, after one has examined them better. So, e.g., it went at the beginning with the writings of Descartes. At the beginning they met with very much contradiction, and 30 and more years passed without their truth being established.
blocks.blomberg-s08-451: Through this establishing of the truth no new cognition is really added to it, but nothing else happens than that all other people cease to judge about it and agree with it. As long, therefore, as a matter is still being disputed, as long as disputes are still being exchanged about it from this side and from that, it is not yet established at all.
blocks.blomberg-s08-452: We can often have complete certainty of this or that matter, but the grounds of the certainty are often such that one notices still very much uncertainty in the manner of inferring. E.g. The soul is immortal: this is completely certain. But the grounds of philosophy for it are not so evident that one should be completely convinced by them. The philosophical form of it is still very uncertain.
blocks.blomberg-s08-453: Every uncertainty is a ground of a rightful doubt, since I still find it possible to seek out grounds for the opposite of the cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-454: Being aware of the insufficiency of a ground for truth is at least useful for assuming as still possible that there are still grounds for the opposite of the matter. Doubt in the proper sense does not yet take place with the uncertainty of a cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-455: The uncertainty of one matter or another, however, makes doubt entirely possible, so that one has grounds for the opposite. Often there actually arises from the fact that one has seen and noticed that reason errs, very often a kind of hatred of reason, misology, roughly in the way that misanthropy is hatred of human beings, which arises from a suspicion against the whole human race, which one draws from the observation of how little justly human beings act.
blocks.blomberg-s08-456: “That author and writer undoubtedly deserves the greatest thanks who teaches in his writings what will hold for a hundred years or so,” says Terrasson. The world then still moves by its prejudices, which that author wanted to root out, until it finally begins to reflect correctly on them,
blocks.blomberg-s08-457: and with the course [685/6] of time also gradually calms down, and grants this.
blocks.blomberg-s08-458: One also cannot always investigate the grounds of the conflict of speech. With people who have themselves written large books and works on this or that matter, it is not good or advisable to dispute further about this matter; for one can well infer for oneself that they cannot so easily be brought to esteem their own labor of many years etc. so lightly, to value it little, or to refute themselves.
blocks.blomberg-s08-459: In an inner proof one is immediately aware of the uncertainty in a cognition. An outer proof, however, is the awareness of the uncertainty of a cognition, and indeed not immediately, but mediately, according to the judgments of others. In many a quaestion of reason a plausibility is to be encountered and found such that I cannot withhold my assent from it at all; but if I present it to others, they nevertheless often hold quite the opposite of it, and I then first become aware that, according to the minds and insights of others, my cognition is still not entirely and wholly indubitably certain.
blocks.blomberg-s08-460: In common usage the word doubt means any uncertainty whatever, and in this respect and in this sense doubt is either dogmatic or skeptical. The former is a doubt of decision, the latter, however, is a doubt of retardation, of postponement. From the former arises certainty, from the latter, however, closer investigation and inquiry, in order thereby to arrive at last at the right and indubitable certainty of the cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-461: In dogmatic doubt we reject all inquiry, and do not accept something against which we have, or believe we have, a well-grounded doubt. We then decide briefly, and say: In this matter it is not at all possible to attain any certainty. Dogmatic doubt therefore regards very many cognitions as if absolutely nothing could be established and settled about them. A dogmaticus is accordingly that philosopher who passes the judgment on universal truths of reason that they can be brought to complete certainty and reliability, but who does not engage at all in the consideration of such truths of reason as are, or can be, exposed to one doubt or another. The mathematicus, e.g., is of this constitution; all his proofs are decisive at once; he presents a proposition positively, proves it straightaway decisive, so that it is entirely impossible that the judgment should not hold.
blocks.blomberg-s08-462: The methodus dogmatica of philosophy will therefore consist in our attaining in all judgments a completely secure certainty, not being content with indecision, and leaving nothing undecided. Through this dogmatic method, however, one will never completely establish the actual certainty of a matter; one will thereby not teach truths, but rather very often help to propagate errors, in that one sets oneself, as it were, upon the judgment-seat of human reason, and makes the pronouncement: that of this or that cognition no certainty at all is to be attained, so that all inquiry is applied in vain. So, and in this way, one sets, as it were, boundaries and barriers to the human understanding.
blocks.blomberg-s08-463: All reflection, all efforts to procure for oneself a true certainty of something [691a] and to arrive at conviction, is thereby entirely removed, and what else can arise from this than ignorance, indeed even error?
blocks.blomberg-s08-464: The dogmatic spirit of philosophy is therefore the proud language of the ignorant, who gladly decide everything and care to investigate nothing: whereas our understanding is properly very much inclined to test everything beforehand and to investigate it closely before it accepts and asserts it, and also to look around well beforehand, without blindly rejecting what presents itself to us. The dogmatici could be set against the dialectici.
blocks.blomberg-s08-465: Cognitions are, 1mo, those whose certainty can be cognized apodictically. These are cognitions a priori, which are seen through mere reason. In testimonies an apodictic certainty can never be attained. Apodictic judgments are judgments a priori, and such cognitions are dogmata; of this kind, e.g., is mathematics.
blocks.blomberg-s08-466: In cognitions of experience, however, no apodictic certainty can take place at all. It is no pure impossibility that all those who tell us much of praxis in thinking, acting, judging, inferring, nevertheless deceive us, without having to be ill-disposed on that account. Everything that is apodictically certain is capable of a dogmatic, but everything else only properly of a dialectical kind of cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-467: The ancients divided their philosophers into dogmatici and scepticici, into seekers, inquirers, speculatores of truth, which they always sought but could never find.
blocks.blomberg-s08-468: Further there were intellectual philosophers: among whom Plato said: “everything good that we want to cognize and rightly see must take place a priori through reason merely and alone. The senses alone contain nothing but delusion.”
blocks.blomberg-s08-469: The sensual philosophers, on the other hand, among whom Epicurus was counted as the foremost, said in turn:
blocks.blomberg-s08-470: “Everything that we are in a position to cognize a priori through reason is nothing but chimerical. The senses alone give true certainty.”
blocks.blomberg-s08-471: Thereupon, however, a third came and made peace between these two heated, quarrelsome parties, by exclaiming: “I believe both equally little or not at all
blocks.blomberg-s08-472: Neither the intellectual nor the sensitive has certainty; everything in the human understanding is nothing but confusion.” And from this arose formal skepticism, which seems to originate from so famous and highly esteemed a man as Socrates is. When the dogmatici either quarreled among themselves or asserted one proposition or another with all gravitas and certainty, he at first listened to them quite humbly, but soon began, as a learning-eager listener and pupil of the heated and pathetic dogmatici, to ask them for advice while they disputed with one another, and thereby he could then catch them with their own words and knew how to confuse them in such a way that they finally contradicted themselves entirely, and thus often had to become ridiculous to whole assemblies. He did this so often, and at the right time, that the enemies of the proud dogmatici already rejoiced beforehand when Socrates visited their lecture halls, and these feared him already when he began to ask, since they had to answer him, as he knew how to present himself to them as a pupil eager for knowledge. From this there finally arose a pernicious inclination in his followers to doubt entirely all and every dogmatic cognitions and their certainty. Pyrrho, however, can rightly be regarded as the actual founder and propagator of the skeptical sect. His non liquet, which he called out indifferently against the proud assertions of the dogmatici, and thereby at least often made them quite taken aback, as well as his careful and indefatigable efforts to examine carefully all the propositions of the dogmatici, are known everywhere.
blocks.blomberg-s08-473: The sceptici, however, in the meantime, if we consider it rightly, have in a certain way created far more benefit for philosophy than the proud dogmatici, although it is indeed also true that the former finally degenerated into bitter mockery through abuse. Skepticism, however, or the method of skeptical doubt, in which one places a mistrust in oneself, considers the grounds for and against the cognition that one has, and in this way endeavors to arrive at complete certainty of it, this is the katharkticon, the best means of purification of reason. This prevents errors as far as possible, leads man to further inquiry, and is the way to attain the truth of the matter (though indeed not at once and suddenly, but slowly and gradually through a more extensive and closer examination).
blocks.blomberg-s08-474: The doubt of postponement is therefore actually a more secure mark of the maturity of reason, and of experience in the truth of cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-475: But if we wanted to ask here which method of philosophizing will be the most suitable and the best at academies and will please the most, the dogmatic or the skeptical?
blocks.blomberg-s08-476: We must nevertheless necessarily answer: the dogmatic.
blocks.blomberg-s08-477: When a scholar mounts the podium here and establishes something dogmatically about this or that cognition, nothing can be easier for the listener; he need not test anything, investigate anything, but only impress upon his memory the little that the teacher tells him and presents. In this way he remains in complete rest and comfort; he need only memorize; whereas doubt about cognitions is far from so commodious, but rather far more disquieting, and requires one's own reflection and inquiry.
blocks.blomberg-s08-481: The school of Plato, the great dogmaticus, was called the Academy. Academic doubt is very much different from skeptical doubt.
blocks.blomberg-s08-482: 1.) “The academic doubter proved and demonstrated per definitionem that properly nothing could be proved, nothing defined, which was yet a contradictio in adjecto, and this was the dogmatic-seeming doubt.”
blocks.blomberg-s08-483: 2do The Pyrrhonian, i.e. the skeptical doubter, on the other hand, said: against all and every one, or at least against most of our judgments, another judgment can always be set and opposed, which asserts accurately the opposite of what is contained in the first judgment; this was therefore to be regarded actually more as a kind of very fine and excellent observation than as a reprehensible doubt. And it would actually be to be wished that this observation had been made correctly and carefully; very advantageous consequences would certainly have sprung from it for the whole of human cognition.
blocks.blomberg-s08-484: But how? Is it not a contradictio to establish something firmly in the case of error, and to be a dogmatic doubter?
blocks.blomberg-s08-485: Answer. Both can very well subsist together. Dogmatic doubt is always connected with persuasion of the certainty that of this or that cognition absolutely nothing is to be established or asserted.
blocks.blomberg-s08-486: Dogmatic doubt therefore consists in nothing other than that one judges that one can never attain complete certainty of a cognition, and all inquiry is therefore henceforth always applied in vain and for nothing.
blocks.blomberg-s08-487: Skeptical doubt, on the other hand, consists in this, that one is aware of the uncertainty in a cognition, and is therefore driven to inquire into it more and more; so that one may nevertheless finally arrive at certainty with the help of careful investigations. The former, that of the dogmatici, rejects certainty entirely at once. The latter, that of the sceptici, seeks it little by little. The origin of the expression skepticism is properly the following σκέπτεσθαι. This word means in Greek: to inquire, scrutari, investigare, indagare. The scepticus therefore constantly inquires, he tests and investigates, he places a mistrust in everything, but never without ground. He therefore resembles in this a judge who weighs the grounds for as well as against the matter, and hears the plaintiff as well as the defendant before and prior to deciding the matter and passing a judgment. He postpones his final judgment for a very long time until he ventures to establish something completely. These were the old and pure characteristics of skepticism, and of an unadulterated scepticus.
blocks.blomberg-s08-488: Skepticism was actually very reasonable at the beginning; only the pupils spoiled it and brought it into such bad repute.
blocks.blomberg-s08-489: These latter were so subtle that they even went so far and said: everything is uncertain, even this is uncertain, that everything is uncertain. That was actually a kind of purgative for human reason, which was of such a constitution that, after it has entirely cleansed our understanding of all impurities, i.e. of all false delusion, prejudices, incorrect judgments, it discharged itself again.
blocks.blomberg-s08-490: Nothing, however, is in fact more harmful to the learned world than a universal calm and agreement and peace; at least this always hinders an improvement and increase of learning; it is roughly almost the same with the English, who, as soon as the court stands in proper agreement with the subjects and they are fully at one with each other, already hold themselves in danger and believe that they have lost all their freedom.
blocks.blomberg-s08-491: A universal resolution to doubt everything is of no use at all; it is entirely absurd; but there are also few, or we might even say no human beings at all, who would be inclined to so childish and harmful a mania for doubt.
blocks.blomberg-s08-492: True skepticism, however, is certainly of great utility; and as such it is nothing other than an exact, careful investigation of all dogmata put forward as apodictic, which, insofar as they really are so and thus hold water, shine forth and strike the eye in their whole valeur, in their whole strength only after this examination.
blocks.blomberg-s08-493: All skeptical method is a true investigation of the truth through postponement, in that one does not at once name or reject anything, but first lets it be disputed. By our nature we are actually not at all inclined to postponement. In our times one calls sceptici partly such people as do not in the least deserve the name of philosophers (e.g. a Voltaire), partly such people as are not real academici, but merely have a skeptical method about them and, as it were, affect it, e.g. a Hume. Among the new sceptici, however, one can count Bayle etc.
blocks.blomberg-s08-494: Among us at present, therefore, the name of a scepticus is for the most part regarded as something hateful; one thinks of such a one as does nothing, applies himself to nothing else, than to strive to overthrow the most undeniable and most certain truths; one therefore actually holds him to be a dogmatic doubter, who believes he is in no position to judge about anything, and that one can attain from no matter a complete certainty that nothing can overturn. Formerly, however, an upright scepticus meant nothing other than one who merely postpones his judgment until he has had occasion and time to take this or that matter into closer consideration, and only then ventures to conclude whether a cognition is to be taken as true, or rather rejected as false. The skeptical method is directly opposed to the dogmatic.
blocks.blomberg-s08-495: The method of judging, however, in which one doubts more than one decides, in which one therefore believes that our cognitions can be false sooner than true, that is the suspensio, or that kind of mistrust toward the cognition that we have, in which we indeed likewise actually establish nothing, but nevertheless judge, and first investigate whether the grounds for or against the cognition retain the upper hand.
blocks.blomberg-s08-496: In this method we collect grounds of assent or of rejection, but we establish nothing at all, we do not yet decide at all. This kind of suspension is therefore directly opposed to dogmatic pride. The dogmaticus asks: is something true or not? He therefore decides at once; but he who suspends his judgment trusts himself not very much; he inquires, tests, and always investigates everything well beforehand, in order precisely thereby to find the way to truth and to arrive at genuine true insight.
blocks.blomberg-s08-497: Human nature is actually far more inclined to decide than always to test and to establish, than always to inquire. For we are not at all content when we must leave something, and something in particular, incomplete in our cognition, but we want gladly to establish everything, so that we can have recourse to it, as to a fully certain and reliable cognition, in an emergency that may arise.
blocks.blomberg-s08-498: Through decision and determination our understanding is actually more satisfied; one believes, namely, that one has thereby already acquired something with which one can establish further cognitions.
blocks.blomberg-s08-499: The dogmatic way of philosophizing is therefore directly opposed to, and contradistinguished from, the problematic way of philosophizing.
blocks.blomberg-s08-500: In the former one establishes everything, in the latter, however, one does not decide at all, but postpones one's judgments until one has duly sought out the grounds and counter-grounds and can then pass a judgment.
blocks.blomberg-s08-501: In physics one must philosophize preeminently problematically, and every cautious scholar will undoubtedly make use of this way of philosophizing. The doubt, however, in the problematic way of philosophizing is either a skeptical one, an inquiring, investigating, testing one, or else a dogmatic, establishing and deciding doubt.
blocks.blomberg-s08-502: The history of philosophy, when it comes to this point, namely to the point of the origin of the sect of the sceptici, mostly refers first of all to Socrates. The sophists, who in earlier times, from vain ambition and imagined knowledge, believed they had the right to decide everything, and defended a matter from whichever side it pleased them, were hateful to Socrates, in that he held them to be merely sham-wise (which they also properly were) and declared them so publicly.
blocks.blomberg-s08-503: He judged that it was not necessary for us to know many things, whence he also had the motto that bore sufficient witness to his wisdom: “quod supra nos, nihil ad nos.” He therefore established that our best cognition was to get to know ourselves, that man was the proper object of all philosophy. Hence he accepted nothing except what he had tested. He gave his assent to no cognition blindly, but inquired and investigated.
blocks.blomberg-s08-504: If, therefore, someone was inclined to decide something at once, he showed him the counter-grounds and difficulties that would compel him to suspend his judgment. This inclination to decide nothing without testing proceeded in him from no pride, but from a high degree of modesty, in that he did not trust himself too much, but actually placed a kind of mistrust in his cognitions. And this modesty he especially impressed upon all his pupils, yet it did not remain with them for long, for his immediate pupil Plato already began to become somewhat more dogmatic, and from him arose and originated the sect of the academici, which was opposed to the sect of the sceptici.
blocks.blomberg-s08-505: These endeavored to philosophize problematically, but those, the dogmatici, decided everything; their whole philosophy consisted in deciding.
blocks.blomberg-s08-506: Pyrrho was the first to bring the sect of the sceptici into vogue, and his followers were therefore also called Pyrrhonists.
blocks.blomberg-s08-507: This sect did not properly doubt all truths, but prolonged the investigation and postponed the decision. Hence it proved through the doubts that the grounds for decision were not yet complete, and thus led the dogmatici, who wanted to decide everything, onto the path of caution.
blocks.blomberg-s08-508: The sceptici, however, are also called zetetici, seekers and inquirers, and indeed for the reason that they sought and inquired. In the case of all propositions they will therefore neither at any time decisively doubt them, nor decisively hold something to be true and accept it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-509: The zeteticus is therefore not the one who has the maxim of rejecting everything and every particular, and of deciding positively on everything and every particular without distinction, or of asserting blindly, but the one who reflects on cognitions and tests them.
blocks.blomberg-s08-510: Pyrrho had a certain motto of his sect: non liquet.
blocks.blomberg-s08-511: To everyone who asserted his propositions with the greatest and most settled gravitas he called out in reply non liquet, it is not yet established, and then began to present his counter-argument.
blocks.blomberg-s08-512: A skillful and learned way of humbling many a proud dogmaticus and showing his weak side. This is a secure motto for every pure reason. One must not accept everything at once, but test, and investigate and consider the objects. This sect of the Pyrrhonists, however, deviated so far from its originator that it was afterwards assumed that Pyrrho himself had entirely denied the certainty of all and every dogmata.
blocks.blomberg-s08-513: That Pyrrho denied many dogmata, and placed in them a just and well-considered mistrust, and further that in particular he rejected many rational judgments, is indisputable and not to be denied; but that he denied all and every dogmata, that is utterly false. He who accepts no dogmata at all can teach no morality. There are certainly certain, so to speak, eternal fundamental propositions of our reason, which cannot be contested at all. But Pyrrho was also further blamed for having doubted the truth of all empirical judgments and not having trusted them. This, however, is nothing but a fiction that has no ground at all. Pyrrho was a very wise man, but he would certainly have been a fool if he had wanted to reject all empirical judgments, whatever they might be; a Pyrrhonist therefore did at the beginning nothing but moderate his judgment, but afterwards the sceptici indeed sought to place everything in uncertainty, they endeavored to demonstrate that in all our cognitions no certainty at all can take place. And hence arose skepticism, problematicus et dogmaticus. The former doubted indeed, but investigated beforehand, and wanted thus by means of this investigation to arrive at certainty. The latter, on the contrary, decided, and assumed that in no matter was a complete certainty to be attained.
blocks.blomberg-s08-514: This inclination to want to hold nothing as certain springs really from nothing other than a desire for [724a] completion. Whoever saw that one cannot attain certainty in very many things, who doubts the truth of many things and dogmata, and had not accepted them until an examination had taken place, considered it better to doubt everything, and to contest the truth of all and every principle by adducing counter-grounds.
blocks.blomberg-s08-515: Of Pyrrho himself we really have no writings left, except that Diogenes Laertius cites something of them. Meanwhile this much is certain, that, much as with Epicurus, far more is imputed and foisted upon him than he really did. It is said of him, for example, that he denied the certainty of all experience, that he therefore walked straight into all swamps and marshes, that he feared neither the racing of horses nor deep abysses and ditches; and yet, in spite of these reports so unfavorable to him, it is added that he lived to be 90 years old, as a manifest proof that all such accusations, which people had devised about him, must be false, for with such recklessness he would surely have lost his life sooner.
blocks.blomberg-s08-516: Carneades, the founder of the last academic school, departed very much from the teachings of Pyrrho, however, and really asserted that in no matter can one attain proper certainty or arrive at certain truth.
blocks.blomberg-s08-517: Skepticism, however, is either logical, the logical. To this belongs, for example, the diallelus: truth is supposed to consist in the agreement of a cognition with itself.
blocks.blomberg-s08-518: Many of the arguments of the skeptics had and received their names often from the terminus medius of the syllogism. Thus one of their arguments, for example, is called the Liar, which ran as follows: if you say you are lying, and in saying this you speak the truth, then you speak the truth in lying, atqui you say you are lying, and in saying this you therefore speak the truth in lying. The correct conclusion, however, should be: Ergo you speak the truth in saying that you are lying.
blocks.blomberg-s08-519: or skepticism is also physical, the physical, where one called into doubt the certainty of all physical laws, e.g. the possibility of motion. Thus the ancient skeptics had a certain argument, which, on account of the medius terminus, they also called the Achilles. They inferred as follows: if the running Achilles were to run a race with a tortoise that has a mile's head start, and Achilles were also capable of running a hundred times faster than the tortoise, he would nevertheless never be able to overtake the tortoise.
blocks.blomberg-s08-520: The grounds he used in defense of this argument were: that all numbers are divisible in infinitum, so that however fast Achilles may run, there would still always be a space, though a very small one, between him and the tortoise.
blocks.blomberg-s08-521: Here, then, they inferred merely through reason, without recurring to experience, for otherwise they would have found that Achilles must necessarily overtake the tortoise within 1¼ miles, provided he could run only 1000 times faster than the tortoise. Skepticism was furthermore vel moralis, and this consisted in this, that one passed off all the rules of virtue as fashions, or customs, and usages in the actions that human beings undertake. Thus, for example, close marriages in Egypt were not forbidden at all, as they now are with us; among some Negroes, for example, the greatest, most excellent, and last service of love that children who tenderly love their parents can render them is that they strangle them as they advance in age. Among the Spartans, for example, theft, provided it could be done without being publicly noticed, was not punished at all, and it was even permitted to steal, provided it happened in secret.
blocks.blomberg-s08-522: Skepticism was furthermore vel Historicus, the historical, which consisted in this, that one believed all and every history and report, also the narratives of ancient times, to be uncertain, invented, and fabulous.
blocks.blomberg-s08-523: Yet another kind of skeptic had the habit of always speaking and conversing at great length about the uncertainty of the senses. They straightway denied the certainty of all and every experience. Thus, for example, there was a skeptic who, after he had often asserted with many grounds that one cannot trust the senses at all, wanted to convince his friend of it quite surely and incontestably, by saying to him: I have a great store of provisions in my pantry every day, but when I go into it, count the provisions over, and come again the next day, this store is nevertheless smaller than it was yesterday, a sure and irrefutable proof that the senses must deceive. His friend, who noticed well what must lie behind it, advised him to keep the key to the pantry as carefully as possible. The skeptic's servant, however, who was very sly, soon knew how to get hold of the key, and under this cover diminished his master's store as before, until his master once caught him in the act after all, and let him feel the just punishment for his theft, but also had to learn in this matter that one may well trust the senses.
blocks.blomberg-s08-524: Such a skepticism could well be called dogmaticus, for the skeptics themselves were dogmatists, in that they did indeed doubt things etc., but yet believed they had a right to demand that every human being should give assent to their proofs and accept their doubts. They thus contradicted themselves, for they said: everything is uncertain without distinction, and yet they asserted their propositions and ascribed to them an infallible certainty. They had, for example, the proposition: Everything is uncertain, and indeed in such a way that it is even uncertain that everything is uncertain –
blocks.blomberg-s08-525: As for the more recent times with regard to skepticism, the dogmatic method was very common at the beginning of the Reformation. At that time philosophy was held, and regarded, as a necessary support of religion; one therefore raised not many doubts and counter-grounds against the certainty of philosophical propositions, but taught and established. But after a free way of thinking had subsequently crept in among many nations, one began, with greater and greater steadfastness and certainty, to doubt the truth of many previously unchallenged propositions, and not to believe and accept everything straightaway. One therefore soon also took pains to resist the proud dogmatists somewhat, and to show the groundlessness of many of their propositions. In the most recent times David Hume in particular is known as a skeptic, though one who had a predominant, indeed somewhat excessive inclination to doubt. His writings, which appear before the learned world under the title: Philosophical Inquiries, and are also otherwise called miscellaneous writings, contain political articles, treatises on literature, moral and also metaphysical articles, but all of them issue in skepticism. In these writings of Hume, however, there is found a gentle, composed examination free of prejudice. For he considers therein first of all the one side of a matter; he seeks out all possible grounds for it, and presents them in the best oratorical style. Then he takes up the other side as well, likewise presents it for judgment quite impartially, again presents all the counter-grounds with just the same eloquence; but at the end, and at the conclusion, he appears in his true shape, as a proper skeptic: he complains about the uncertainty of all our cognitions in general, shows how little they are to be trusted, and finally doubts, instead of concluding and deciding which cognition of these two is true and which false. He would surely be one of the best and most readable authors, if only he did not have the predominant propensity to doubt everything, but sought rather, by means of the examination and investigation of cognitions, to arrive at true certainty.
blocks.blomberg-s08-526: Cardanus, in his book de vanitate Scientiarum, also expresses skepticism, and likewise asserts that everything is uncertain.
blocks.blomberg-s08-527: Voltaire is the skeptic of the more recent skeptics of our times. His skepticism, however, is far more harmful than it is useful. He brings forward neither grounds for nor against the matter. He investigates and examines nothing at all, but doubts without any proof that a cognition is to be trusted at all. His grounds are therefore also nothing other than sham grounds, which can deceive a simple man, but never a sharp-witted and reflective learned man. And precisely for that reason Voltaire is very dangerous to the great multitude, and especially to the common man. For he supplies them with quite false grounds for doubting the truth of this or that matter. But if one wants a closer instruction on the skepticism of more recent times, one can read with great profit for this purpose the work which Haller published under the title: Examination of the Sect that Doubts Everything. The above-mentioned writings of Hume, too, are in a certain way really to be recommended.
blocks.blomberg-s08-528: In this paragraph the author speaks of an opinion in general. It is, however, contradistinguished from persuasion. Both are uncertain cognitions, but in persuasion one holds them to be certain; in opinion, by contrast, one does not hold them to be certain. We must therefore take pains above all to distinguish persuasion well from conviction. The very same person who holds something as an opinion cannot yet hold it as a persuasion, and really errs as soon as he does so. Persuasion is therefore always blameworthy, since in it one holds something to be certain from insufficient grounds.
blocks.blomberg-s08-529: The difference between persuasion and conviction, however, is rather difficult, and is therefore very seldom properly determined. This comes from the fact that one has perhaps never yet tasted a true conviction, but only a sham conviction.
blocks.blomberg-s08-530: Opinion, however, is properly no error, but only an imperfect cognition, a lack, in that something in our judgment has no sufficient grounds.
blocks.blomberg-s08-531: We can always put forward many opinions, if only we do not hold them as persuasions, without thereby erring. The rabble does this very often. Even if a cognition is quite false, the opinion of it can nevertheless be quite certain and agree with the rules of the understanding and of reason. E.g. when someone in ordinary life chooses a servant who is of good parents and also has a good upbringing, he thinks he is good and that one can trust him. Here all reason is present and applied, although the opposite of it may very often occur, and my cognition may be false. Wolff held a quite reasonable opinion that there were inhabitants on the moon, for at that time the discoveries were not yet as numerous as now, when it has been seen that the moon has no atmosphere.
blocks.blomberg-s08-532: The opinion can often be false in terms of matter although it is true in terms of form; and conversely it can be true in terms of matter but false in terms of form; in the first case it is false, in the other, however, always true.
blocks.blomberg-s08-533: If my cognition agrees with the constitution of the thing itself, it is true. But if it is contrary to the constitution of the thing, it is false. An opinion, however, can also be very true, reasonable, and well-grounded in terms of form, although in terms of matter it does not agree with the constitution of the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s08-534: An opinion is never a certainty; the opposite of it can always take place; in the meantime it can nevertheless very often be reasonable and right.
blocks.blomberg-s08-535: One gets an opinion about something from certain grounds which one cognizes. The outcome of the matter, however, instructs us as to whether our opinion was true or false in terms of matter. But whether the form of the opinion was right, this the eventus of the matter cannot properly show us.
blocks.blomberg-s08-536: The chief error of our cognitions consists in the formal, and not in the material of the cognitions. One can hold something to be true according to every form of reason, and have a well-grounded opinion about something, if the data one now has for the matter are weightier than the grounds of the opposite, although the outcome of the matter first properly instructs one whether the opinion was true in terms of matter, and the eventus was different from what one had thought.
blocks.blomberg-s08-537: All and every opinion is very changeable. Today one can have more grounds for, tomorrow against the opinion, whereupon one must at once alter one's opinion, and often adopt another opposed to that one, which indeed can in fact be nothing disadvantageous to a true philosopher either.
blocks.blomberg-s08-538: Hypotheses are a quite particular kind of philosophical opinions. Not all philosophical opinions, however, are hypotheses, but only some. They serve not to explain the appearances of the world, but only to explain something in general, whether it spring from reason, or from experience, or from appearance.
blocks.blomberg-s08-539: An opinion about the truth of a ground from its sufficiency for the consequence is a hypothesis. If, namely, I hold something to be true a priori on account of its grounds, this is nothing other than an opinion. But if, on the contrary, I cognize the ground from the sufficiency of the consequences for a ground, this too is an opinion, but not a priori, rather a posteriori, and thus a hypothesis. A hypothesis is, as it were, a presupposition. Thus a physician makes hypotheses when he treats the patient; he must subsume everything under hypotheses, and see whether the consequences arise from them that he now sees before his eyes.
blocks.blomberg-s08-540: If all the consequences that follow from an assumed hypothesis are true and agree with what is given, then it is no longer an opinion, but a certainty
blocks.blomberg-s08-541: A demonstrated truth it is furthermore, but since we are not at all, or only very rarely, in a position to draw all and every consequence from it, they are still for the most part only pure opinions; we must therefore say: if all the consequences that we have been able to draw from the hypothesis are true, I have great cause to infer that the hypothesis itself is certain and true. If a hypothesis, besides its sufficiency for its consequences, is also strengthened by other assurances, then it is confirmed. A hypothesis subsidiaria, however, is such a hypothesis as presupposes a new hypothesis. The more I must assume in it, the less steadfast it is. The more unity there is in the hypothesis, the better it is, for otherwise fiction for the most part comes in besides, and in this way a philosophical romance arises. A romance of reason, as e.g. that of Descartes etc. etc. A world-edifice out of pure chimeras. But note the rule: I may indeed invent in order to philosophize, but not invent while philosophizing itself
blocks.blomberg-s08-542: Every presupposition, however, has infinite consequences. In relation, however, something is certain when the grounds of assent surpass all the grounds of the opposite; that is then a comparative certainty.
blocks.blomberg-s08-543: Absolutely, however, something is certain whose opposite is impossible or absurd. Two presuppositions, if they are so constituted that one and the very same consequences flow from the one as from the other, are one and the very same representations, and not at all different.
blocks.blomberg-s08-544: Thus the Copernican system is a hypothesis. The opposite can still always be represented as possible, however difficult that is; and however easy this system is, and in accordance with reason, and in agreement with all the phenomena of the heavens. –
blocks.blomberg-s08-545: With all hypotheses one is compelled, in order to procure for them entry and certainty, to see that they can be confirmed and derived not merely a posteriori through the relation to their consequences, but also through the nexus a priori, that is, through the relation to their grounds.
blocks.blomberg-s08-546: From the sufficiency of a ground for a given consequence one can never infer with complete truth that this is the true ground of the consequence: for this is only an opinion. There is a ground of possibility there, but not of certainty, for a consequence can often spring from several grounds, and originate from more than one ground. The more sufficient a ground is, however, the more one will infer that it is the ground of the consequence. For all hypotheses are posited arbitrarily. I assume something, namely, and see whether something is sufficient to derive a certain consequence from it, or not.
blocks.blomberg-s08-547: If a ground suffices for all the determinations that are contained in a certain given consequence, no more, and no fewer, if it is therefore adequate, so that neither fewer determinations are to be inferred from it, and it is thus complete, nor more, and it is thus precise, then it is the true ground, in that it is so constituted as it ought to be.
blocks.blomberg-s08-548: More grounds than those which are to be quite adequate to one consequence are impossible. Grounds that are different from one another also cannot agree with one another in all cases. Grounds, however, that agree in all consequences are not different grounds, but one and the very same ground.
blocks.blomberg-s08-549: If a ground suffices for some of what is contained in the consequence, then according to logical rules an opinion takes place that the ground is the true one. If the ground suffices for several determinations of the consequence, the opinion is so much the more probable.
blocks.blomberg-s08-550: Until finally, when the ground suffices for all determinations, but also for no more determinations than are contained in the consequence, then a true ground is there, and then the hypothesis ceases. The ground becomes a theory. A certainty.
blocks.blomberg-s08-551: If a consequence is given to me, and I am to find the ground for it, this is a hypothesis. But if a ground is given to me, and I am to derive the consequences from it, this is indeed an opinion, but no hypothesis. In the hypothesis the consequences are given, but the ground is invented.
blocks.blomberg-s08-552: One of the most famous hypotheses is the Copernican. Copernicus assumed that the sun stands still and the planets move around it, and saw whether all the appearances of the heavenly bodies could be explained from it; this hypothesis of his, however, subsequently becomes a true opinion and a complete system, which deserves approval everywhere. If it is asked: why do all bodies have just an inclination to fall to the earth? then here the consequence is there, and the ground is to be found.
blocks.blomberg-s08-553: Cartesius assumed that bodies made certain vortices; still others assumed that these vortices intersected, and so they sought to explain from this the fall of bodies, and indeed always toward the center of the earth.
blocks.blomberg-s08-554: In metaphysics there are many hypotheses. The proof of the existence of God is first of all a hypothesis. One assumes a being that is the most perfect among all others, and then investigates whether explanatory grounds of it can be derived from this, of which nature, experience, and the creatures that are on the earth instruct us.
blocks.blomberg-s08-555: Plato and Malebranche assumed it as a hypothesis that human beings stand in a quite particular connection with the Godhead, and saw whether they would be able to explain from it the consequences which they perceived.
blocks.blomberg-s08-556: Hypotheses, however, really have a very great use, and can never be wholly banished from human cognition. All judges make hypotheses, which they often reject again upon better investigation. Hypotheses are the way to theory, and often to a truth quite opposed to it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-557: Through hypotheses one does not always find what one wants, but often something else; one tries, one tests, assumes something, and investigates whether one can explain the known consequences from it or not; if the first takes place, one accepts the hypothesis, if the latter takes place, one rejects it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-558: Since from the sufficiency of a ground for the consequence the truth of the ground can be inferred, and this ground is invented, it follows from this: the more is invented in a ground, the more follows licite from it, and the newer it is. And the more hypotheses must be assumed in order to explain something, the more invention takes place in it.
blocks.blomberg-s08-559: In some inferences one must invent many hypotheses subsidiarias. When we have consequences and invent the ground for them, it can often happen that we have still more consequences than the ground suffices for.
blocks.blomberg-s08-560: We must therefore invent new grounds, and these new grounds are nothing other than the hypotheses subsidiariae.
blocks.blomberg-s08-561: These, however, are really contrary to true philosophy, and show effrenis fingendi licentia. If I want to invent everything, then I want to explain everything. Unity is therefore a chief property of hypotheses, namely that one assumes a ground which suffices to explain from it all the determinations and consequences of the thing that we cognize, without, however, having to help oneself further by hypotheses subsidiarias and the assumption of them.
blocks.blomberg-s08-562: The unity of the hypothesis is a great ground for the ground's being the true one, and for no other being possible from which one could just as well explain as many consequences.
blocks.blomberg-s08-563: A chief ground of the truth of the hypothesis is also this: if one shows that the ground which one has devised for the sake of the sufficiency for the consequences deserves to be accepted on other grounds as well. Here, namely, one shows from other grounds that what is invented must be accepted; one thus confirms the truth of the hypothesis.
blocks.blomberg-s08-564: All holding-to-be-true derives from a twofold connection, namely either because the ground is sufficient to derive all the consequences from it, or because it also agrees with other grounds that have a similarity to it, and is, so to speak, aequivoce. In all hypotheses we shall therefore first show the sufficiency of the fictio historica for the consequences, and also the agreement of the fiction with other grounds, so that there are still other grounds from which some consequences can be derived. Hypotheses must first be probable as inferences, but at the same time also be capable of being confirmed through other grounds. E.g. whoever wants to explain thunderstorms assumes in the air an electrical kind of matter, and then shows from other grounds that a sulphurous and electrical matter must really be found in the air. Hypotheses have, from one side, something very disadvantageous to philosophy, insofar as they give permission to invent. From the other side, however, they are again very advantageous, namely when the fictiones are heuristic, or have as their purpose to discover something.
blocks.blomberg-s08-565: The hypothesis is thus in philosophy a really quite indispensable method of our reason and of our understanding; all hypotheses must absolutely be assumed problematically, and consequently one must not be obstinate about any hypothesis straightaway, nor hold fast to it, so that one could not soon let it go as soon as one sees its falsity or uncertainty. Often many attempts at invention are quite in vain, in that one thereby discovers no truth. Hypotheses therefore also have this harm, that, when they have been artfully devised and one has noticed in them the agreement with many consequences, they take very deep root in our understanding, and one, even when one subsequently sees their falsity, nevertheless does not let them go so easily. Thus, e.g., if this or that hypothesis were sufficient for new and correct consequences, and there is only one, e.g. the hundredth, that contradicts the ground, one rather rejects this one, although it is evidently true, than that one should let go of that hypothesis which seems to be so good. It is therefore very sad when in an age nothing but hypotheses prevail which are false, and thus do not suffice to find out the true ground of the matter. Such hypotheses harm more than they benefit, for they do not suffice to explain everything, and if one also assumes them as true, one gets, instead of true ones, nothing but false cognitions and representations. He who will not let go of false hypotheses because he has hatched them, and they seem so probable to him, is like a man who has brought up a child with much trouble and care, which he afterwards does not like to cast away, so as not to lose all his labor, trouble, and expense.

blocks.blomberg-s08-599: The word knowing is the origin, or the root word, of certainty. We have already explained a certainty above. A science, however, is nothing other than a cognition through which we know something. The word science is contradistinguished from art; hence one also commonly says in ordinary life, and the other way around, that is no science, but an art. E.g. this takes place with riddles; there one exclaims, that is no science but an art (a great difference).
blocks.blomberg-s08-600: There are actions for which a certain art, but there are also, on the other hand, certain actions for which a science is required and necessary. Something, however, is called (in order to set these concepts apart) an art for which a specific perfection of practice is required. Something is called a science, however, for which a specific perfection of theory is necessary. Every art involves a practical skill in acting. The practical skill one has in art, however, cannot be attained merely according to rules and particular certain precepts, but one must in addition have a particular talent. Furthermore, science is opposed to critique. All theoretical cognition is either a doctrine or a critique. Critique, however, is in fact nothing other than a species of theoretical (thus not practical) cognition about any product that is there, which shows us the rules according to which this product is produced. Doctrine, however, is that theoretical cognition in which one finds the grounds for how a thing can be produced, or finds the rules according to which a good product can be brought forth.
blocks.blomberg-s08-601: A critique is properly no science, for otherwise we might be able to produce good products ourselves at once. blocks.blomberg-s08-602: In certainty, what is needed is not the truth itself of the thing that we cognize, but the holding-to-be-true of it. This necessity of accepting the thing, however, does not lie in the object itself, but in the subject, because the grounds of the opposite by no means come up to those which I cognize for the truth of the thing. blocks.blomberg-s08-603: The author here also speaks of mathematical certainty, of the first and second rank. blocks.blomberg-s08-610: In this paragraph the author calls hypotheses arbitrary truths. An arbitrary proposition makes something be true, only it must not contradict itself. Such an arbitrary proposition is called positio. Nothing that is objective can ever be assumed arbitrarily, but only the subjective is fixed through arbitrariness. All arbitrary propositions bear on what one ought to do, on the practical, and thus never teach what the thing is. A positio takes place only with regard to practice, and thereby it is distinguished from the hypothesis. Arbitrary positiones that bear on actions occur chiefly in mathematics, e.g. in the circle, that one divides it into 360 degrees, in logarithms, the relation of the arithmetical to the geometrical number, proportions, progressions.
blocks.blomberg-s08-611: The word hypothesis therefore means no arbitrary proposition at all, but an opinion from certain grounds a posteriori, which are sufficient for this or that consequence.
blocks.blomberg-s08-612: In positions I really posit nothing at all that lies in the object, but that which I arbitrarily wish and want in it. And all propositions that have this constitution can be cognized only intuitively, not through reason. Through reason one can cognize no coordination at all, for reason only subordinates. blocks.blomberg-s08-623: To prove something directly means to prove something in connection with the grounds. That is an ostensive proof, whereby one shows that what is the opposite is false, hence an apagogic proof.

It is thus also far easier than the direct proof, since it brings the opposite ad absurdum, and it is established that absurdity always strikes the eye far more strongly than any and every truth, just as the greatest pleasure that has ceased is by far not so sensible to me as the opposite pain, and a pleasure is heightened through the pain that preceded it. blocks.blomberg-s08-626: The apagogic proof, however popular it may be, is thus used only so ad interim etc. The true, genuine insight, however, one obtains properly only through the direct genetic proof. blocks.blomberg-s08-660: In coordination, however, I prove first wholly from reason alone, and then wholly from experience alone, so that the proof from experience serves the proof from reason for the proof ad Evidentiam. In this way the Connubium rationis et Experientiae is produced. Experience has no need at all of the proof of reason, and conversely the proof of reason has no need of the proof of experience. Neither is subordinated to the other; both make up not one but two proofs. For in the proofs there is merely a coordination. But one can be very much deceived in this. If the proof of reason is a demonstration, or a complete proof, the proof from experience serves it for no greater strengthening at all but only for illustration, and if the proof from experience is a complete proof, the proof of reason also helps it not at all. Proofs from experience and from reason make no coordination at all, and still less, if they are already coordinated, a distinctness. Many mutually coordinated insufficient proofs never give a demonstration but are mere Probationes, and can bring about no apodictic certainty. Proofs from experience and from reason can therefore not possibly possess their evidence if they are not subordinated and subordinate to one another. Where we already find very many proofs of one thing, there we can already infer that we shall never attain to an apodictic certainty; a single proof from sufficient grounds is far better than 1000 insufficient proofs that are subordinated to one another, because one is after all not in a position to attain complete certainty through them. It does indeed often happen that in mathematics, as in the other sciences, more than one sufficient proof of one and the same thing is given, but this happens for the most part more in order to show one's art in demonstrating than because one demands still more proofs for the evidence of the thing. But if several mutually coordinated insufficient proofs are nevertheless adduced, these serve for no greater distinctness and certainty, but the thing remains, as before, unsettled.
blocks.blomberg-s08-661: One can opine without believing, namely if one has more grounds for than against the cognition. Here I hold something to be true without its having an influence on our actions. To know something, however, means nothing other than to cognize something with certainty. In belief, however, there is a great degree of holding-to-be-true, so that one would like to wager that something is true.
blocks.blomberg-s08-662: Belief is either a belief in things or in a person. One can hold a thing immediately to be true merely because one has grounds for the thing, and then it is called believing a thing. Conversely, however, one can also believe a thing immediately because a person gives it out as true, which one would otherwise not have held to be true in itself, and then one believes in a person. But this belief, which relates to a certain kind of person, is twofold. One sometimes believes everyone, be he who he may, merely because he says something, without attending to his person or his caractère or station. If someone says, e.g., that it has snowed in his region, or that many ships have arrived, one believes this simply, without investigating much; one therefore does not judge at all about the credibility of the witnesses. But in certain matters one does not believe everyone at all, but a particular credibility is required by us of the one who gives something out as true, in order that one accept it and hold it true. Belief in a person, however, is either moral or historical. The former consists in trust in the rectitude of the other, although he has made no statement of the narrative. The other, however, consists in holding true what the other asserts, merely because he affirms it. For historical belief no particular morality need be in the other, but one holds something true because he relates something that has happened. Moral belief, however, requires that one have a particular trust in a person, that he will be kind and upright. E.g. if a faithful servant, in the absence of his master, in an arising great danger, leaves his own affair in the lurch and saves the affair of his master, in the hope that he will richly reward him for these services, this is a moral belief. Historical belief is required alone in theology, that one hold something true on account of a statement. But everyone can have this belief, even the most wicked. Without fidelity and belief no republic, no commonwealth could subsist, nor could any pacta take place. Fidelity is always required with regard to him who promises something, that he also keep what was promised; belief, however, with regard to him to whom something is promised, that he namely assume as true that the other will keep his promise. Both must be joined together. For even if everyone kept faith but no one believed, no agreements etc. could take place, and just as little if all believed but no one wished to keep faith. Belief is therefore very necessary in common life; if no one wished to give credit, things would indeed very often look bad, for one cannot always pay in cash at once. It also indicates a very bad way of thinking if one trusts no one with anything, but wants to see everything that is promised and pledged to one immediately present and fulfilled. The Greeks were of such a kind; they believed no one, but wanted to have everything paid out in cash at once. Hence the proverb arose: graeca Fide mercari.
blocks.blomberg-s08-663: Theological belief trusts someone merely on his statement, and holds it true. In historical belief the object of belief is always a thing that has happened, an experience of the other, but not a judgment of reason; hence, e.g., if someone said to me with confidence: Believe me, there are inhabitants on the moon, I shall naturally be able to answer him: Have you been there? Have you seen them? What you have produced merely through reason I cannot believe of you. Consequently all judgments where the other subtilizes are no objects of historical belief. Theological belief is therefore merely historical. But religious belief is not merely historical but moral, in that one holds something true because of a promise, and therefore undertakes certain actions, in the hope of one day reaping good consequences from them in the future. Through this belief one must hope that there will be a future world, and future rewards or punishments for these actions. The natural, moral belief is found in all the virtuous, in that one believes that good actions will be rewarded of themselves, although one also sees no particular promise for oneself in this. Such a virtuous person is to be compared to a creditor; he hopes for the future good, supposing that he has as yet not a trace of it. But here we are not speaking at all of this moral belief, although it is the most worthy of consideration and the most excellent, in that one receives credit, and trusts not merely the present but the future, in that one wants to have paid not everything in the world but also some things in a future life.

It is one of the greatest human faults that they are so much inclined, when they are hearsay witnesses of a thing, to be eyewitnesses gladly. They relate a thing with such certainty and confidence as if they had seen it themselves, though they have only received it from others. But what is the difference in credibility between eyewitnesses and hearsay witnesses? The hearsay witness has, as it were, only half as much credibility as the eyewitness, for in his case I must first examine his own credibility, and then also that of him who saw the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s08-677: In the series of witnesses subordinated to one another, credibility decreases. In the series of witnesses coordinated with one another, however, the probability and credibility of the testimony always increases. E.g. if someone describes the history of a scholar or of a king, but his successor does not hand down the history itself but clothes it in his own style, and this goes on continuo ever further, the credibility thereby becomes smaller and smaller; but if many at the same time assert one and the same thing, the credibility is only the greater, especially if these are people who love honor.
blocks.blomberg-s08-678: The series of witnesses coordinated with one another is called public rumor, sive Rumor. The series of assertions subordinated to one another is called an oral transmission, Traditio oralis. But if in the series of witnesses, both coordinated and subordinated to one another, the first originator, i.e. the eyewitness, is unknown, this is a mere common saying, sive rumor sine capite; and such an assertion is little or not at all to be trusted; little belief is to be attached to it. But there are certain assertions in which one has no need at all to investigate the credibility of the witness, but which one rejects before all investigation.
blocks.blomberg-s08-679: This seems at first sight to be very harsh, but it is nevertheless certain. Cognitions that are wholly and entirely and manifestly false need no investigation at all, and altogether deserve complete contempt. Of such a kind are the assertions about the divining rod; these deserve no investigation, one can reject them at once, they deserve no refutation, for they are false in and for themselves.
blocks.blomberg-s08-680: There are thus grounds for rejecting a testimony that are not historical or taken from the constitution of the witness, but are rational and lie in the constitution of the thing itself. Yet one must be very cautious in this, and not reject a cognition at once until it is evident that the thing is manifestly false. Much seems at first sight wholly false, but on closer investigation one finds the opposite of it. All empirical judgments about the possibility or impossibility of an eventus do not yet entitle us to reject the cognition at once without examining the credibility of the witness. If someone testifies to something that is very improbable and contradicts the ordinary events in nature, he cannot yet demand that one should believe him at once on his assertion; rather, if he wants to have this, he must furnish the proof. Thus, e.g., if Pontoppidan writes that in certain seas there is an exceedingly large fish that looks like a piece of land and that he calls the Crac, he must, since such an animal has never been seen, prove it. But if someone testifies to something that agrees evidently and well with experience and reason, one believes him without proof. But if the credibility of the witness cannot be made to waver at all, while the narrative or testimony that he gives contradicts reason and experience in the highest degree, the question arises: must one in this case give assent to his assertion, and as it were disown one's reason, or not?
blocks.blomberg-s08-681: Answer: The best thing then is neither to reject the cognition nor to accept it as true, but to postpone one's assent until one has more grounds for or against it. There are sometimes persons who assert something, whose credibility one cannot doubt in the least, of whom one also cannot assume that they had the animum, or intention, to deceive others, and whom one nevertheless may not trust. The fault in their assertion then lies for the most part only in experience not having been made, or in a Vitio of memory, which does not retain it faithfully enough. Hence it also happens that people who have put forward something very probably and asserted it as true, when one asks them whether they could swear to this assertion of theirs, hesitate and must resort to all sorts of evasions. They then commonly say that they might well have forgotten something since that time. The imagination can also quite well reproduce for them other images than the experiences were that they have had.

blocks.blomberg-s08-686: The union of all these three sources of cognition rests on their having not one but many proofs as their ground. But if one source of cognition is sufficient to give a complete proof of a thing, then one does not need the others. If something can be demonstrated completely and evidently through reason, then one does not need experience to make the proof still more complete. blocks.blomberg-s09-001: If a cognition contains in itself motive grounds for actions, then it is practical. All practical cognition is either a cognition of ends or of means; the latter must be distinguished from the former. Practical geometry teaches no ends, no motive grounds for actions, but only means of attaining certain ends. It shows the conditions under which an end can be reached with respect to measuring.
blocks.blomberg-s09-002: All doctrine of skill is a practical cognition of means. All doctrine of morality, however, is a practical cognition of ends, as is also the doctrine of prudence. Our author speaks in this whole section generally of cognition as it relates to the free will. In logic, however, the relation of cognition to the will is not considered at all, but this belongs in morals. The relation of the free will is not an objectum domesticum of logic. The practical science of skill gives us no motive grounds at all for certain actions. For any science whatever that shows only means and no ends contains no motive grounds; all motive grounds, namely, must be derived from the end. A cognition is called practical insofar as it is contradistinguished from the theoretical
blocks.blomberg-s09-003: cognition, or from mere contemplation and speculation. A cognition, however, is practical either explicite or implicite. Explicite when it itself shows the rules for actions; implicite when it offers the motive grounds or presents such truths from which certain practical rules for actions can be derived. E.g. the proposition: you shall not lie, you shall be faithful and honest, is practical explicite. But the proposition: There is a God, consequently one is obliged also to arrange one's actions in such a way as is in conformity with the holy will of this divine being, is practical implicite. In metaphysics there are for the most part pure speculationes, not practical but theoretical, which therefore have no influence on the free will. Such speculationes are neither harmful nor useful. For they contain no grounds at all for actions. Many subtleties and errors devised by human beings are nothing other than pure speculations. We therefore pass over this section, because it is introduced here unsuitably and belongs more in morals than in logic, and no advantage is to be hoped for in logic from treating it, for logic likewise occupies itself with speculative cognitions.

If I only have an object first, I can soon ascribe to it an enormous magnitude, which can indeed cause admiration, but no emotion. But there are also involuntary inventions, or involuntary

blocks.blomberg-s10-041: The distinctness of a concept is a property of a logical perfection. Making distinct occurs through analysis. If, however, I make distinct a concept that contains, e.g., many marks, then I shall have to seek to avoid tautology among these marks; I shall thus promote the precision of the marks, i.e. I shall restrict the quantity of the marks, without however being detrimental to their quality. Also the totality of the distinct representation of a thing is asked about, and this totality I often need very much. In all distinctness of concepts I can be content with partiality, but if my marks are sufficient for the whole concept of the thing, then I have a totality. But if precision is also asked for, then I have a complete, precise concept of a thing, and that is a definition. The definition, and the action of our soul in it, can be compared completely with the reduction of fractions ad minimos Terminos occurring in arithmetic, e.g. 4/2 3/6 2/3 1/3 = 4/12. And this is also the aim of defining. We want 1) a distinct, 2) a complete, and then 3) a precise concept of a thing. In order therefore to seek whether a definition is correct, we always ask 1) whether this alleged definition is true as a proposition, and so we can use many definitiones as true propositions, in which many marks otherwise imperceptible occur to us. False definitiones can sometimes even be of use to us as true propositions; indeed, one can often even do quite well without the usefulness of such a true proposition of the whole definition. Supposing it does not fulfill what it promised, it can nevertheless be so useful, it can always create benefit, even though it does not attain its aim.
blocks.blomberg-s10-042: 2:) One asks whether the definition is distinct as a concept, whether I can cognize it clearly. For all distinctness, however, it is required that a mark be a clear ground of cognition of the thing. All tautology in the definitions is therefore a lack of distinctness, and such a definition is not only no definition, but also no distinct concept. All empty propositions are tautological. The soul, e.g., is in an animal a ruling monad; this proposition is not empty, but in it a comparative obscurum is explained per aeque obscurum. The uselessness of this proposition, however, can still be removed here. With tautology, however, this is not possible at all. 3:) One asks whether the definition as a distinct concept is exhaustive, that is: distinct. nam definire est fines conceptus alicuius ponere. I.e. the definition is a determination of everything that belongs to the thing.
blocks.blomberg-s10-043: 4to It is asked whether this distinct and exhaustive concept is also commensurate, that is precise, namely that the marks of the definition do not flow out of one another, or are not subordinated to one another, but are coordinated to one another.
