If everything were omitted without which a concept nevertheless remains distinct and complete, then such a concept is called: conceptus rem adaequans. Completeness, therefore, and the precision of a concept together make up its adequation. An Adaequatum therefore admits no Comparativum. As regards the matter, I think to myself indeed always the same object, but not in the same, but in another manner; what I previously represented to myself of the Definitum confuse, that I represent to myself in the definition distinctly, and accordingly every definition must be distinct. For distinctness in general, however, and thus also with the distinctness of a definition, marks are required; these marks, however, must first be clear concepts, they must also be still clearer than the concept of the Definitum, and from this flows this canon: ne definiatur obscurum per aeque obscurum. E.g. if I wanted to say to someone who does not know what a Monas is: the soul is a monad thinking in the body, this would again violate this rule. Secondly, however, these marks must also be clear grounds of cognition. For as a ground of cognition it is still supposed to be distinguished from the consequence, consequently it must be thought differently, and far more clearly, than in the Definitum, for he names no ground to me who says merely one and the same thing. And from this flows this rule: ne Notae in definitione Sint Tavtologicae. Otherwise one also calls this defining per circulum. The Circulus vitiosus in definiendo is either implicitus (concealed) or Explicitus, namely when even according to the expressions the marks are the same. It is certainly curious that the means of cognizing identity are exactly opposed to those I make use of in order to see their diversity from others. blocks.blomberg-s10-071: But what aim, we ask, do we have in this?
blocks.blomberg-s10-072: The aim in this is not to obtain the cognition of the Definitum through its dissection, but only to give the Definitum a meaning. The end here is thus only the prior signification, so that this, namely, may not be lost altogether from the language. For example, in the Harz mountains one already calls the spruces firs, and again the firs spruces. I define an Empirical concept in order afterwards always to add something to it per Synthesin. But I never define a concept of experience in order to get to know the object through dissection. I do not define a concept of experience, e.g. gold, in order to infer something from it and to draw consequences out of this definition, but only in order thereby to fix the meaning of the word of the Definitum. Here we remark this: the definitiones of morals are analytic, and serve so that I may draw from this concept all possible consequences. The definitiones of morals are all real, and I therefore need only analyze them; so it is really curious that one can infer their particular kind from the use of definitions. Empirical definitions go only to the understanding, but not at all to reason (for only through the understanding do I see the meaning), and they therefore also have no Philosophical use at all. From this it follows that the Definitiones of Empirical concepts are wholly unnecessary, for even if there could really be some, they would still be only nominal definitiones. For I do not say of them: all this taken together makes up the whole concept of the thing, but only: this is all that I think in the concept of the thing. All Empirical concepts are capable only of Description, all arbitrary concepts are Synthetic, and their Definition real. Finally, all concepts of reason are, because they are given, analytic, and their Definitiones likewise real. Now all distinctness of definitiones can be attained only through reason per analysin, and the concept of reason becomes complete only Successive, namely when I weigh one clear mark after the other; and since every cognition, when it has clear marks, is a judgment, all definitiones are at the same time judgments. blocks.blomberg-s11-001: Properly we already know judgments from the previous Section, since we have dealt with distinct concepts, which, however, can arise only through a judgment, for to cognize distinctly means to cognize everything through a clear mark. But to cognize something through a clear mark means likewise to judge. We can therefore also say: distinct concepts are those that are cognized through a judgment. Now: the 2 concepts that are compared with one another, and indeed in such a way that the one contains the marks and the other the clarity, make up the matter of the judgment. That concept which is to be made distinct through comparison with its mark is called the Subject; that concept, on the other hand, which is added to the mark as a ground of distinctness, is called the Praedicate.
blocks.blomberg-s11-002: The comparison is twofold, for I can compare 2 concepts either through the relation of connection, or through the relation of conflict with one another. A judgment in which the predicate is thought as connected to the subject is called an affirmative judgment. A judgment, however, in which the predicate is thought as in conflict with the Subject is called a negative judgment. The form of the judgment is the relation. The sign that indicates this relation or the form is the copula est. And since every relation is either affirmative or negative, the copula est, when it is simply affirmative, is accompanied with yes (id est simply with est), but when it is negative, with an id est non. The negation no, or the non, does not affect the matter at all, but only the form of the judgment; it must therefore be set not at the subject or at the Praedicate, but at the Copula, e.g. anima non est mortalis but not anima est non mortalis, for otherwise the negation does not affect the form of the judgment of reason but the matter of the judgment, and consequently it is then also no negative judgment but a so-called Judicium infinitum.

blocks.blomberg-s11-010: The following remark is well to be annotated: Omnia Judicia sunt vel problematica, vel assertoria (decisive). A problematic judgment is one in which I merely consider the relation of two concepts indeterminately, but do not posit it; I weigh something in it as given, for investigation, i.e. I fix no relation in it, but only see what, were it actual, would follow from it. They have, notwithstanding this, a great use. For through the relation of two such judgments one can nevertheless learn to use a certain caution in judging, and to make our judgments advantageous.
blocks.blomberg-s11-011: All relation in judgments is either a relation of connection or a relation of conflict. That judgment through which the relation of connection of two judgments with one another is indicated is called a Hypothetical judgment. That judgment, however, in which the relation of conflict of two judgments is indicated is called a Disjunctive judgment. One calls, namely, those judgments in which one thinks the relation of two judgments with one another, relation judgments (relative); these judgments now consider the relation of one judgment to the other, either according to connection, and then they are Hypothetical judgments, or according to conflict, and they are then disjunctive judgments. In the former one always finds the relation of ground to consequences. In conditional judgments, then, that which contains the ground is called antecedens or also prius. But that which contains the consequences is called in them consequens or posterius. As for the disjunctive judgments, however, the relation of conflict in them is again of two kinds: either it is a relation of two or more judgments that contradict one another; but we shall show that a true disjunctive judgment occurs only with two, and not at all with more judgments, for no true and pure contradiction can occur otherwise than only with two concepts that stand precisely opposed to one another in opposition. It is then also called a bimembris propositio, and since the disjunctive judgments thus contain in themselves the relation of a true contradiction, they can comprehend only 2 judgments. If we judge merely rationally, the Propositio disjunctiva in the judgment must be Bimembris; but all those disjunctive judgments whose propositio disjunctiva is not bimembris have arisen from Induction, for how else do I know that I have enumerated the cases rightly, than only from experience, and so per inductionem. A Disjunctive judgment, if it is to become certain without Induction, must be bimembris. A disjunctive judgment is nothing more than a representation of a logical division, or Repraesentatio Divisionis Logicae.

Logic now has the duty, it must express the exponible judgments. What do the questions mean: Quae? Qualis? Quanta? 1. The question Qualis est propositio? aims at the quality, namely whether the judgment was affirmative or negative. 2. Quanta est propositio? contained the question whether it was a universal or a particular judgment. 3. quae est propositio? is the question whether the Judicium is purum or modale. Modal, however, a judgment is called which carries a condition of judgment with the Praedicatum. To these questions one must answer according to the constitution of the judgment. If now an empty judgment came up, one was therefore accustomed to say: Quae? qualis? Quanta? i.e. there is not the least thing in the judgment.
blocks.blomberg-s11-013: A judgment is expressed practically when it enunciates a possibly necessary action. This seems indeed to be contradictory, something is possibly necessary. But it is entirely correct here, for the action is indeed always necessary if I want to bring the thing about, but the case is not necessary, but merely possible. It is very good that with this kind of judgments one does not set the Imperativum, [965a] but only the Infinitivum, and expresses them with it, as when etc.
blocks.blomberg-s11-014: Provably certain means nothing other than a mediately certain judgment. A judgment, however, is on the other side absolutely unprovable if it is immediately certain. And such judgments must also be met with in the human understanding, for even if we have ever so many consequences, and can cognize these from their grounds as from their marks, we must nevertheless finally come to a ground which is no further a consequence of another ground, but is itself the very first mark of all consequences, and this is then immediately certain, or an unprovably certain judgment. Whether there is only one such absolutely first ground, or many of the kind, is dealt with in Metaphysics.
blocks.blomberg-s11-015: All unprovable judgments, in so far as they are the ground of all judgments, are called Principles and are either Theoretical or practical. A practically unprovable proposition is called a Postulatum. All these Principia are either material, in so far as they have a medium terminus, or Formal, which have no medium terminus. These have no determinate Praedicate at all, but go only to the relation of predicates to subjects in general. To these belong the Principium contradictionis and the Principium Identitatis. For these there is no determinate Subject and Praedicate, or no determinate case, but it can be applied to every subject and predicate. We have now in our judgments a twofold form, namely the Synthetic and the analytic form; the Principium contradictionis, however, is only analytic.
blocks.blomberg-s11-016: Here the author gives an instruction for Demonstration. One has, just as Tavtological Definitiones, so also Tavtological Resolutiones, where one answers just the same as what one asked. And so our author does here too. If a Quaestion is at hand, one should attend very well whether the pretended answer and Resolution of the Quaestion is not merely a dissection of the Quaestion itself. For then I have not taught the other to resolve the Quaestion, but merely made known to him, through dissection, what was in it. I have thus done nothing more than made him understand better that which he asked me. So the author too often does. It is curious, he shows me merely that I am to do that about which I ask him, and does not show me at all how I am to do it. In my last Disputation de mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et Principiis I also had various quaestiones to resolve, but I did not merely dissect the Quaestiones, but in fact also indicated quite correct and complete marks of the things. E.g. pag. 30 § 25 (vid. Dict. Metaph. where this Disputation is bound in) There, namely, this infallible mark of sensibility is adduced: Si de conceptu quocunque intellectuali generaliter quicquam praedicatur, quod pertinet ad respectus Spatii atque Temporis: objective non est enuntiandum et non denotat nisi conditionem, sine qua conceptus datus sensitive cognoscibilis non est. vid. ibid.
blocks.blomberg-s11-017: Where the author speaks of intuiting judgments. An intuiting judgment is properly a singular judgment, in so far as it is immediately cognized, but a Judicium discursivum is a concluded judgment. All immediate judgments, however, are intuiting only for this reason, that they are immediately cognized, in so far as their form is Sensitive; for otherwise, when the form is rational, the immediate judgments are nevertheless not intuiting judgments at all; to intuiting judgments only the Discursive could be Contradistinguished, and the ancients called the universal
blocks.blomberg-s11-018: judgments Discursiva, but the singular ones intuitiva, and so we want to take it here too. This was now about intuiting or experiential judgments. Whether a judgment is an experiential judgment or not belongs to Metaphysics to investigate. Logic does not consider judgments at all in so far as they are given, as Metaphysics does, but in so far as it is to compare them. Logic shows only whether the judgments are universal or particular, and so it occupies itself only with opposition and identity. All propositions are either theoretical or practical. The first are those that show only the relation of concepts to other concepts, but the others indicate the relation of action to concepts. Both kinds of propositions, however, are provable or unprovable. Theoretically provable propositions, when they arise through a ratiocinium polysyllogisticum, are called Theoremata. Every provable proposition, however, that is only monosyllogistic is called a Corollarium. A practically provable proposition is a Problema, a practically unprovable proposition, however, a Postulatum. With all theoretically provable propositions the proposition itself is the Theorema, but the proof of the proposition the Demonstration; the action that is to be done in it is called the Quaestio; the propositions according to which it is cognized, the Resolution of it. A lemma is a proposition that is indeed provable, but not in this discipline but in another, from which it is taken. One must be very much on one's guard with this, so that one does not assume something and give it out as already proved in another science, when it has not yet been proved in it at all; indeed one often finds in the authors something that they assume at the beginning, which they promise to prove at the end, but the proof is forgotten. Scholia are propositions that are added to a doctrinal edifice not as essentialia but only as accidentalia.
blocks.blomberg-s11-019: Every inference is in general a judgment, only with this difference: if the judgment is mediate, it is an inference of reason, or a mediate inference. But if the judgment is immediate, the inference is only an inference of the understanding; namely, one is judged from the other absque medio Termino, and then the judgment, or also the Conclusio, is immediata; or one is inferred from the other per medium Terminum, and then the inference is mediate, or also an inference of reason. We now want to consider only mediate inferences. As for their manner of arising, it is 5-fold, for they can arise either
blocks.blomberg-s11-024: 5) per Contrapositionem. As for the consequentia per Judicia aequipollentia, since both judgments in it are wholly one and the same with one another, there is properly no Consequens at all, and so the so-called inference per Judicia aequipollentia is no inference. The Consequentia per Judicia Subalternata occurs without any change in the position of the Termini; the quality also remains the same, only the Quantity is changed in it. In the consequentia per Conversionem Logicam likewise the quality must never, but only the Quantity, be changed. In the conversio Logica, however, both the position of the Termini and the quality must be changed in it. With the oppositio Judiciorum the Logicians have made the following division:
blocks.blomberg-s11-025: 1: Contradictorie 2 judgments are opposed to one another when a particular negative judgment (or conversely) is set against an affirmative judgment, e.g. all men are mortal, but some are not mortal.
blocks.blomberg-s11-026: 2 Subcontraria are judgments when, in 2 Particular judgments that have the same Subject and Praedicate, the one is affirmative and the other negative.
blocks.blomberg-s11-027: 3 there is also a Contrarietas Judicii, which occurs when, in 2 judgments, the one is universal affirmative and the other universal negative. The Judicia Subcontraria contain less, or not enough, than belongs to a correct opposition; the Judicia contraria contain more, and the Judicia contradictoria just as much as is enough for a proper opposition. And we can therefore say: Judicia subcontraria, because they do not contain enough, can 1) both be true, but they can 2) not both be false.
blocks.blomberg-s11-028: Secondly, Judicia Contraria can both be false, for there is too much in both, and in their very too much they can also be false. Of 2 pure oppositions this must always be able to hold: posito uno tollitur alterum. et vice versa In all Logical Conversion (vid. ant. § 346) of judgments the judgment that is to be turned around is called conversum, the judgment that is to arise from this reversal, convertens. A Conversio in which the quality of the judgment is not hindered is called Simplex, but where it is hindered, conversio per accidens. Universal affirmative judgments can be converted per accidens, but all negative judgments can be converted Simpliciter, and finally the particular ones can all be converted Simpliciter; that is the sole rule of logical conversion. The rule of Contraposition is this: universal affirmative judgments can only be contraposed.
blocks.blomberg-s12-001: Inferences of reason are judgments which occur mediately by means of a medius Terminus. There are also, namely, as said before, certain judgments and consequences, which we called immediatas; these were indemonstrable. We also called these consequences of a judgment from other judgments that are unprovable not an inference of reason but an inference of the understanding. But from the other side there are still certain consequences from other mediate judgments, and these are always provable. There are uncertain Apparent inferences, which are not inferences of reason but only mere Themata for them, and of this kind are the so-called Ratiocinia Disjunctiva, and Hypothetica, or also Speciosa. Of these inferences, which are only Themata for inferences of reason, we do not want to treat here at all, but only of the inferences of reason themselves.
blocks.blomberg-s12-002: If two concepts are put together, one of which is the mark of the other, a certain relation is posited in these concepts. This relation can now be represented immediately, and then it is a Judicium; but if it happens per notam intermediam, then it is a Ratiocinium. Or the inference of reason is nothing other than the comparison of a nota remota with the thing itself, by means of a Nota intermedia. The mediate relation of a Nota remota is always remota with regard to the thing, but also nota proxima of the Nota intermedia, and thus a Nota rei ipsius, with the given concept; that is a Judicium medium, or a ratiocinium.
blocks.blomberg-s12-003: An adaequate inference consists in an inference of reason whose rule is this: nota notae rei est nota rei ipsius; and this is also the fundamental rule of all syllogistic, and at the same time the whole difference between a judgment and an inference of reason. For a Judicium requires an immediate clear mark, but a Ratiocinium in addition a mediate clear mark. Consequently the Ratiocinium is the relation of the nota remota, through a nota mediata, vel intermedia, to a certain given concept of a thing. In a Ratiocinium, then, these 3 actions occur: 1mo the Nota proxima or intermedia is compared with the nota remota, 2 the Nota proxima is compared with the thing, et 3tio the Nota remota is compared with the thing itself. The nota intermedia is also called the medius Terminus. Since now in every judgment the predicate constitutes the majorem Terminum, we can say: in every inference of reason there are 3 Termini. 1. the proposition that I am to cognize by means of the nota intermedia, 2: the Nota remota, and 3rdly the Terminus medius, or the nota intermedia, which contains in itself the ground of the relation of the thing to the nota remota. And these make up the 3 Terminos, namely Majorem, minorem et conclusionem. In every inference of reason 1. the Terminus major is compared in the Termino medio, or the nota proxima with the nota remota, 2 the Terminus medius with the minor, or the subject, and finally 3: the minor with the Major, or the predicate.
blocks.blomberg-s12-004: Thus to infer requires only the synthetic kind of reason; this now always requires that one descend from the general to the particular. If one reverses this, it is again against reason, and a leap is immediately committed. And therefore the major propositio must also always come first, or the predicate of the conclusion; or first I must go per notam remotam to the nota proxima, then I must go again from the Nota proxima to the thing, and finally from the thing to the nota remota. That is the synthesis of reason, and if one loses sight of it, one also fails to observe the order. In every inference of reason there are thus certain Termini, of which there must be no more than 3, and in every proper inference of reason there are likewise no more than 3 iudicia. The first 2 are called the premises, but the 3rd judgment is called the Conclusion. The premises now make up the matter, but the conclusion the form of inferences of reason; hence the correct form of an inference of reason will rest solely and alone on the correct following of the conclusion. In both inferences the medius Terminus or the Nota intermedia always occurs (but not at all in the Consequens itself). Every inference of reason is nothing other than a representation of a mark by means of a Terminus medius. It belongs to an inference of reason that one mark be subordinated to another mark of the thing, as to a Nota notae. Thus in an inference of reason I compare the Nota remota with the Nota proxima, then the thing with the nota proxima, and finally also the nota remota with the thing itself. All form of inferences of reason is only twofold, and there are no more, for the judgment is either immediate or mediate
blocks.blomberg-s12-005: The fundamental rules of all affirmative inferences are these:
blocks.blomberg-s12-006: 1: Nota Notae rei est nota rei ipsius
blocks.blomberg-s12-008: 2:) of all negative inferences will therefore be this:
blocks.blomberg-s12-009: Repugnans Nota Notae rei, repugnat rei ipsi. This is now the fundamental rule of all inferences of reason.
blocks.blomberg-s12-010: The logicians have a certain Dictum de omni et nullo, which they hold to be the very first ground of all ratiociniorum. But these fundamental rules cited here precede even this.
blocks.blomberg-s12-011: The Dictum de omni et nullo reads thus among the logicians: what belongs to a general concept belongs also to all concepts that are contained under it.
blocks.blomberg-s12-012: If in an inference of reason the relation of two judgments (not of two concepts) is weighed, that is called a Ratiocinium Extraordinarium; or if an inference of reason is adopted in which the major propositio is not a Judicium ordinarium but a Judicium Extraordinarium, then it is likewise called a ratiocinium Extraordinarium. All ratiocinia Extraordinaria are either Hypothetica or Disjunctiva. For either the relation of connection or the relation of opposition is indicated in them; if the first, it is called a hypothetical, but in the other case a disjunctive inference of reason. The Judicium Hypotheticum consists of only 2 propositions, and so no Judicium Hypotheticum can produce a ratiocinium. In a Judicium Hypotheticum only the consequens needs to be proved, for nothing is enunciated and asserted in it. But with Judiciis Categoricis not only the Consequens but also the Assertion itself must be proved from correct grounds. The conditioned inference is no inference of reason, but only the Substratum for an inference of reason, for it must first still be proved per ratiocinium. It is first the Quaestion itself, and the Datum, that is still to be proved; thus properly nothing is yet proved by it, but only a ground stated, of which one at the same time affirms that its consequence is correct; but how it is correct, that I do not see at all thereby. It is merely, so to speak, the ground of proof, not the proof itself; that is to say: thereby only the matter but not the form of the proof is given. This analysis is certainly not at all unnecessary, and quite correct. For in a Judicio conditionali no subject is connected with a predicate through a mediate mark at all, and there is no major propositio in such an inference at all; and so they are also not proper inferences of reason at all, but only Substrata for them. One does not really infer according to them, but only says there what one wants to infer. All proof goes either to the truth of the antecedens or of the consequens. Every Syllogismus Hypotheticus has 2 modos, namely a modum ponentem, where an affirmation is inferred in the Conclusion, and the modum tollentem, where a negation is inferred. An affirmation is here inferred according to the rule: atqui verum est prius, ergo quoque posterius. But the negation from the falsity of the consequens to the falsity of the antecedens, and indeed according to the rule: atqui falsum est prius, ergo quoque posterius remoto antecedente non tollitur consequens sed sublata consequentia tollitur antecedens. Thus I can never infer here a negatione antecedentis to the negationem consequentis, but certainly conversely.
blocks.blomberg-s12-013: As for disjunctive inferences, these are inferences in which the major propositio is disjunctive. A disjunctive inference is a logical division; in it I represent to myself a divided concept, and all membra that are equal to the Diviso. The subject of the major propositio in it is the Divisum, and the predicate is all the membra dividentia. Consequently the correctness of a disjunctive inference rests on the correctness of a logical division: namely, everything must stand in true disjunction and opposition to one another, and moreover everything must also be complete.
blocks.blomberg-s12-014: A Dilemma is properly a ratiocinium Hypotheticum whose consequence is disjunctive. One therefore proceeds in it according to the rules of the hypothetical as well as of the disjunctive kind of inference. atqui falsum est prius, ergo etiam posterius. One never has a Dilemma as modum ponendi, but always as modum tollendi. By a Dilemma we seek not to prove a proposition properly, but only to convince someone of falsity. The Dilemma is otherwise also called Cornutum, because by it one refutes the other and at the same time cuts off all his ways: whichever way he may go, he is caught. And therefore this Dilemma is also much used in dialectic. On that account the Sceptici, too, were very fond of it.
blocks.blomberg-s12-015: Here the author speaks of immediate inferences, but this is not at all fitting, for they are not inferences of reason at all but only inferences of the understanding. For they have no medium Terminum.
blocks.blomberg-s12-016: Are either formal inferences of reason, or ratiocinia cryptica. Ratiocinia Cryptica are those where I enunciate only 2 judgments but think the 3rd along with them. In such a Syllogismo one always says less than one arbitrarily thinks, and that is the so-called dissimulating, which is very often salutary and fair. But simulating means that one speaks otherwise than one thinks, and is of course to be wholly rejected as unfair.
blocks.blomberg-s12-017: Enthymema: this is an inference in which only 2 judgments, namely a praemissa and the conclusio, are posited. To these belong also the ratiocinia Contracta. These are syllogisms where there are not 2 propositions at all, but only one proposition and the medius Terminus. Further, induction also belongs here, which is especially noteworthy. The rule of reason in apodictic certainty in inferences always goes from the general to the particular. But there are nevertheless still inferences in which we infer from the particular to the general. The former is the ratiocinatio rigida; the latter, however, the ratiocinatio laxa. To the latter now belong 1.) the Inductio, 2.) the Analogy. Induction is the inference where I hold that which belongs to many things under a general inference and concept to be true, as if it belonged to all. I infer thus: what belongs to so many things that I have ever cognized must also belong to all that are of this kind and species. This kind of inference is indeed quite contrary to the logical rule, but one cannot do without it at all, and with it most of our cognitions would at the same time have to be abolished.
blocks.blomberg-s12-018: As to 2ndly the inference according to an analogy, this is nothing other than an induction, but only an induction with regard to the predicate. Namely, if 2 things have agreed in all the properties that I have been able to cognize in them, then they will also agree with each other in the remaining properties that I have not cognized in them, and so the inference reads with regard to analogy. Analogy and induction are merely the crutches for our understanding. For in general propositions of truth we will indeed always be able to proceed with logical rigor, but in the use of our cognition (a posteriori) we must often make do with the probable.
blocks.blomberg-s12-019: There is a complete and also an incomplete induction. Complete, when its membra are equal to the given concept, or when everything can be derived from a particular concept.
blocks.blomberg-s12-020: Every inference false in form is a Paralogismus. But every false inference that is supposed to be a means of producing an error in another is called a Sophisma. There are various Sophismata that could be given many names, which however is not at all necessary. Otherwise there are still some Sophismata that deserve a place in logica, for some of them can be truer than the others. Otherwise the author also mentions here the Sophisma ignorationis elenchi. But for us only this is to be noted about it: he who in a dispute forgets the point in dispute commits a Sophisma ignorationis elenchi.
blocks.blomberg-s12-021: If inferences of reason are coordinated with one another, a Ratiocinium Compositum arises from it, also polysyllogisticum. The Polysyllogisticus is called a Ratiocinium when the Conclusio of one inference of reason is the Praemissa of another. That Syllogismus whose Conclusio is the premise of another is called Prosyllogismus. But that Syllogismus whose Praemissa is a conclusion of the previous one is called Episyllogismus. Or, more briefly: the Prosyllogismus contains the ground, but the Episyllogismus the consequence, of an inference of reason. vid. auct: § 406: § 408: There are Sorites per Syllogismos Hypoth: and then it is also called Sorites Hypotheticus, or the Sorites can arise per Syllogismos Categoricos, and then it is also called Categoricus.
blocks.blomberg-s12-022: The formalia ratiocinia are used only in disputing, not in books and the like, for otherwise this would become too tedious. And as for the many inferences of reason otherwise, they make things more indistinct than distinct. But they are expressed only on this account, as reason actually thinks.
blocks.blomberg-s12-023: Where the author speaks of the leap in proof, of the legitimate as well as of the illegitimate, we note here only this: nullus Saltus in intellectu est possibilis, et non aliter Saltus possibilis est, quam in enunciando. The immediate connection of a remote ground with the consequence is namely a leap. In thought such a leap is wholly impossible, but in the Enunciation it can certainly take place, and in this case it can sometimes certainly be legitimus too, namely if I believe that the other will unfailingly know what is omitted, and so Supply it in thought.
blocks.blomberg-s12-024: The actual omission of a proposition that deserves a proof is called Petitio Principii. This comes from Peto, I ask. For with such a kind of conviction I must, as it were, ask the other for his assent, and from this we see that this can be called no proof at all.
blocks.blomberg-s12-025: The Circulus in demonstrando is that fault when one assumes the conclusion in a proof as its own premise. This happens
blocks.blomberg-s12-026: 1:) when one wants to prove that which is indemonstrably true, or immediately certain.
blocks.blomberg-s12-027: 2:) when one wants to prove indemonstrably false propositions; in both these cases the circle in proving is always necessary. But it arises chiefly
blocks.blomberg-s12-028: 3:) when, namely, one is already certain of the truth of a proposition that is demonstrable before any proof; then one already grants the proof to the other, and therefore a circle in proving can always creep in.
blocks.blomberg-s12-029: A proof proves too little if it proves only a part of the proposition. It proves too much if it proves more than can be proved. A proof that proves too little can be true, but a proof that proves too much is always false. For when it is said: the proof proves too much, that is as much as: it proves more than is true, but this is nothing other than that it is false.
blocks.blomberg-s12-030: The author finally still says something about the utility of inferences of reason, which seems almost unnecessary, for who indeed will not hold the use of reason to be useful?
blocks.blomberg-s13-001: The method of teaching is nothing other than the form of a whole of cognitions, insofar as it is arranged according to the rules of logical perfection
blocks.blomberg-s13-002: Since, however, logical perfection is twofold, namely either logical perfection according to healthy reason, or logical perfection according to learnedness and science, the method of teaching can be divided in the same way. For the rules of healthy reason are distinguished from the rules of science. To be sure, in all sciences and learnedness the method of healthy reason must prevail; but conversely not everything that is found in learnedness need also be in healthy reason. In all sciences I do not look to how something appears in practice, but to how it can also be judged before all practice. I look to how something can also be thought in abstracto; but if I go, on the contrary, according to the rules of healthy reason, I must always show everything in concreto. The other kind is a cognition that carries a certain life with it; the first, however, serves merely for speculation and the desire for knowledge. The methods of the learned are now distinguished:

blocks.blomberg-s13-016: Analysis and synthesis are either according to coordination or according to subordination
blocks.blomberg-s13-017: α) the synthesis of coordination is the combination of the parts with the whole.
blocks.blomberg-s13-018: β) but the analysis of coordination is the resolution of the whole into its parts.
blocks.blomberg-s13-019: γ) the synthesis of subordination is the combination of the grounds with the consequences

blocks.blomberg-s13-021: In all historical cognitions the connection is that of coordination, but in all rational cognitions only the connection of subordination takes place. In history I namely count one thing after another, whether according to space or to time. But in rational cognitions and sciences we always derive one thing from another. In analytic coordination I namely go from the whole to its parts, but in synthetic coordination from the parts to the whole.
blocks.blomberg-s13-022: The analytic method is most advisable in historical cognitions. First I must namely form for myself an idea of the whole, and then I make an idea and concepts of the parts contained under it. In all rational cognitions the form is that of subordination, and this is now either synthetic or analytic. With the former I go from the ground to the consequence, with the latter from the consequence to the ground.
blocks.blomberg-s13-023: The artificial method of teaching is contradistinguished from the natural, just as a distinction is to be made between a reasonable cognition, i.e. one that does not contradict reason, and a rational cognition, if one understands by it one that arises from reason. The method of teaching must be natural not so much subjectively as objectively, i.e. appropriate to the object.
blocks.blomberg-s13-025: Methodus Tabellaris, i.e. to comprehend and to sketch a whole science in tables, is very fine. blocks.blomberg-s13-027: The Socratic method of teaching takes place through conversations, in which by well-arranged questions one brings everything out of the pupil and leads him to answers. It has great utility. It is a kind of catechetical method, but it is very tiring.

blocks.blomberg-s13-034: Science is a complete Disciplin. With Doctrin I direct my attention only to what is taught, with Disciplin I look to the method. Doctrin and Disciplin thus take place in historical cognitions just as well as in dogmatic ones. With sciences there must always be Doctrin.
blocks.blomberg-s13-035: One thinks tumultuarily when one thinks without method.
blocks.blomberg-s13-036: To meditate does not mean to recall cognitions that one has had, but to produce new ones that one has not yet had. Methodical meditating hinders one from procuring enough materials for meditating. In the beginning one meditates Tumultuarily; one must write down what occurs to us, as thoughts sometimes come into our mind that we would not otherwise have. One first writes down all thoughts as they come, without order; afterward one begins to Coordinate, and then to Subordinate. In every elaboration 3 labors must precede
blocks.blomberg-s13-037: 1) One writes down all thoughts without order
blocks.blomberg-s13-039: 3) One works out all the parts
blocks.blomberg-s13-040: Doubting exercises one in reflection, but so does the endeavor to understand everyone's opinion correctly and to be able to put oneself in it. It is good if one alternates meditating with other sciences that are restorative.
blocks.blomberg-s14-002: The constitution of words is a worthy object of the philosopher's reflections. The right use is that they designate a thought precisely.
blocks.blomberg-s14-003: A Terminus inanis is one whose meaning we believe we understand, but in fact do not understand. An expression is deceptive (d ecept rix) where we believe something is possible, and yet it is impossible.
blocks.blomberg-s14-004: A Terminus Familiaris is the expression whose sense has never been investigated, because it has never been noticed. Every language has such. I say, e.g., süchtig; such Termini are on closer investigation also often deceptive.
blocks.blomberg-s14-005: The words, the peddling of the learned, is a deceptive trade, in which one passes off words for things; what is more common than this expression, and deception! An expression is called intelligible that can be understood. Something can be intelligible without being distinct. If 2 expressions have one meaning, or where at least the meanings are not very different, they are called synonymous expressions. If an expression has more than one meaning, it is called Terminus vagus ambiguus anceps.
blocks.blomberg-s15-002: Style properly means the tool of a sculptor. Here it means the character of expressing one's thoughts. Everyone has his own particular style, just as everyone writes his own particular hand. Style is to be considered 1) insofar as it is appropriate to its object, 2) to the person (subject) and his station, 3) to those for whom one writes. A particular style suits each, and not everyone can bring his thoughts into the form of another.
blocks.blomberg-s15-003: The propriety of the manner of writing consists in its being so constituted that it is not too grand but fitting for the matter. The euphony of the manner of writing is something that belongs more among the chimeras than to the true. The English say that Virgil's poems sound well, but if one hears an Englishman recite the verses, this would be intolerable to our ears. The Sonorum consists in the measure of the syllables. Congruence consists in the style's being suited to the matter. This can be learned only through experience.
blocks.blomberg-s16-002: On the Donum Didacticum and the requisites of a teacher. In general 2 things must be found in a teacher. He must possess 1) a Condescendenz to the weaker, and 2) a Coadscendenz to the higher capacities
blocks.blomberg-s16-003: 1. Every teacher must know how to put himself in the place of his listeners; I can instruct another only through his own understanding, hence I have a matter to work on that already lies in the other's head. This is called Condescendenz; it presupposes that one knows how to put oneself in the place of those whom one instructs. Very few teachers of religion, and others, can do this.
blocks.blomberg-s16-004: 2): the 2nd Requisitum of a teacher is Coadscendenz, namely that one ascend to the talents that are raised above the middling level. He who knows little certainly cannot. It is the best case that one choose a middle degree. But how must one conduct oneself in public lectures, where one does not know the capacity of the Auditorum?
blocks.blomberg-s16-005: A distinction is to be made between: instilling an opinion in someone, and refuting someone's opinion. In the first case the subject is empty, but in the other I must empty it. Before all instruction I must first have the Data wherein the other errs. Every error is to be regarded as a Phaenomenon that is worthy of an explanation. I must first see how he could have come to the error. There I must also track down the part of truth in his error.
blocks.blomberg-s16-006: A dispute about words is when different persons believe they are contesting different opinions and yet are at odds only in the words, but agree in the matter itself. Of predestination some have believed that it is more a dispute about words than a dispute about things. An Argumentum ad hominem is an argument that is indeed not true for everyone but nevertheless serves to bring someone to silence, if I fetch up something, e.g., ex concessis and from the particular propositions that another holds. These are good means of keeping someone off one's neck and of ending the dispute, but not of finding the truth. Retorsiones and Reprehensiones are personal quarrels; the Distinctiones serve very well to extricate oneself from a tight spot. Instantia is when something is used generally and I show that it is not general. A defense that goes to the person is called Apologie; if it goes to the judgments of others, it is called Refutatio.
blocks.blomberg-s16-007: A Formal Disputation is the action in which, in the presence of learned people, one exposes some propositions in order to defend them against all objections. Disputing could bring great utility if it were not a Certamen Personarum, and if one did not want to seek the truth through strife but through agreement.
blocks.blomberg-s17-002: All learned writings are either historical or dogmatic. A writing can be historical as to matter, if it is something that has actually happened or a cognition of an individual, and also as to form. The form is called historical which is not rational, where I do not derive through general cognition of the grounds.
blocks.blomberg-s17-003: A cognition is called historical-dogmatic as to form when the data are dogmata but are presented historically; but as to matter, when some of it is historical, some dogmatic. Everything that happens is considered in connection with space and time. If one considers what happens insofar as it is at different times, that is called history; but insofar as it is at the same time, it belongs to the field of geography. There are various kinds of geography and history.
blocks.blomberg-s17-004: The distinction that the author makes, in dividing history into political, ecclesiastical, learned, and private history, is determined by different objects of historical cognitions. There could also be a moral history, which considers the morals of common life, and also the moral data. Biography is the life of a single subject. All history, of whatever kind it may be, should have the purpose of broadening reason; it should furnish the material for the use of reason.
blocks.blomberg-s17-005: History is called pragmatic that becomes useful through general rules; this can have a relation either to speculation or to practical reason. If one merely learns the names of rulers and knows their reign, this gives little material for the use of reason, i.e. for speculation or for practical rules. Meanwhile one must in the beginning already abstract from the use of reason and provide oneself, in good hope, with many historical items of knowledge. Learned history becomes pragmatic thereby, when one considers learnedness merely in relation to human reason, looks at its growth, or at the causes by which it was held back. There are 2 methods of composing dogmatic writings, either tumultuarily or methodically. The latter method brings a system into being. A system is any whole whatever. Systematic writings are distinguished from Tumultuary writings in that they make up a coherent whole. Abridgments,
blocks.blomberg-s17-006: Epitomes, are actual systems. In dogmatic writings the Principia of the dogmatists must be set forth, then drawn together and weighed in Concreto; and upon this one must interpose something historical in order to give evidence.
blocks.blomberg-s17-007: The method in which one does not draw a cognition from the proper sources but takes it from those who have drawn from the source is called compiling. History is compiled if I have written it together not from the first sources but from later ones. One can also compile philosophical propositions, in that one reads together what others have thought through reason. Nevertheless one shows skill if one gathers the most important with prudent choice from the authors who possess great acuteness, from the most thorough histories. The Plagiarius is distinguished from the Compilator. The latter pretends that he has himself drawn from the first learned sources, even though he displays only a product of another.
blocks.blomberg-s17-008: The French are especially of the caractère that among them the sciences grow more extensively than intensively. To the Epitomes belongs much understanding, in order to be able to choose the most important and most comprehensible.
blocks.blomberg-s18-002: The character of a learned person is twofold, the character of the head and of the heart. The first goes to cognition, the latter to inclination. The character of the heart has a great connection with the character of the head, if learnedness is to be furthered. The constitution of the heart has a great influence on the direction of the understanding, and it is therefore not a matter of indifference even in merely speculative sciences.
blocks.blomberg-s18-003: The character of the head concerns understanding, reason, and taste. The faculty of imitation is just opposed to the faculty of genius. Those who possess the capacity of genius sometimes lack the spirit of imitation, which, on the other hand, is peculiar in a great degree to most of those who show no genius. The Russians are said to have the fault that genius is lacking in them, and for just that reason they cannot teach it. Therefore science always dies out among them. For philosophy genius is required, likewise for the fine sciences, but for the useful sciences the spirit of imitation. Mathematics requires only imitation. Learnedness and good taste are distinguished from one another.
blocks.blomberg-s18-004: Mother wit is the natural capacity of healthy understanding and healthy reason. This cannot be learned; what is afterward learned, however, is called school wit. All instruction already presupposes certain cognitions, or at least the capacity for them. Thus school wit Supposes mother wit. It is more tolerable to lack school wit than to have it without mother wit. What is learned is beautiful in the human being, but he himself is absurd in the application. Hence comes pedantry, and through school wit one becomes still more absurd than otherwise, because one then has more materials. School wit is a perfection of mother wit.
blocks.blomberg-s18-005: To the particular learned exercises belongs
blocks.blomberg-s18-006: 1: learning. This happens through oral lecture or through reading books. One learns either by producing a cognition, or by reproducing cognitions one has had. To teach properly means to let cognitions be produced by others. The learner is in this respect purely passive, but he must also be active. He must have receptivity, i.e. capacity of the understanding, and also apply it. The oral lecture has a great advantage over the written, for the oral is not so artificial as the written. It is also more comprehensible, for it is one action of the mind less than in reading. For in reading I must namely also hear in thought.
blocks.blomberg-s18-007: 2: The reading of learned writings. It depends very much first on the order in which one reads, and on the choice of writing, where one begins. The question is: should compendia or great works be read first? One should not begin with the compendia, which contain many thoughts in little space, but with those that contain few thoughts in a wide space. In mathematics and in history one must first make the general known to oneself. One must proceed chiefly at first. Historical books that one chooses for reading must at first concern not so much the exact events as the general. One must go by a certain order, and read books of speculation in the morning and evening, historical books at midday. One must read much and, so to speak, digest what is read, and the field must not be changed much. Every book one must read at least 2 times, once quickly, marking the passages that need an explanation. Some books are of great importance and require much investigation; these one must read often. E.g. Hume, Rousseau, Locke, who can be regarded as a grammar for the understanding, and Montesquieu on the spirit of the laws
blocks.blomberg-s18-008: Repetition too frequent is just as harmful as an interruption too long. § 546: Imitation in matters of style is not advisable. § 548: no rule is to be given for the discovery of new truths. § 549 Avtodidactus is he who makes himself learned through meditating and reading. This is always a great genius. An oral lecture, however, is always to be preferred. One can make more Reflexiones.
blocks.blomberg-s18-009: Learned diligence means the strength of the exertion that one applies to learn something. The human being is by nature indolent, and laziness is itself the final end of his diligence. The future rest is the spur that sets human beings in activity. The greatness and worthiness of the objects can nevertheless exercise diligence very much. Learned diligence, when it Continues, is called steady diligence. Distinguished from this is vehement diligence, which consists in an all too strong exertion.
blocks.blomberg-s18-010: The mind suffers under vehement diligence; the representations soon die out.
blocks.blomberg-s18-011: A student must first weigh well the end and the extent of his powers; it is bad that others prescribe the end to us, and that one does not yet know oneself when one begins to study. One must never study with vehement diligence, but one must never cease to learn. One knows how to judge what one has to learn only when one is near the end. It also belongs to the character of a learned person that he be a person without title, rank, and civil standing; chiefly that he be a man of all estates, and that his cognition be generally usable and not suited merely to the form of the school. The final end of learnedness should be to give the human race its true form, to free it from prejudices, to refine morals, and to elevate the powers of the soul; then it is a benefit to the human race; but if it is used merely for operation, it is to be regarded only as a kind of luxury
